recipe_title: Strengthen by Adding a Missing Link
stimulus: When prewashed salad greens began appearing in resealable pouches, sales climbed sharply; shoppers prized that, once opened, the greens stayed crisp for days longer than they had in the old tear-open bags. A neighborhood bakery is now weighing whether to sell its sliced sandwich loaves in resealable pouches instead of twist-tied bags. Just as with the salad greens, this is a shrewd commercial move.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choice_a: Resealable pouches occupy less space on the bakery's shelves than twist-tied bags do.
choice_b: Before resealable pouches existed, shoppers often complained that opened bags of salad greens wilted by the next day.
choice_c: Producing loaves in resealable pouches would cost the bakery no more than its current twist-tied bags.
choice_d: Most bread shoppers say that packaging has little influence on which loaf they choose.
choice_e: Selling the sliced loaves in resealable pouches would keep the bread noticeably fresher after the package is first opened.
prediction_text: Pouches helped the greens by keeping them fresh after opening; the analogy holds only if pouches deliver that same freshness benefit to the bread.
correct_answer_job: Add a consideration on which the target case gains the same operative advantage that drove the model case.
conclusion: Selling the sliced loaves in resealable pouches is a shrewd move.
support: Resealable pouches boosted salad-greens sales by keeping them crisp longer after opening.
gap: Nothing yet says pouches would keep bread fresher; the salad benefit may not transfer.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it names a real convenience of pouches, but it is a benefit to shelving, not the after-opening freshness that made the model case succeed, so it does not carry the analogy.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it reinforces why pouches helped the greens, but it strengthens only the model side of the analogy and says nothing about whether bread would benefit likewise.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it clears a practical hurdle to switching, but removing a cost objection is not the same as showing the switch would help sales; the freshness link is still missing.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting as a packaging-related fact, but it cuts the other way: if packaging barely affects choice, the switch is less likely to be shrewd, so it weakens rather than strengthens.
explanation_e: Choice E supplies the missing link: pouches drove the salad's success by preserving freshness after opening, and this gives the bread that same advantage, which is what the analogy needs.

stimulus: Restaurant critic: As a rule, the more celebrated a chef is, the more lavishly diners praise the meal they are served. To my mind this is only right, and it gives us no reason to grow cynical about whether ordinary diners can tell genuinely fine cooking from the merely mediocre.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strongly supports the critic's view?
choice_a: A chef's level of celebrity usually reflects the genuine quality of that chef's cooking.
choice_b: Some of the most skilled chefs working today are unknown to the dining public.
choice_c: The more celebrated a chef is, the larger the crowds the restaurant can draw.
choice_d: Even the most skilled chefs cannot cook equally well on every night.
choice_e: Celebrated chefs often prepare dishes whose subtleties ordinary diners struggle to appreciate.
prediction_text: The optimism holds only if a chef's celebrity generally tracks genuine skill, so that praising the celebrated is praising the skilled.
correct_answer_job: Add a consideration on which diners' greater praise for celebrated chefs reflects real cooking quality rather than celebrity alone.
conclusion: There is no reason for cynicism about diners' ability to distinguish fine cooking from mediocre.
support: Diners praise the meals of more celebrated chefs more lavishly.
gap: Unless celebrity tracks skill, the extra praise could reflect reputation rather than diners' discernment.
explanation_a: Choice A supports the view: if celebrity tracks real skill, then praising the more celebrated chef is praising the more skilled one, so the pattern is no evidence that diners are fooled by fame.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns skill and fame, but it points the other way: skilled yet uncelebrated chefs suggest fame and quality can come apart, so it undercuts rather than supports the critic.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it echoes the more-celebrated-more pattern, but it speaks to crowd size, not to whether diners' praise reflects real cooking quality, which is what the view needs.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting as a caveat about skill, but night-to-night variation says nothing about whether celebrity tracks quality, so it leaves the cynicism worry untouched.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links celebrity and diners' judgment, but it implies ordinary diners may miss what celebrated chefs do, cutting against their discernment, so it works against the view.

stimulus: By splicing a gene borrowed from a jellyfish into ornamental orchids, growers have produced orchids that glow softly in the dark. This line of work is pointless, however. However striking the effect, buyers will simply refuse to purchase orchids that carry genes taken from an animal.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
choice_a: The glowing orchids the growers produced have not yet been tested to see how long the glow lasts.
choice_b: The same splicing technique can make orchids glow using a gene taken from a naturally luminous fungus rather than from any animal.
choice_c: Buyers of ornamental plants have eagerly embraced other novelties, such as orchids dyed in vivid, unnatural colors.
choice_d: Any orchid grown from animal genetic material must be labeled as such at the point of sale.
choice_e: Some prized ornamental orchids are cultivated in greenhouses that stay dark for much of the day.
prediction_text: The pointless verdict rests on buyers rejecting animal genes; showing the technique yields an acceptable glowing orchid by another route defeats it.
correct_answer_job: Add a consideration on which the research has value despite buyers' refusal of animal-gene orchids.
conclusion: The line of work is pointless.
support: Buyers will refuse orchids carrying genes taken from an animal.
gap: The technique might produce a saleable glowing orchid with no animal gene at all.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it raises a doubt about the orchids, but how long the glow lasts does not bear on the claim that consumer refusal makes the work pointless.
explanation_b: Choice B weakens the argument: it shows the technique can yield a glowing orchid with no animal gene, so the buyers' objection to animal genes does not render the work pointless.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it suggests buyers welcome novelty, but the stated obstacle is specifically genes taken from an animal, which dyeing does not involve, so it does not meet the argument's reason.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the animal-gene issue, but mandatory labeling would make the very refusal the argument relies on more likely, so it strengthens the pointless verdict rather than weakening it.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because darkness relates to a glow, but where orchids are grown says nothing about whether consumer refusal makes the research pointless.

stimulus: In a laboratory study, forty volunteers were each shown a concealed number and paid to deny, to an interviewer, that they had seen it. Whenever a volunteer lied, an eye-tracking camera recorded a marked dilation of the pupils, a response long known to accompany heightened mental effort. The researchers concluded that pupil-dilation tracking could eventually serve as a reliable detector of deception.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
choice_a: Existing deception detectors, such as the polygraph, have never been shown to be dependable.
choice_b: The degree of mental effort that lying requires differs widely from one person to the next.
choice_c: When the volunteers answered truthfully about other concealed numbers, their pupils dilated to much the same degree as when they lied.
choice_d: A lie prepared in advance tends to require less mental effort than one invented on the spot.
choice_e: Many volunteers reported feeling uneasy about lying even though they had been paid to do so.
prediction_text: If the same dilation appears when volunteers tell the truth, the marker cannot pick out lies and the detector inference collapses.
correct_answer_job: Add a consideration on which the observed marker fails to distinguish lying from truth-telling.
conclusion: Pupil-dilation tracking could serve as a reliable detector of deception.
support: When volunteers lied, their pupils dilated markedly.
gap: The dilation may accompany truthful answers too, not lying specifically.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it disparages lie detection generally, but the reliability of other devices says nothing about whether this pupil-based marker works, which is the argument's claim.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting and does raise a reliability worry, but variation in effort across people does not show the dilation fails to mark lying; the decisive problem is that truth-telling produces it too.
explanation_c: Choice C weakens the argument: if truthful answers produce the same dilation as lies, the marker does not distinguish deception from honesty, so it cannot ground a reliable detector.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it suggests some lies may dilate the pupils less, but that at most limits sensitivity to certain lies; it does not undercut the inference the way shared truthful dilation does.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because unease relates to arousal, but whether volunteers felt uneasy does not address whether dilation distinguishes lies from truths, so it leaves the inference intact.

stimulus: Okoye: Cities have tried to ban provocative street murals, but such bans seldom work, since residents crave public art and muralists always find sly ways to needle officials who treat them harshly. Since muralists will not needle a city that employs them as honored artists, a city can both control its murals and keep residents content by putting muralists on the public payroll as honored employees.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken Okoye's argument?
choice_a: Few cities are willing to bear the ongoing cost of keeping muralists on the payroll.
choice_b: Even entirely unregulated street murals rarely provoke residents to turn against city officials.
choice_c: Some muralists needle city officials even when those officials have treated them generously.
choice_d: Residents generally have little appetite for murals they know were painted by artists on the city's payroll.
choice_e: Most street murals neither criticize city officials nor praise them.
prediction_text: The plan must both control murals and please residents; if residents shun murals made by city-employed artists, the second aim fails.
correct_answer_job: Add a consideration on which the plan fails to satisfy residents' craving for public art even if it curbs provocation.
conclusion: Employing muralists as honored public employees can both control murals and keep residents content.
support: Muralists will not needle a city that honors and employs them; residents crave public art.
gap: Residents may not embrace murals produced by city employees, leaving their craving unmet.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it raises a practical obstacle, but whether cities will pay does not show that the plan, if adopted, would fail to control murals and please residents, which is what the argument asserts.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns murals and officials, but whether murals endanger officials is beside the point; the plan's promise is control plus resident contentment, which this does not touch.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting and does press the claim that honored muralists will not needle the city, but it challenges only the control prong; it is the resident-contentment failure that the plan truly cannot survive.
explanation_d: Choice D weakens the argument: if residents shun city-employee murals, the plan fails to keep residents content even if it curbs provocation, defeating one of the two aims claimed.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting as a fact about mural content, but murals that are neutral neither help nor hurt the plan's two aims, so this leaves the reasoning untouched.

stimulus: Books columnist: Unlike most eagerly awaited novels, the forthcoming thriller Nightglass has not been sent to critics as an advance copy for early review. Pre-orders are running at record levels, and surveys show that most readers who know of the book intend to buy it. So the publisher must have decided to avoid doing anything that could cool readers' enthusiasm for Nightglass.
question_stem: The columnist's explanation for why no advance copies were sent to critics relies on assuming that the publisher believes that
choice_a: the money saved by not printing advance copies is better spent on other forms of promotion
choice_b: sending advance copies to critics might dampen the enthusiasm of readers who would otherwise be eager to buy Nightglass
choice_c: the critics who would ordinarily receive advance copies of Nightglass would not enjoy the novel
choice_d: because most readers are aware of Nightglass, most readers intend to buy it
choice_e: roughly the current number of readers will buy Nightglass only if no advance copies are ever sent
prediction_text: Withholding copies counts as avoiding a risk to enthusiasm only if the publisher believes sending them could cool that enthusiasm.
correct_answer_job: State the belief the publisher must hold for avoiding a cooling of enthusiasm to explain withholding the copies.
conclusion: The publisher decided to avoid anything that could cool readers' enthusiasm, and so sent no advance copies.
support: Pre-orders are high and most aware readers intend to buy.
gap: The explanation works only if the publisher believes advance copies might reduce, not raise, enthusiasm.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it offers a reason not to send copies, but it is a different explanation (cost) than the one the columnist gives (protecting enthusiasm), so it is not what that explanation assumes.
explanation_b: Choice B is the required assumption: only if the publisher believes early copies could cool enthusiasm does withholding them count as avoiding a risk to that enthusiasm, which is the columnist's whole explanation.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns the critics, but the explanation turns on protecting readers' enthusiasm, not on critics' tastes, so this belief is not required.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it echoes the survey figures, but the explanation does not depend on equating awareness with intent to buy; it depends on a belief about what advance copies would do.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links copies and sales, but the explanation needs only the belief that copies risk cooling enthusiasm, not the far stronger claim that sales depend on never sending any.

stimulus: City officials flatly deny that any of their decisions worsened downtown flooding. The record says otherwise. Two years ago, at the urging of several developers, the council relaxed a longstanding requirement that new parking lots be surfaced with water-absorbing pavement. Since the requirement was relaxed, three low-lying blocks that had never before flooded have been swamped after nearly every heavy rain.
question_stem: The argument relies on which one of the following assumptions?
choice_a: Without the developers' urging, the council would not have relaxed the pavement requirement.
choice_b: The officials who deny worsening the flooding do not actually believe their own denials.
choice_c: The developers who urged relaxing the requirement built the very lots on the flooded blocks.
choice_d: The council is generally more responsive to developers than to residents worried about flooding.
choice_e: Had the requirement that new lots use water-absorbing pavement not been relaxed, considerably less downtown flooding would have occurred.
prediction_text: The argument blames the relaxed rule for the flooding; it must assume that without the relaxation there would have been considerably less flooding.
correct_answer_job: State the counterfactual link on which relaxing the requirement, rather than something else, accounts for the new flooding.
conclusion: The officials' decisions worsened downtown flooding.
support: The council relaxed the pavement requirement, and afterward previously dry blocks flooded.
gap: The new flooding must trace to the relaxed rule rather than to some unrelated change.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because the developers' urging is mentioned, but why the council relaxed the rule is beside the point; the argument needs the rule change to explain the flooding, not an account of what prompted it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it targets the officials' denial, but the argument's force does not depend on whether they are sincere, only on whether their decision in fact worsened flooding.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it ties the developers to the flooded area, but the argument blames the council's decision generally; it need not assume the same developers built the lots that flooded.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it fits the story's politics, but a general tilt toward developers is not something the causal claim about this rule change requires.
explanation_e: Choice E is required: the argument pins the flooding on the relaxed rule, which holds only if keeping the rule would have meant substantially less flooding; deny this and the timing is mere coincidence.

stimulus: Ethicist: One cannot defend the clinic's paid overnight sleep-deprivation study merely by observing that every participant was told the risks in advance and accepted payment for shouldering them. Although hiring someone to take on a task raises no objection when the person settles on it entirely of their own accord, that justification lapses the moment a decision has been driven by sheer financial desperation.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ethicist's argument?
choice_a: Being told about the possible consequences of a choice does not by itself guarantee that the choice is freely made.
choice_b: Nothing at all can be rendered acceptable simply by the fact that the parties involved took part willingly.
choice_c: Anyone whose choice falls even slightly short of being fully free is thereby acting under duress.
choice_d: There is nothing objectionable about accepting money in exchange for exposing oneself to risk.
choice_e: A person ought to be allowed to carry out whatever they have settled on of their own free will.
prediction_text: The rebuttal works only if being told the risks does not guarantee a free choice; otherwise informed and paid would suffice to defend the study.
correct_answer_job: State the link on which being informed of the risks fails to establish that the choice was free.
conclusion: One cannot defend the study merely by noting that participants were informed and paid.
support: Paying is acceptable only when the choice is free, not when coerced.
gap: Being informed of risks may leave the choice unfree, as under economic coercion.
explanation_a: Choice A is required: the ethicist grants that free choice justifies payment, so the rebuttal succeeds only if being informed leaves open that the choice was coerced, exactly what this supplies.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it sounds like the moral of the passage, but the ethicist needs only that informing does not secure freedom, not the sweeping claim that willingness never justifies a transaction.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because freedom and coercion are the poles in play, but the argument does not require that every shortfall from complete freedom counts as coercion; that overshoots what is needed.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because payment for risk is the topic, but the ethicist's point is about coerced choice, not risk-for-pay as such; assuming this does not move the argument along.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because free choice appears in it, but a permission principle about what people may do is not needed to show that informing fails to establish freedom.

stimulus: Historian: Many collectors hold that the world's first adhesive postage stamp was Britain's Penny Black, issued in 1840. They are mistaken. Fully two years earlier, a small Caribbean colony, short of coins for its postal fees, engraved little paper labels that senders bought at the post office, affixed to their letters, and used to prepay delivery. The colony's labels therefore came first.
question_stem: The historian's conclusion is properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: Britain did not issue any adhesive postage stamp before the Penny Black of 1840.
choice_b: The Caribbean colony issued its paper labels because it lacked the coins to collect postal fees.
choice_c: The engraved paper labels the colony issued in 1838 were themselves adhesive postage stamps.
choice_d: No government issued an adhesive postage stamp during the 1830s except the Caribbean colony.
choice_e: Every early postal authority kept detailed records of the fees it charged senders.
prediction_text: The conclusion follows only if those 1838 labels count as adhesive postage stamps; otherwise being earlier is beside the point.
correct_answer_job: Supply the premise on which the colony's affixed, prepaid paper labels qualify as adhesive postage stamps.
conclusion: The colony's 1838 labels, not the Penny Black, were the earliest adhesive postage stamps.
support: In 1838 the colony issued engraved paper labels that senders bought and affixed to prepay delivery.
gap: Nothing yet establishes that those labels were adhesive postage stamps.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns the Penny Black's priority, but even granting it, nothing yet makes the 1838 labels count as stamps, so the conclusion still does not follow.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the coin shortage is in the passage, but why the colony issued the labels does not help establish that they were postage stamps, which is the gap the conclusion needs closed.
explanation_c: Choice C makes the conclusion follow: if those affixed, prepaid paper labels were adhesive postage stamps, then an adhesive postage stamp existed in 1838, before the Penny Black.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it sounds supportive, but the conclusion only compares the colony's labels with the Penny Black; a sweeping uniqueness claim is neither needed nor sufficient to make the labels stamps.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting as historical color, but recordkeeping has no bearing on whether the 1838 labels were adhesive postage stamps, so it cannot complete the argument.

stimulus: When a startup and the firm acquiring it share a compatible working culture, the buyout negotiations between them proceed smoothly. And wherever such negotiations proceed smoothly, neither side comes away feeling that it has abandoned its core mission. It follows that the acquisitions that turn out best are to be found among those in which the startup and the acquiring firm share a compatible working culture.
question_stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: Acquisitions succeed most often when the issues most debated in negotiations are not ones of company culture.
choice_b: If a buyout negotiation proceeds smoothly, then the two firms share a compatible working culture.
choice_c: Only when an acquisition leaves a side feeling it has abandoned its mission does that acquisition turn out poorly.
choice_d: The acquisitions that turn out best include those in which the buyout negotiations proceed smoothly.
choice_e: Whenever two firms lack a compatible working culture, their negotiations leave at least one side feeling it abandoned its mission.
prediction_text: Given culture leads to smooth, the conclusion needs smooth leads to among-the-best, so culture chains through to best.
correct_answer_job: Supply the link on which smooth negotiations place an acquisition among those that turn out best.
conclusion: The acquisitions that turn out best include those in which the two firms share a compatible working culture.
support: Compatible culture yields smooth negotiations, which leave neither side feeling it abandoned its mission.
gap: Nothing yet says that smoothness makes an acquisition one of the best.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it links success and culture, but it concerns which issues are debated, not the smooth-negotiations link the conclusion actually needs, so the chain stays broken.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it joins the same two terms, but it reverses the given conditional; the argument already has culture leads to smooth and gains nothing toward best from its converse.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it ties abandoned mission to poor outcomes, but it does not establish that not feeling so puts an acquisition among the best; the needed bridge to best is still missing.
explanation_d: Choice D completes the chain: compatible culture yields smooth negotiations, and if smooth negotiations are among the best acquisitions, then compatible-culture acquisitions are too, exactly the conclusion.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it mirrors the premises' terms, but reasoning about firms that lack a compatible culture does nothing to link the smooth cases to the best acquisitions, which is what the conclusion requires.

stimulus: Every subway map lays out the network's lines and stations. Yet any such map is bound to leave a great deal out. choice_e: It is impossible for anything to represent completely something more complex than itself.

explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it resembles the reasoning's principle, but it overstates it into a universal claim the argument neither makes nor needs, and it is not the specific conclusion drawn about the map.

choice_d: Generating its own power would shield the co-op from rising utility rates.

stimulus: Alvarez: The 1855 Athenaeum Hall is widely described as the town's oldest public library. That description is mistaken, since the Cedar Street reading room first opened its doors back in 1840, a full fifteen years earlier. choice_d: There is not enough evidence that the Cedar Street reading room opened in 1840.

explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because dates are central, but Booker never disputes when the room opened; he disputes whether it was a public library, leaving the date untouched.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because Booker discusses the earliest collections, but his criticism is specifically that Cedar Street was members-only, not a general claim that no early collection was ever public.

choice_a: At least one roof vent is open.
choice_b: The irrigation system is working.
choice_c: The irrigation system is not working.
choice_d: The soil moisture is continuing to fall.
choice_e: All of the roof vents are shut.

stimulus: Can every judgment about a work of art be grounded in objective standards? stimulus: A philosopher has proposed that courage is simply acting to pursue a worthy goal in spite of feeling afraid. stimulus: A recent roadside survey found that, when asked to compare themselves with others, most drivers believe they take fewer risks at the wheel than most other drivers do. But it cannot possibly be the case that most drivers take fewer risks than most other drivers. Therefore, ______.

stimulus: Throughout last summer's heat wave, no greenhouse fitted with a misting system lost any plants. This summer every greenhouse at the Fairview nursery has been fitted with a misting system. So during this summer's heat wave none of the Fairview greenhouses will lose any plants.

stimulus: Mara usually shops at the farmers' market, because getting the freshest produce is what matters most to her.
