explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because a colleague is contradicted, but Reyes disputes the advice itself, offering a competing remedy; no attack on the colleague's character or standing is made.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because individuals and a wider public both appear, but the argument moves the other way, from a public remedy to individual advice, so this description is backward.
explanation_c: Choice C names the flaw: the colleague gave advice to individuals, and Reyes answers it with a society-wide pollution measure, as if refuting a policy proposal, which the advice never was.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the advice targets a specific group, but Reyes's error is not an assumption about who else should limit sun; it is answering personal advice with a policy fix.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the pollution remedy is asserted, but the flaw does not depend on whether that remedy is feasible; even a feasible public fix would not refute advice to individuals.

stimulus: Editorial: Students who pull an all-nighter before an exam are very likely to do poorly on it the next morning. Priya did poorly on yesterday morning's exam. So Priya very likely pulled an all-nighter the night before. Plenty of students do exactly that during exam week, trading sleep for a few extra hours of review. Her low score, the editorial insists, points squarely to the same choice.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the editorial's reasoning?
choice_a: It fails to consider that a particular member of a group may be unrepresentative of that group.
choice_b: It treats a condition that would be enough to secure the conclusion as one the conclusion positively requires.
choice_c: It confuses a consistent association between two things with one of them always causing the other.
choice_d: It treats the fact that all-nighters make a poor score likely as showing that a poor score makes an all-nighter likely.
choice_e: It dismisses a position by going after someone who holds it instead of engaging the position.
prediction_text: That all-nighters make poor scores likely does not make an all-nighter likely given a poor score; many other causes produce poor scores.
correct_answer_job: Name the flaw: it reverses the direction of a likelihood claim.
conclusion: Priya very likely pulled an all-nighter.
support: All-nighters make a poor next-morning score very likely, and Priya scored poorly.
gap: Poor scores can arise from many causes, so a poor score does not make an all-nighter likely.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because Priya is a single case, but the error is not treating her as typical; it is inferring the cause from the effect against the stated direction of likelihood.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because conditions are in play, but the argument confuses the direction of a likelihood claim, not the roles of sufficient and necessary conditions.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because causation is discussed, but the premise is already causal and probabilistic; the flaw is running that probability backward, not mistaking association for cause.
explanation_d: Choice D names the flaw: the premise runs from all-nighters to a likely poor score, and the argument reverses it, treating a poor score as making an all-nighter likely, ignoring the many other causes of poor scores.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it names a familiar flaw, but the editorial attacks no one; it draws a faulty inference about Priya, so an ad hominem charge does not fit.

stimulus: When orchards are sprayed with a certain pesticide, the number of pollinator species visiting them drops by an average of twenty percent. So if the Hollowbrook orchard is sprayed with that pesticide, some pollinator species will surely stop visiting it. That result, the argument holds, is all but certain for this one particular orchard.
question_stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?
choice_a: It ignores the possibility that other factors might offset the decline at a particular sprayed orchard.
choice_b: It fails to allow that the total count could stay steady even as particular species stop visiting.
choice_c: It ignores that some pollinator species might stop visiting Hollowbrook even if it is never sprayed.
choice_d: It assumes the orchards studied were alike in the pollinator species that visited them.
choice_e: It overlooks that visiting species could fall an average of twenty percent across sprayed orchards even if some sprayed orchards lose none.
prediction_text: A twenty-percent average can come from big drops at some orchards and none at others, so Hollowbrook could lose none.
correct_answer_job: Name the flaw: an average decline across many orchards need not occur at any particular orchard.
conclusion: Some pollinator species will stop visiting Hollowbrook if it is sprayed.
support: Spraying lowers visiting pollinator species by an average of twenty percent.
gap: An average across orchards does not fix what happens at this single orchard.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns a single orchard, but the flaw is not about counteracting factors; it is that an average drop need not appear at any one orchard at all.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it separates totals from particulars, but the conclusion is precisely that some species stop, and the flaw is reading a cross-orchard average onto one orchard.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it raises an alternative, but the conclusion is about the effect of spraying; the flaw lies in applying an average to one case, not in ignoring background change.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it questions the study group, but the argument needs no such uniformity; its error is moving from an average to a guaranteed effect at one orchard.
explanation_e: Choice E names the flaw: a twenty-percent average is consistent with some orchards losing no species, so it does not guarantee that Hollowbrook in particular will lose any.

stimulus: Coach: The new athletic director argues that we should drop any sport that fails to fill its stands, reasoning that a team is a product, fans are its customers, and any business must meet customer demand. But running a team is not like selling a product. So the director is wrong that we should keep only the sports that fill their stands.
question_stem: The coach's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
choice_a: concludes that the director's position is mistaken merely because one argument the director gives for it is inadequate
choice_b: appeals to what is popularly believed in order to support its own conclusion
choice_c: treats two things that are merely analogous as though they were identical
choice_d: defends a position without showing that the argument against that position fails
choice_e: improperly attacks the character of the athletic director rather than the director's reasoning
prediction_text: Even if the director's product analogy fails, that does not establish that the director's conclusion is false.
correct_answer_job: Name the flaw: it treats a weak argument for a view as showing the view itself is false.
conclusion: The director is wrong that only stand-filling sports should be kept.
support: Running a team is not like selling a product, so the director's analogy fails.
gap: A flawed argument for a claim leaves open whether the claim is nonetheless true.
explanation_a: Choice A names the flaw: the coach shows only that the product analogy is weak, then treats the director's conclusion as false, when a weak argument for a claim does not show the claim is wrong.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because crowds are in view, but the coach cites no popular belief as support; the reasoning turns on rejecting the analogy, so this does not describe it.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because an analogy is central, but that is the charge the coach levels at the director; the coach's own error is inferring the view is false from the analogy's weakness.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the coach defends a stance, but the coach does engage the director's argument; the flaw is the leap from that argument's failure to the falsity of its conclusion.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the director is opposed, but the coach addresses the reasoning, not the director's character, so no personal attack occurs.

stimulus: Historian: Medieval village blacksmiths are often pictured as devoting themselves chiefly to making swords and armor. In truth, most of what they produced was everyday hardware, such as nails, hinges, and farm tools. Weapon commissions were rare and irregular, and few village smiths could have stayed in business on such work alone. Most of a smith's day, in fact, went to mending and forging the plain fittings a village needed.
question_stem: The claim that medieval village blacksmiths are often pictured as devoting themselves chiefly to weapons plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
choice_a: It is a premise offered in support of the historian's overall conclusion.
choice_b: It states a widely held view that the historian then argues against.
choice_c: It clarifies the meaning of one of the premises the historian relies on.
choice_d: It is an objection the historian raises against a competing historical theory.
choice_e: It is the overall conclusion that the historian's argument is designed to establish.
prediction_text: It is the popular view the historian sets out to correct with the everyday-hardware evidence.
correct_answer_job: Identify the role of the 'often pictured as weapon-makers' claim.
conclusion: Most of what village blacksmiths produced was everyday hardware, not weapons.
support: Weapon commissions were rare and irregular; few smiths could survive on them.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it opens the passage, but the historian argues against this picture rather than leaning on it, so it does not support the conclusion; it is the target.
explanation_b: Choice B captures the role: the common picture of smiths as weapon-makers is set up precisely so the historian can correct it with evidence that everyday hardware was the bulk of their work.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it precedes the evidence, but it does not explain a premise; it is the mistaken view the evidence is marshaled to overturn.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because opposing views are in play, but the claim is not an objection the historian raises; it is the popular impression the historian himself rejects.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it is a prominent claim, but the historian denies it; the conclusion is that everyday hardware, not weapons, made up most of the smiths' output.

stimulus: Consultants say that ranking employees on a public leaderboard is meant to lift everyone's performance by holding all to the same visible standard. In reality the practice backfires. It pushes staff to chase the posted metric rather than do the work well, and it breeds resentment toward whoever sits at the top. In practice the ranking shapes how people behave far more than it lifts how they perform.
question_stem: The claim that public leaderboards are meant to lift everyone's performance plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
choice_a: It is a claim the argument sets out to refute outright as simply false.
choice_b: It is put forward to back a claim the argument then declares untrue.
choice_c: It presents a rationale people sometimes give for a practice the argument then goes on to call harmful.
choice_d: It describes a phenomenon that the argument says is far less damaging than people assume.
choice_e: It gives an example of something whose effects differ entirely from what everyone assumes.
prediction_text: It is the stated rationale for a practice the argument goes on to call harmful.
correct_answer_job: Identify the role of the 'meant to lift performance' claim.
conclusion: Public leaderboards backfire and do harm.
support: They push staff to chase the metric and breed resentment toward top performers.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because the argument opposes the practice, but it does not deny that lifting performance is the stated aim; it grants that aim and argues the practice fails to serve it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it names a claim's function, but the rationale is not evidence for anything; it is the justification given for a practice the argument judges harmful.
explanation_c: Choice C captures the role: the stated purpose of lifting performance is the rationale for leaderboards, and the argument concedes it only to conclude that the practice actually does harm.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because harm is central, but the claim states a purpose, not a phenomenon the argument downplays; the argument stresses the harm, not its mildness.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because outcomes defy the stated aim, but the claim is the aim itself, not an example whose effects the argument contrasts with universal assumption.

stimulus: Neighborhood bake-offs can never really achieve their headline goal of crowning the single best baker, since taste is a matter of preference and many superb home bakers never enter. Even so, these contests draw neighbors together and spark fresh interest in baking, and sustaining that interest is something a community needs if the craft is to stay alive. That second benefit is a real and lasting one.
question_stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?
choice_a: Keeping the craft of baking alive in a community requires holding neighborhood bake-offs.
choice_b: Some matters of personal preference get in the way of keeping a craft alive in a community.
choice_c: A bake-off limited to the bakers who never enter the usual contests would not help keep the craft alive.
choice_d: The headline purpose of neighborhood bake-offs is not the strongest reason for holding them.
choice_e: Neighborhood bake-offs are worth holding only if they succeed in crowning the best baker.
prediction_text: Since the headline goal is unreachable but a different benefit is real and valued, that headline goal is not the best reason to hold bake-offs.
correct_answer_job: Draw the claim best supported by the contrast between the unreachable headline goal and the real benefit.
conclusion: The headline purpose of bake-offs is not the strongest reason for holding them.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because bake-offs are said to help sustain interest, but the passage never says they are required; other things could sustain it, so this overstates the support.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because preference and craft survival both appear, but preference is said only to block fair judging, not to hinder keeping the craft alive, so the link is unsupported.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because non-entrants are mentioned, but the passage says nothing about a special contest for them, so no conclusion about such a contest is supported.
explanation_d: Choice D is best supported: the headline goal of crowning the best baker cannot be met, yet the contests deliver a real and valued benefit, so that unreachable goal is not the best reason to hold them.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it echoes the headline goal, but the passage points the other way: the contests are valued for a different reason, so their worth does not hinge on crowning the best baker.

stimulus: Botanists found pollen from several plant species sealed in a peat layer of a lowland bog, a layer dated to about three thousand years ago. Those species no longer grow anywhere near the bog, but they flourish today a day's walk away in a wetter stretch of highland. So the land around the bog was probably wetter three thousand years ago than it is now, since ______.
question_stem: The conclusion of the argument is most strongly supported if which one of the following completes the passage?
choice_a: the wetter highland where the species now grow is also somewhat cooler than the bog
choice_b: those plant species did not grow near the bog at any time much earlier than three thousand years ago
choice_c: those plant species grow only in lowland areas and never at higher elevations
choice_d: fewer plant species grow near the bog today than grew there three thousand years ago
choice_e: the plant species whose pollen was found can grow only within a narrow band of moisture conditions
prediction_text: If the species grow only where it is wet, their pollen at the bog 3,000 years ago shows the bog was wet then.
correct_answer_job: Complete the passage so the past presence of the species implies past wetness.
conclusion: The land around the bog was probably wetter three thousand years ago.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it describes the highland, but a difference in temperature does not connect the species' past presence at the bog to past wetness, which is what the conclusion needs.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it fixes a date, but ruling out earlier growth does nothing to show that their presence three thousand years ago indicates the bog was wet then.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it restricts where the species grow, but it points to elevation rather than moisture and even conflicts with their thriving in the highland, so it cannot support a wetness conclusion.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it compares then and now, but a change in the number of species says nothing about whether the past climate was wetter, so it leaves the conclusion unsupported.
explanation_e: Choice E best completes the argument: if those species can grow only where moisture falls in a narrow band, then their presence at the bog three thousand years ago shows the bog then supplied that moisture, so it was wetter.

stimulus: The relationship between a password and the online accounts it lets a person reach is much like the relationship between a key and the doors it opens for whoever holds it. A key, however, is worthless in a building that happens to have no locked doors at all. So, reasoning in the very same way, it follows that ______.
question_stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choice_a: a password is worthless in a system where nothing at all is kept locked
choice_b: a password is no more useful than the key it is being compared with
choice_c: any key that succeeds in opening a door has value
choice_d: a password should be thought of as a kind of key rather than as a secret
choice_e: a password's value comes entirely from the accounts it lets a person reach
prediction_text: As a key is worthless without locked doors, a password is worthless where nothing is kept locked.
correct_answer_job: Complete the analogy the way the key case licenses.
conclusion: A password is worthless in a system where nothing is kept locked.
explanation_a: Choice A best completes the argument: the analogy carries the point about keys straight over, so just as a key is worthless without locked doors, a password is worthless where nothing is locked.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it echoes the comparison, but the argument draws a conclusion about when a password is worthless, not a ranking of how useful passwords and keys are.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns keys, but it makes a claim about keys that open doors, the reverse of the worthless-without-doors point the argument extends to passwords.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because passwords and keys are likened, but the passage uses the likeness to draw a conclusion about worth, not to reclassify what a password is.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it sounds sensible, but the argument's parallel yields a claim about worthlessness where nothing is locked, not a claim about where a password's value comes from.

stimulus: Principle: A researcher whose study appeared in a journal may publish a rebuttal in that same journal to a harsh review of the study, provided either that the review appeared in that journal too, or that it appeared in a different journal and misrepresented the study. Application: Okonkwo ought to be permitted to run a rebuttal in Coastal Ecology answering Vance's review, which harshly criticized Okonkwo's study.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, justifies the above application of the principle?
choice_a: Okonkwo's study appeared in Coastal Ecology as well as in several other journals.
choice_b: Both Okonkwo's study and Vance's review appeared in Coastal Ecology.
choice_c: Vance's review appeared in Coastal Ecology as well as in several other journals.
choice_d: Okonkwo's study appeared only in Coastal Ecology, while Vance's review ran in many other journals.
choice_e: Vance's review appeared in Coastal Ecology and was unfair to Okonkwo's study.
prediction_text: If both the study and the review appeared in Coastal Ecology, the first branch is met and the rebuttal there is licensed.
correct_answer_job: Supply the fact that makes one branch of the principle apply to Okonkwo's case.
conclusion: Okonkwo should be allowed to rebut Vance's review in Coastal Ecology.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it places the study in Coastal Ecology, but it says nothing about where the review ran, so neither branch of the principle is shown to be satisfied.
explanation_b: Choice B justifies the application: the study ran in Coastal Ecology, so a rebuttal there is the right venue, and the review also ran there, satisfying the first branch of the principle.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it puts the review in Coastal Ecology, but it does not establish that the study appeared there, so it is not shown that Coastal Ecology is the journal in which Okonkwo may rebut.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the study is placed in Coastal Ecology, but with the review only elsewhere the first branch fails, and nothing says the review misrepresented the study, so the second branch is unmet.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it adds unfairness, but misrepresentation matters only for reviews in a different journal, and this choice still does not establish that the study itself appeared in Coastal Ecology.

stimulus: A sprawling new data center was built to meet the strictest energy-efficiency codes any facility has ever satisfied, consuming enormous quantities of steel, concrete, and power in the process. Yet it now sits nearly idle, its servers rarely called upon. So it is, in the end, no real triumph of energy efficiency after all.
question_stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the argument?
choice_a: Achieving energy efficiency is no harder in a data center than in other kinds of buildings.
choice_b: A backup facility ought to meet the same efficiency codes as the primary one it supports.
choice_c: Devoting resources to build capacity that the market leaves unused undercuts a project's claim to energy efficiency.
choice_d: To limit financial risk, very large facilities should not be built during economic downturns.
choice_e: The energy a building uses while operating matters more than the energy used to construct it.
prediction_text: If building capacity the market leaves unused undercuts an efficiency claim, then an idle center is no efficiency triumph.
correct_answer_job: Supply the principle linking unused capacity to a failed claim of efficiency.
conclusion: The data center is no real triumph of energy efficiency.
support: It meets strict codes but sits nearly idle after consuming enormous resources.
gap: A principle is needed tying wasted, unused capacity to the failure of an efficiency claim.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns efficiency, but a claim that efficiency is equally hard across buildings gives no reason to deny that this idle center is efficient, so it does not justify the reasoning.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because standards are at issue, but a rule about matching codes across facilities does nothing to connect the center's idleness to a failed efficiency claim.
explanation_c: Choice C justifies the reasoning: the argument's sole ground is that the center was built at great cost yet goes unused, and this principle makes exactly that a reason to deny it is a triumph of efficiency.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it counsels caution about big projects, but timing and financial risk are not the argument's ground, which is wasted capacity, so this principle does not support it.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it weighs kinds of energy, but if operating energy mattered most, an idle center would look efficient, which cuts against the conclusion rather than supporting it.

stimulus: Opposing counsel: The arbitrator recently spent a holiday weekend at a lodge owned by one of the parties, and for years her household has accepted free courtside seats from that party's parent company. Even granting her word that the dispute never came up during the weekend, these ties give real reason to doubt she can rule even-handedly. She ought to do the right thing and withdraw from the case.
question_stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in opposing counsel's argument?
choice_a: An arbitrator, being human, can never be expected to be wholly impartial in deciding a dispute.
choice_b: An arbitrator's denial that a case was discussed should be doubted if she has accepted something of value from a party.
choice_c: An arbitrator should never accept anything of value from a party to a dispute over which she presides.
choice_d: An arbitrator should step aside from any dispute in which a reasonable doubt about her impartiality could be raised.
choice_e: An arbitrator should withdraw only when it is plainly shown that a party actually swayed her.
prediction_text: Counsel infers withdrawal from mere reasonable doubt about impartiality; the principle must make such doubt sufficient grounds to step aside.
correct_answer_job: Supply the principle whose truth licenses the call for withdrawal.
conclusion: The arbitrator ought to withdraw from the case.
support: Her ties to a party give real reason to doubt she can rule even-handedly.
gap: A principle is needed making a reasonable doubt about impartiality enough to require withdrawal.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns impartiality, but if perfect impartiality were never expected, that would undercut singling this arbitrator out, so it works against the call to withdraw.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because gifts and a denial both appear, but counsel grants the denial and argues from appearances anyway, so a principle for disbelieving the denial is not what the reasoning needs.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it condemns the free seats, but a rule against accepting gifts does not by itself establish that this arbitrator must withdraw from the case, which is the conclusion drawn.
explanation_d: Choice D justifies the reasoning: counsel's ground is that the ties raise a reasonable doubt about even-handedness, and this principle makes exactly such a doubt sufficient reason for the arbitrator to withdraw.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it addresses withdrawal, but it demands proof of actual bias, a higher bar than counsel meets; it would block the conclusion rather than justify it.

stimulus: Analyst: The town's average summer temperature has climbed about two degrees over the past thirty years. This warming is chiefly the result of the spreading expanse of dark asphalt across the town, which soaks up sunlight through the day and releases the stored heat well into the night. Nothing else about the town, the analyst maintains, has changed enough to account for the rise.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would count as evidence against the analyst's explanation of the town's warming?
choice_a: Only some of the dark asphalt now in town was laid down by the municipal government.
choice_b: Over the thirty years the town received slightly more sunshine in some summers than in others.
choice_c: Pale-colored rooftops across the town reflect a good deal of sunlight before it can warm the ground.
choice_d: The area covered by dark asphalt has grown more in the past thirty years than in any earlier period.
choice_e: Most of the two-degree rise had already taken place before most of the town's asphalt was laid down.
prediction_text: If most of the warming happened before most of the asphalt existed, the asphalt cannot be its chief cause.
correct_answer_job: Add a fact on which the asphalt cannot be the chief cause of the warming.
conclusion: The town's warming is chiefly caused by the spread of dark asphalt.
support: Asphalt absorbs sunlight and releases heat, and its expanse has spread across the town.
gap: If the warming preceded the asphalt, the asphalt cannot explain most of it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it qualifies the asphalt, but who laid it has no bearing on whether the asphalt as a whole is warming the town, so it does not tell against the explanation.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because sunlight drives the mechanism, but small year-to-year swings in sunshine do not challenge the claim that the growing asphalt is the chief cause of the overall rise.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it introduces sunlight and heat, but a factor that keeps things cooler does not show the asphalt failed to cause the warming that did occur, so it does not weaken the claim.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it engages the asphalt, but a surge in asphalt matching the warming period would support the explanation, so it strengthens rather than weakens it.
explanation_e: Choice E weakens the argument: if most of the warming came before most of the asphalt existed, the asphalt cannot be the chief cause of that warming, which is exactly what the analyst claims.

stimulus: Naturalist: The claim that the marsh warbler still nests in this valley is mistaken. The wetland it depended on was drained for farmland years ago, and ever since, surveyors combing the valley have turned up no nests, no eggs, and no feathers. Whatever people believe they have glimpsed, the marsh warbler no longer lives here. The evidence, in the naturalist's view, all points in one direction.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the naturalist's argument depends?
choice_a: The marsh warbler did not simply move to a different area and go on nesting there after its wetland was drained.
choice_b: Draining the wetland killed off the last marsh warblers by starving them where they were.
choice_c: Some animals in the valley can destroy a warbler's nest and eggs without leaving a trace.
choice_d: Every surveyor who has worked in the valley searched systematically for signs of the warbler.
choice_e: The people who report glimpsing the warbler are not experienced birdwatchers.
prediction_text: From lost habitat plus no physical evidence, the naturalist concludes absence, which needs that the bird did not just move elsewhere and persist.
correct_answer_job: State the assumption ruling out that the warbler simply relocated within reach and still nests nearby.
conclusion: The marsh warbler no longer lives in the valley.
support: Its wetland was drained and no nests, eggs, or feathers have been found since.
gap: The bird might have shifted to another spot and gone on nesting, leaving the old area empty.
explanation_a: Choice A is required: the naturalist reads lost habitat and missing evidence as extinction from the valley, which holds only if the bird did not relocate and persist elsewhere; if it had, the empty old site would prove nothing.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it ties draining to the birds' fate, but the argument needs only that the bird is gone, not a particular mechanism of death, so this stronger claim is not required.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns the missing evidence, but it would explain away the absence of traces, weakening the argument rather than being something it must assume.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because thorough searching supports the conclusion, but the argument does not require that every single surveyor searched systematically, only that the bird is in fact gone.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it would discount the sightings, but the argument can set the glimpses aside without assuming the observers are inexpert, so this is not a required assumption.

stimulus: Admission to the Pilots' Guild requires a current medical certificate, and no one who has failed the annual vision exam may be admitted to the Guild. So Reyes, a decorated navigator who failed last month's vision exam, cannot be hired as the ferry's relief captain, the officer who takes the helm whenever the regular captain is away. That post is a demanding one, not a mere formality.
question_stem: The argument's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: Anyone who holds a current medical certificate and has not failed the vision exam is eligible for Guild admission.
choice_b: Only those eligible for admission to the Pilots' Guild can be hired as the ferry's relief captain.
choice_c: A current medical certificate is not required in order to be hired as the ferry's relief captain.
choice_d: If Reyes had not failed the vision exam, he would be hired as the ferry's relief captain.
choice_e: Reyes's trouble with the vision exam bears on what a ferry's relief captain must actually do.
prediction_text: Reyes is barred from the Guild, so to conclude he cannot be relief captain the argument needs that only Guild-eligible people can hold that post.
correct_answer_job: Supply the link tying Guild eligibility to being hired as relief captain.
conclusion: Reyes cannot be hired as the ferry's relief captain.
support: Reyes failed the vision exam, and no one who failed it may be admitted to the Guild.
gap: Nothing yet says the relief-captain post requires Guild eligibility at all.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it recites the Guild's requirements, but it tells us who is eligible for the Guild, not that the relief-captain post requires Guild eligibility, so it does not close the gap.
explanation_b: Choice B makes the conclusion follow: Reyes is barred from the Guild by his failed vision exam, and if only Guild-eligible people can be relief captain, then Reyes cannot hold that post.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it mentions the certificate, but what the relief-captain post does or does not require of certificates does not connect Reyes's Guild ineligibility to the post.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it links the exam to the post, but it supplies a sufficient condition for being hired, not the bridge from Guild ineligibility to being barred, which the conclusion needs.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it connects vision to the job, but mere relevance does not make the conclusion follow; the argument needs that the post itself requires Guild eligibility.

stimulus: Standard clay bricks are identical in the amount of clay each contains. Forty percent of the clay in a certain batch (P) of standard bricks was reclaimed from an older batch (Q) of standard bricks that had been ground up. Since all of Q's bricks were reclaimed into bricks in P, and since the non-clay material in a brick is negligible, it follows that P contains two and a half times as many bricks as Q.
question_stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: The clay in the bricks of batch P cannot be reclaimed yet again into future bricks.
choice_b: Reclaimed clay is of poorer quality than clay that has never been reclaimed.
choice_c: All of the clay in a brick is recovered when that brick is ground up and reclaimed.
choice_d: None of the bricks in batch Q had themselves been made from previously reclaimed clay.
choice_e: Clay bricks are easier to reclaim than bricks made from other materials.
prediction_text: The count follows only if all of Q's clay ends up in P, so nothing is lost when the bricks are ground up and reclaimed.
correct_answer_job: Supply the assumption that lets Q's clay equal exactly forty percent of P's.
conclusion: P contains two and a half times as many bricks as Q.
support: Forty percent of P's clay came from Q, whose bricks were all reclaimed into P.
gap: If some clay were lost in reclaiming, Q's clay would exceed forty percent of P's and the ratio would fail.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns reclaiming, but whether P's clay can be reused later has no bearing on how much of Q's clay ended up in P, so it does not secure the ratio.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it distinguishes the clay, but quality does not affect the amount of clay carried over, and the conclusion turns entirely on amounts, so this is beside the point.
explanation_c: Choice C makes the conclusion follow: if no clay is lost in reclaiming, then Q's clay is exactly the forty percent of P's clay that came from it, so P has two and a half times Q's clay and thus two and a half times as many bricks.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns Q's history, but where Q's clay originally came from does not affect how much of it transfers into P, so it does not close the quantitative gap.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it praises clay's recyclability, but a comparison with other materials says nothing about whether all of Q's clay ended up in P, which is what the count requires.

stimulus: Suppose I have vowed always to tell my mentor the whole truth, and one day she asks me something I cannot answer fully without revealing a friend's secret I swore to guard. Plainly I cannot both reveal and conceal the very same secret. So no one can be bound both to tell a mentor the whole truth on every occasion and to guard every secret entrusted to them.
question_stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?
choice_a: Some shops can draw enough customers only by advertising falsely; and every shop needs customers; so some shops must advertise falsely.
choice_b: If we price the tickets high, patrons will call us greedy; if we price them low, they will think the show second-rate; so however we price them, we invite complaint.
choice_c: If tenants have a valid grievance and the landlord can fix it, the landlord must act; and if a landlord must act, the board will compel it. The board did not compel this landlord, so either the grievance was invalid or the landlord could not fix it.
choice_d: We are told we have a free hand to spend our earnings however we like, and also a duty to support our aging parents. But supporting them means not spending entirely as we like. So we cannot both have a free hand to spend as we like and a duty to support our parents.
choice_e: To open a second location we would have to borrow heavily or sell equity; both would strain our finances, which we cannot allow; so we will keep to a single location.
prediction_text: Form: duty-to-always-X and duty-to-always-Y conflict in a case; can't do both there; so one cannot be bound to both universally.
correct_answer_job: Match the form: two universal duties that collide in a case, so both cannot hold without exception.
conclusion: One cannot be bound both to tell the whole truth always and to guard every secret.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it reaches a must-conclusion, but it chains a need to a single means, rather than showing two universal duties that collide, so its form differs from the original.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because two options both go badly, but it is a dilemma about outcomes of a choice, not a demonstration that two standing obligations cannot both hold, so it does not match.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it involves obligations, but it runs a conditional chain backward from a denied consequent, a different structure from showing two universal duties in conflict.
explanation_d: Choice D matches the form exactly: two universal entitlements or duties are posited, a case shows they cannot both be honored, and the argument concludes one cannot be bound to both without exception, just as with truth and secrets.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because options are ruled out, but it eliminates both branches of a disjunction to reach a practical decision, not a conflict between two universal obligations, so the pattern is different.

stimulus: Editor: Every newspaper chases online clicks, since clicks bring in advertising revenue and help keep the paper afloat. But not every tactic that wins clicks serves the paper's deeper interests. Chasing clicks often means running shallow, sensational stories, which erodes readers' trust and demoralizes the reporters who want to do serious work. The pull of the click count, in short, does not always run with the paper's real good.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the editor's argument?
choice_a: If a tactic that keeps a paper afloat fails to help its reporters, then it cannot be good for the paper.
choice_b: Only when reporters also own the paper will their interests and the paper's fully coincide.
choice_c: There is no newspaper that does not chase online clicks.
choice_d: Running shallow, sensational stories demoralizes the reporters who want to do serious work.
choice_e: Not every tactic a newspaper uses to win online clicks serves the paper's deeper interests.
prediction_text: The main point is that not every click-winning tactic serves the paper's deeper interests; the rest supports it.
correct_answer_job: Identify the editor's main point, as opposed to the supporting premises.
conclusion: Not every tactic a newspaper uses to win clicks serves the paper's deeper interests.
support: Chasing clicks often means shallow stories that erode trust and demoralize reporters.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it echoes the theme, but the editor never asserts this general conditional; it goes beyond the argument, so it is not the conclusion actually drawn.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because interests are discussed, but the editor says nothing about ownership, so this claim is neither stated nor the point the argument builds toward.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the editor does say every paper chases clicks, but that is a premise setting up the argument, not the main point it is offered to establish.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it is stated in the passage, but it is offered as support for the main point, explaining why click-chasing can fail the paper, rather than being that point itself.
explanation_e: Choice E is the main conclusion: the surrounding claims about shallow stories, lost trust, and demoralized reporters are all offered to support precisely this point, which is what the editor is arguing for.

stimulus: Cafe owner: Our competitors say we should stop handing out single-use cups, on the principle that any business whose cups end up as litter ought to phase them out on its own. Their claim that our cups become litter has never actually been established. And even if it were, their argument would deserve no attention at all, because their own shops hand out single-use cups too, and they have not phased theirs out either.
question_stem: The cafe owner's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
choice_a: rejects an argument on the ground that those who advance it have not themselves done what the argument says ought to be done
choice_b: rejects an argument on the ground that those who advance it stand to gain if others accept its conclusion
choice_c: concludes that because a claim has not been proved true, that claim must be false
choice_d: tries to support its conclusion with two reasons that cannot both be true at the same time
choice_e: treats a condition under which cups would be objectionable as though it were enough by itself to make them objectionable
prediction_text: The owner brushes the argument aside because the competitors don't practice what they preach, which is no reason the argument is wrong.
correct_answer_job: Name the reasoning error: dismissing an argument because its proponents do not themselves follow its recommendation.
conclusion: The competitors' argument deserves no serious attention.
support: The competitors also hand out single-use cups and have not phased them out.
gap: Whether the proponents follow their own advice is irrelevant to whether the advice is correct.
explanation_a: Choice A correctly names the error: the owner sets the competitors' argument aside merely because they do not follow its recommendation, which has no bearing on whether the recommendation is sound.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the competitors are rivals, but the owner's stated reason is that they fail to follow their own advice, not that they would profit if the advice were accepted.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the owner does note the littering claim is unproven, but the argument does not treat it as thereby false; it goes on to attack the competitors for not following their own rule.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the owner gives more than one reason, but the two reasons are not in conflict with each other, so the flaw is not an incompatibility between them.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because conditions for objectionable cups are in play, but the owner never confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one; the real error concerns dismissing the rivals' argument.

stimulus: Head librarian: Here at the central branch, every one of our full-time clerks attends the weekly shelving workshop, because their contracts require it, while only about half of our part-time clerks attend it. Some workshop attendees, including several of our most accurate shelvers, also serve on the events committee. Therefore we can conclude that some events-committee members are full-time clerks and some are part-time clerks.
question_stem: The reasoning in the head librarian's argument is flawed because this argument
choice_a: takes for granted that more of the strong shelvers than of the other clerks serve on the events committee
choice_b: overlooks the possibility that those who both attend the workshop and serve on the events committee do not include both full-time and part-time clerks
choice_c: takes for granted that more full-time clerks than part-time clerks serve on the events committee
choice_d: overlooks the possibility that clerks have many ways of spending their time besides the events committee
choice_e: uses the word "attend" in one sense at first and then shifts it to a different sense
prediction_text: The attendees who also sit on the committee could be entirely full-time, or entirely part-time; nothing guarantees both are represented.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: assuming the overlap group must include members of both subgroups.
conclusion: Some events-committee members are full-time clerks and some are part-time clerks.
support: All full-timers and half the part-timers attend the workshop, and some attendees serve on the committee.
gap: The workshop-and-committee overlap need not contain both full-time and part-time clerks.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because the strong shelvers are mentioned, but the argument makes no comparison of how many strong versus other shelvers join the committee, so this is not its error.
explanation_b: Choice B correctly names the error: the people in that overlap could all be full-time, or all part-time, so the conclusion that both groups are represented on the committee does not follow.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because full- and part-time clerks are compared elsewhere, but the argument never assumes one group outnumbers the other on the committee; that is not the flaw.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it raises other activities, but what else clerks might do is beside the point; the gap is about who is in the workshop-and-committee overlap.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because a describe-the-flaw answer often points to a shifted term, but "attend" keeps a single meaning throughout, so no equivocation occurs.

stimulus: Linguist: Most scholars accept that the Talvic language descended from Old Rhenish. A few have resisted this view, because the earliest known Talvic inscriptions are older than the earliest known Old Rhenish inscriptions by several generations. That reasoning goes wrong, though: the absence so far of any Old Rhenish inscription from the relevant era does nothing to show that none such ever existed.
question_stem: The linguist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?
choice_a: It overlooks that even if one particular objection to a theory is misguided, the theory itself may still be false.
choice_b: It takes for granted that if any Old Rhenish inscriptions older than the known Talvic ones exist, that alone would prove the descent.
choice_c: It fails to address the possibility that it can be reasonable to withhold acceptance of a theory solely because the evidence gathered so far is insufficient.
choice_d: It overlooks that there may be strong evidence against the descent that has nothing to do with the ages of any inscriptions.
choice_e: It presumes, without warrant, that the earliest inscriptions of a language are a reliable guide to that language's true age.
prediction_text: Even if the dissenters' particular objection fails, it can still be reasonable to withhold acceptance while the evidence remains insufficient.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: rebutting one objection does not establish the theory, since withholding acceptance on thin evidence can itself be reasonable.
conclusion: The dissenters' reasoning against the descent theory is misguided.
support: Missing old Old Rhenish inscriptions might nonetheless exist.
gap: Defeating one objection leaves open that scant evidence can justify withholding belief.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting and close, but the linguist attacks the dissenters' reasoning, not the theory's truth directly; the sharper flaw is ignoring that scant evidence can justify withholding acceptance.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns the missing inscriptions, but the linguist never claims such a find would prove descent; only that its possibility undercuts the objection.
explanation_c: Choice C correctly names the error: the dissenters may be reasonably withholding belief given thin evidence, and showing their specific point about inscriptions is answerable does not touch that stance.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because unspecified counter-evidence sounds relevant, but the argument concerns the inscription-age objection specifically; positing unrelated evidence is not the flaw committed.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because inscription ages are central, but the linguist does not rely on that presumption; the reasoning fault lies in dismissing reasonable doubt based on insufficient evidence.

stimulus: Blogger: The health press wildly overstates the harm of sitting at a desk all day. We are constantly warned about how a sedentary workday supposedly shortens people's lives, yet my aunt sat behind a desk for forty years and is now a sharp, healthy eighty-eight. Clearly there is far less to these warnings than the experts would have us believe about the risks of a desk job.
question_stem: The reasoning in the blogger's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choice_a: fails to consider factors other than a desk job that can lengthen or shorten a person's life
choice_b: addresses only how long a person lives and not the quality of the life that is lived
choice_c: does not address possible moral objections to spending one's days at a desk
choice_d: relies on a single anecdote to challenge a general claim
choice_e: mistakes the cause of a phenomenon for one of that phenomenon's effects
prediction_text: One long-lived aunt cannot refute a claim about what tends to happen across many people.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: using a single anecdote to rebut a general statistical claim.
conclusion: The warnings about sedentary work are greatly overstated.
support: One aunt sat at a desk for forty years and is healthy at 88.
gap: A general claim about a population is not overturned by a single favorable case.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because other health factors clearly matter, but the argument's central mistake is using one case against a general claim, not neglecting confounding factors.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it distinguishes length from quality of life, but the warnings and the blogger both speak to lifespan, so this shift is not the flaw.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting as an overlooked angle, but moral objections have nothing to do with the health claim at issue, so ignoring them is not the reasoning error.
explanation_d: Choice D correctly names the error: one healthy aunt is a lone example, which cannot by itself overturn a general claim about how sedentary work tends to affect lifespan across people.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it names a familiar reasoning error, but the blogger never swaps a cause for an effect; the mistake is generalizing from one favorable case.

stimulus: Last quarter the plant moved every shift's start one hour earlier, and as a result many workers lost an hour of sleep. Over the following week, according to the safety office, on-the-job injuries ran about eight percent above what the plant normally sees in that season. The most plausible explanation is that grogginess brought on by the lost sleep drove this jump in injuries.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choice_a: Some workers, forgetting the new schedule, arrived an hour late and had to rush through their opening tasks.
choice_b: On-the-job injuries are generally less frequent in that season than during the winter months.
choice_c: The injuries that occurred in the week after the change were no more serious than injuries normally are.
choice_d: The effects of losing a single hour of sleep can persist for several days.
choice_e: The rise in injuries was most pronounced during the first hours of each shift, when workers short on sleep tend to be groggiest.
prediction_text: If the extra injuries cluster exactly when groggy workers would be worst off, the sleep explanation is reinforced.
correct_answer_job: Add a fact that ties the injury spike specifically to sleep-driven grogginess.
conclusion: Grogginess from lost sleep caused the jump in injuries.
support: Injuries rose eight percent the week after workers lost an hour of sleep.
gap: Something must link the timing or pattern of injuries to sleep deprivation specifically.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it could explain some injuries, but rushing due to lateness is a different cause, which if anything competes with the sleep explanation rather than supporting it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it cites injury rates, but a season-to-season comparison says nothing about whether lost sleep caused the eight-percent rise within that week.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns the injuries, but their severity is beside the point; the argument is about what caused the rise in their number, not how bad they were.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns lost sleep, but a general claim about lingering effects does not tie this particular injury spike to grogginess the way a specific pattern would.
explanation_e: Choice E most strengthens the argument: if the extra injuries cluster precisely when sleep-deprived workers would be groggiest, that pattern is just what the sleep-deprivation explanation predicts.

stimulus: The nests of the marsh wren often hold shredded reed, which the birds eat, together with shredded wormwood, which is not a food source. Since the wormwood is not eaten, it is probably tucked into the nest to drive off mites. This view is backed by a test in which mite eggs incubated among shredded reed almost all hatched, whereas among shredded wormwood only about one in five did.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choice_a: Marsh-wren nests that contain no shredded wormwood are, in most cases, infested with mites.
choice_b: Marsh wrens that nest near stands of reed almost always include shredded reed in their nests.
choice_c: The marsh wren is the only bird known to keep shredded wormwood in its nest.
choice_d: Mites are found more often on the bodies of marsh wrens than in their nests.
choice_e: Shredded wormwood is generally harder for marsh wrens to gather than shredded reed is.
prediction_text: If nests lacking wormwood tend to be mite-ridden, that confirms the wormwood keeps mites down.
correct_answer_job: Add a fact confirming that the wormwood is doing the mite-suppressing work in real nests.
conclusion: The wormwood is placed in nests to drive off mites.
support: Far fewer mite eggs hatch among wormwood than among reed.
gap: The lab result should be shown to hold for actual nests.
explanation_a: Choice A most strengthens the argument: if nests lacking wormwood tend to be mite-infested, that is just what we would expect if the wormwood is what keeps mites down.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns nest contents, but that wrens use nearby reed says nothing about whether the wormwood repels mites.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it singles out the wormwood behavior, but whether other birds do it has no bearing on whether it drives mites from the wren's nest.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it mentions mites, but where mites live does not speak to whether the wormwood in the nest is what keeps their numbers down.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the wormwood, but the difficulty of gathering it does not support the claim that its purpose in the nest is to repel mites.

stimulus: A study compared the songs of five inland populations of a finch, all of one subspecies, with those of two coastal populations of a different subspecies, tracking phrasing and rhythm. It found that one inland population's song resembled the coastal populations' songs more closely than it resembled the songs of the other inland populations. The researchers concluded that these song patterns are set mainly by learning rather than by inherited differences.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the argument?
choice_a: Finches new to a population sometimes bring with them both unfamiliar songs and unfamiliar inherited traits.
choice_b: Finches sometimes imitate the songs of other finches whether or not they are closely related genetically.
choice_c: The finch populations studied face markedly different environmental challenges in their various locations.
choice_d: The song differences among the populations are pronounced enough to tell each population apart.
choice_e: The five inland populations live closer to one another than the two coastal populations do.
prediction_text: If finches learn songs from others regardless of kinship, the cross-subspecies resemblance fits learning.
correct_answer_job: Add a fact making learning, not genetics, the better explanation of the odd resemblance.
conclusion: The finches' song patterns are set mainly by learning.
support: One inland population's song matched the distant coastal populations more than its genetic neighbors.
gap: Something must make learning a more plausible source of the resemblance than shared ancestry.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it involves new songs, but by bundling songs with inherited traits it leaves open a genetic explanation, so it does not favor learning over inheritance.
explanation_b: Choice B provides the most support: if finches copy songs regardless of kinship, then an inland population sounding like distant coastal ones is readily explained by learning rather than by genetics.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because environment can shape behavior, but differing environments would if anything predict differing songs, which does not explain the cross-subspecies resemblance by learning.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns song differences, but that the populations are distinguishable says nothing about whether learning or genetics sets their songs.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns location, but relative proximity does not explain why one inland population sings like the distant coastal ones, nor does it favor learning.

recipe_title: Weaken by Undercutting the Safety Claim
stimulus: Installing rumble strips on the approaches to rural intersections is supposed to make those intersections safer, but it does not. Crashes actually rise at intersections that have the strips: there are fewer high-speed cross-traffic crashes, but considerably more low-speed rear-end taps as cars brake suddenly. So the strips do nothing for safety.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
choice_a: The rumble strips cost far less to install than most other intersection safety measures do.
choice_b: The strips are sometimes set off by large animals crossing the road rather than by cars.
choice_c: High-speed cross-traffic crashes are a far graver threat to life than low-speed rear-end taps are.
choice_d: The high-speed cross-traffic crashes are usually the fault of drivers who were speeding.
choice_e: Many of the low-speed rear-end taps at these intersections are never reported to the authorities.
prediction_text: If the crashes that dropped are far deadlier than the ones that rose, safety improved.
correct_answer_job: Show that the change in crash mix is a net safety gain despite more total crashes.
conclusion: The rumble strips do nothing for safety.
support: Total crashes rise, with fewer cross-traffic crashes but more rear-end taps.
gap: A rise in minor crashes may be outweighed by a fall in severe ones.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it favors the strips, but their low cost has nothing to do with whether they make the intersection safer, which is the claim at issue.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns the strips, but what triggers them does not bear on whether they reduce the overall harm from crashes.
explanation_c: Choice C most weakens the argument: if the crashes that fell are far deadlier than the ones that rose, the strips improve safety on balance even though total crashes go up.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it discusses the cross-traffic crashes, but who is at fault does not affect whether reducing those crashes makes the intersection safer overall.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the rear-end taps, but whether they are reported does not speak to the net safety effect of the strips.

recipe_title: Weaken by Offering a Rival Function
stimulus: A blind cave fish that lives far from any light has been found to possess organs sensitive to faint infrared warmth. Ordinary sunlight cannot reach its cavern. If these heat receptors arose as an adaptation to cave life, they are probably for sensing the warmth given off by other living things. In that case, since the fish itself is cold-bodied, it probably uses the receptors to hunt warm-bodied prey.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument?
choice_a: A trait that serves no function at all tends to be lost over many generations.
choice_b: Warm-bodied creatures are scarce in the part of the cave where the fish is found.
choice_c: The cave fish can locate others of its own kind by smell rather than by warmth.
choice_d: The cave fish's most dangerous predators are warm-bodied.
choice_e: Heat-sensing organs of this kind take many generations to evolve.
prediction_text: If the fish's predators are warm-bodied, the receptors more likely serve to avoid them, not to hunt.
correct_answer_job: Offer a rival purpose for the heat sense that fits the facts better than hunting.
conclusion: The fish uses its heat receptors to hunt warm-bodied prey.
support: The receptors likely sense living things' warmth, and the fish is cold-bodied.
gap: The warmth being sensed could belong to predators rather than prey.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns adaptation, but it does not challenge the leap from sensing warmth to hunting prey; it is a general remark that leaves that inference untouched.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because scarce prey seems to undercut hunting, but the argument is about what the receptors are for, and scarce prey does not show they serve some other purpose.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns how the fish senses things, but that it finds its own kind by smell says nothing about what the heat receptors are used for.
explanation_d: Choice D most weakens the argument: if the fish's predators are warm-bodied, the heat receptors are at least as plausibly used to detect and avoid those predators as to hunt prey, breaking the inference.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the receptors' origin, but how long they took to evolve does not bear on whether their function is hunting rather than something else.

stimulus: A recent experiment suggests that crows sometimes act altruistically rather than out of self-interest. Researchers let an unfamiliar crow struggle to reach a scrap of food lodged behind a barrier; most of the crows that were watching then nudged a stick within its reach, even though doing so took effort and brought them nothing. Since the crows were given no reward for helping, the experiment plainly revealed altruism.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choice_a: Had a reward been offered, the crows would have helped in exactly the same way.
choice_b: Crows are the only birds that have been shown to behave altruistically.
choice_c: The crows treated nudging the stick as a form of play.
choice_d: The crows would have behaved differently toward a crow they already knew.
choice_e: The crows did not act in the expectation that they would receive a reward.
prediction_text: If the crows expected a reward, the act would not be altruistic; so they must not have expected one.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for 'no reward given' to establish altruism.
conclusion: The experiment revealed altruism.
support: No reward was given for the helping behavior.
gap: No reward offered does not rule out the crows' expecting one.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns rewards, but the argument does not need this; it needs only that the crows did not expect a reward in the situation as it was.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it praises crows' altruism, but whether other birds are altruistic is irrelevant to whether this experiment shows these crows acted altruistically.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting as an alternative motive, but the argument does not require it; in fact, if the crows were merely playing, that would undercut, not support, the altruism claim.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the helped crow was unfamiliar, but the argument does not depend on how the crows would treat a familiar crow.
explanation_e: Choice E is the required assumption: the conclusion rests on the helping being unrewarded, so if the crows had expected a reward the behavior would not count as altruism, and the argument would collapse.

stimulus: Economist: In many industries, resentment of automation and calls to slow it down are on the rise, chiefly because automation has sharply widened the gap between high and low earners within those industries. Since automation delivers large gains in output to an industry as a whole, firms should adopt measures such as funding worker retraining in order to spread those gains more evenly.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?
choice_a: Funding worker retraining will not significantly undercut the output gains that automation delivers to the industry.
choice_b: The widening income gaps within these industries are not themselves a direct result of automation.
choice_c: In industries with sharply unequal incomes, lower-paid workers gain little or nothing from automation.
choice_d: Slowing automation is one effective way to spread an industry's gains more evenly.
choice_e: Spreading the gains more evenly will increase the total output gains automation brings the industry.
prediction_text: If retraining wiped out the output gains, recommending it while praising automation would be self-defeating; so it must not.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for retraining to be the recommended response given automation's benefits.
conclusion: Firms should fund worker retraining to spread automation's gains more evenly.
support: Automation delivers large output gains, and inequality drives resentment.
gap: The recommended measure must not cancel the very gains it is meant to distribute.
explanation_a: Choice A is the required assumption: the economist urges retraining precisely to distribute automation's gains, so if retraining wiped those gains out, the recommendation would defeat its own purpose.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because inequality is central, but the argument grants that automation widened the gaps; it does not need to deny automation as their cause.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns who benefits, but the argument does not require this; its recommendation stands whether or not low earners currently share in the gains.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because slowing automation is what critics want, but the economist recommends retraining instead, so the argument need not assume slowing automation would work.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links distribution to gains, but the argument needs only that retraining not destroy the gains, not that distributing them makes the gains larger.

stimulus: Ferry operator: Our two companies are the only customers of the regional dry dock, and there is no other dry dock within reach of our route. If our main rival's line were to fold, that dry dock, which both of our companies rely on for every major repair, would close for lack of enough business to sustain it. So, for our own line to keep running, our main rival's line must keep running.
question_stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: The dry dock will not close.
choice_b: Our line will keep running only if the dry dock stays open.
choice_c: Our line will keep running if our main rival's line keeps running.
choice_d: If our line folds, our main rival's line will fold too.
choice_e: Our line will keep running if the dry dock stays open.
prediction_text: If our line runs only when the dry dock is open, then the dock's closing (from the rival folding) would stop us.
correct_answer_job: Supply the conditional that makes the rival's survival necessary for the operator's survival.
