stimulus: Earlier this week, I promised to answer Mara's question about when the recital begins. As it happened, I misheard her and thought she had asked who among the staff gets to decide when it begins. I told her, quite truthfully, that the director makes that decision and has not yet fixed a time. Thus I kept my promise to answer her question.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choice_a: No one can be held responsible for a decision that is another person's to make.
choice_b: The person who decides when an event begins is the one who ought to announce it.
choice_c: All that answering a person's question requires is giving that person some true information in response to it.
choice_d: One need not actually answer a question in order to have made one's best effort to answer it.
choice_e: Making a promise always obliges the person who makes it to keep it.
prediction_text: If answering a question is just giving some true information in response, then my truthful reply counts as answering.
correct_answer_job: Supply the principle equating 'said something true in response' with 'answered the question.'
conclusion: I kept my promise to answer Mara's question.
support: I told her something truthful in response to her.
gap: A link is needed from 'said something true' to 'answered the question I promised to answer.'
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because the reply mentions the director's authority, but responsibility for the decision has nothing to do with whether I answered Mara's question.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns the director, but who ought to announce the time does not bridge my truthful reply to the claim that I answered the question.
explanation_c: Choice C enables the conclusion: if answering just means giving some true information in reply, then since I told Mara something true in response, I answered her question and so kept my promise.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns answering, but the conclusion claims I did answer, not that I merely tried; this principle would not license that stronger claim.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because a promise is involved, but that promises must be kept does not show that what I did amounted to answering the question I promised to answer.

stimulus: Releasing hatchery-raised fish into a river at the start of each fishing season is said to boost anglers' catches noticeably, and supporters treat this apparent benefit as proof that the release does the river's ecology real good. Yet it may do ecological harm even if catches do climb, because it could disturb the wild population's genetics in ways that no one can yet reliably foresee.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that releasing hatchery-raised fish could disrupt the wild population's genetics in ways no one can foresee?
choice_a: It is a summary of the argument's overall position.
choice_b: It is a claim that the argument sets out to refute.
choice_c: It is a claim the argument says is not enough to establish what supporters take it to establish.
choice_d: It is a premise offered in support of the argument's conclusion.
choice_e: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
prediction_text: The genetics claim is the support the argument gives for its conclusion that the practice may be harmful.
correct_answer_job: Locate the claim's function: it is a stated reason for the argument's own conclusion.
conclusion: The practice may be ecologically harmful even if it raises catches.
support: It could disrupt wild genetics in unforeseeable ways.
gap: Distinguish a supporting premise from the conclusion it supports.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it is a prominent claim, but it is not a restatement of the whole argument; it is one reason offered within it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the argument does refute the supporters' view, but this particular claim is the argument's own, not the position it opposes.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting, but this describes how the argument treats the catch-boosting claim, not the genetics claim, which the argument itself endorses.
explanation_d: Choice D correctly describes the role: the possibility of unforeseeable genetic disruption is the reason the argument gives for concluding that the practice may be harmful even if catches rise.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it is a strong claim, but the main conclusion is that the practice may be harmful even if catches rise; the genetics claim is the support for that.

stimulus: Essayist: Since ancient times people have told stories to predict what the future holds. In this respect the pronouncements of modern economic forecasting are no different from an old farmers' almanac. The question of a forecast's truth, as with an almanac's, is simply the question of how useful it is in coping with uncertainty. So although forecasting has a handful of genuine hits to its name, its failure to reach the whole truth is plain from how frequently it has steered public policy astray.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main conclusion of the essayist's argument?
choice_a: Economic forecasting is at least partly responsible for misguided public policy.
choice_b: Economic forecasting is no more true than an old farmers' almanac.
choice_c: Economic forecasting is merely a collection of stories about the future.
choice_d: Economic forecasting, like an old almanac, attempts to predict what is to come.
choice_e: Economic forecasting falls short of being completely true.
prediction_text: The point everything else supports is that forecasting is only partly true.
correct_answer_job: Separate the single main claim from the premises that lead to it.
conclusion: Economic forecasting falls short of being completely true.
support: It is like an almanac, its truth is mere usefulness, and it has misguided policy.
gap: Distinguish the conclusion from the supporting comparisons and observations.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it appears near the end, but this is the evidence the essayist offers, not the conclusion it is offered to support.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the comparison is prominent, but it is a premise used to set up the main point, not the point itself.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting but overshoots: the essayist claims forecasting falls short of complete truth, not that it is nothing but storytelling.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it is stated early, but it is background setting up the argument, not the conclusion the argument reaches.
explanation_e: Choice E is the main conclusion: the comparison to an almanac, the account of truth as usefulness, and the record of misguided policy are all offered to support this single claim.

stimulus: When phytoplankton in the Coral Sea multiply rapidly, they draw down more of the water's carbon dioxide than they give back to it; when they multiply slowly, the reverse holds. Any substantial rise in the carbon dioxide entering the sea warms its surface waters, where the bulk of the plankton live. And the warmer those surface waters get, the more sluggish, on average, is the multiplication of the plankton living there.
question_stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choice_a: The plankton in the surface waters will multiply more slowly, on average, if they give off enough carbon dioxide to raise the sea's total intake substantially.
choice_b: The amount of carbon dioxide entering the sea is bound to climb at a steadily accelerating pace.
choice_c: If the carbon dioxide entering the sea rises substantially, most of the plankton will give off more of it than they take in.
choice_d: If the plankton begin to multiply more slowly, the surface waters will as a result grow substantially warmer.
choice_e: Any warming of the surface waters will be accompanied by a substantial rise in the carbon dioxide entering the sea.
prediction_text: If the plankton release enough carbon dioxide to raise the total substantially, the warming that follows will slow their multiplication.
correct_answer_job: Follow the stated chain to the conditional it best supports.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Slow growth releases carbon dioxide; a substantial release warms the surface; warming slows growth.
gap: Link the plankton's own release to their slowed multiplication via the warming step.
inference_or_resolution: The chain connects a substantial release by the plankton to their own slower multiplication.
explanation_a: Choice A is most strongly supported: a substantial rise in the sea's carbon dioxide warms the surface waters, and warmer surface waters slow the plankton's multiplication, so their own heavy output would slow them.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns released carbon dioxide, but nothing in the passage supports a claim about an ever-accelerating rate of release.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it uses the passage's terms, but the passage does not support concluding that a substantial rise makes most plankton net releasers.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting but reverses the chain: warming slows multiplication, not the other way around, so slower multiplication does not by itself warm the waters.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting but states the converse: a substantial release causes warming, which does not license the claim that every warming is accompanied by such a release.

stimulus: Some good study practices, such as reviewing one's notes each night, tend to raise the grades of the student who follows them; others, such as tutoring classmates, do not. Moreover, no practice counts as a good study practice if it tends to lower other students' grades.
question_stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choice_a: A student who follows no good study practices tends not to have any habits that help other students.
choice_b: Reviewing one's notes each night tends not to lower other students' grades.
choice_c: A student who follows good study practices tends to help other students more than a student who follows none.
choice_d: Tutoring classmates tends to be to one's own disadvantage but not to other students' disadvantage.
choice_e: If a study habit tends to help other students' grades, then it is a good study practice.
prediction_text: Reviewing notes nightly is a good study practice, so it cannot tend to lower others' grades.
correct_answer_job: Combine the definition with the given example to deduce a guaranteed claim.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Reviewing notes nightly is a good study practice; good practices don't tend to lower others' grades.
gap: Apply the disqualifying rule to the stated example.
inference_or_resolution: A good study practice cannot tend to lower other students grades.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it echoes the terms, but nothing links lacking good study practices to lacking habits that help others; this does not follow.
explanation_b: Choice B must be true: reviewing notes nightly is stated to be a good study practice, and no good study practice tends to lower other students' grades, so this practice cannot.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting but goes beyond the premises: the rule forbids lowering others' grades but says nothing about which students help others more.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because tutoring is mentioned, but the passage does not say tutoring disadvantages the tutor, only that it need not raise the tutor's own grades.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting but reverses the rule: not lowering others' grades is required of a good practice, which does not make helping others' grades sufficient to be one.

stimulus: The cafe's new espresso machine has started to rattle loudly in the middle of service. The owner first suspected a loose panel somewhere in the casing, but a failing pump is the likelier cause. If a loose panel were to blame, we would expect the machine to rattle at every pressure setting; but in fact it rattles only at the highest pressure.
question_stem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following arguments?
choice_a: If the shipment had been held up at customs, it would arrive after Friday; but it was not held up at customs, so it will probably arrive by Friday.
choice_b: If the thermostat were broken, the office would be cold; the office is cold, so the thermostat is probably broken.
choice_c: If the new server were configured correctly, the site would load quickly; but the site loads slowly, so the server is probably not configured correctly.
choice_d: I expect the auditor to flag the missing receipt; if she flags it, the report will be sent back; so the report will probably be sent back.
choice_e: If the cafe runs a promotion, its sales rise; the cafe will probably run a promotion this week, so its sales will probably rise.
prediction_text: The parallel rejects a hypothesis because an expected consequence fails to appear.
correct_answer_job: Match the form: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P (favoring the alternative).
conclusion: A loose panel is probably not to blame (a failing pump is likelier).
support: A loose panel would cause rattling at every setting, but it rattles only at the highest.
gap: Find the choice with the same deny-the-consequent structure.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it uses an if-then, but it denies the antecedent (not P, so not Q), which is a different and invalid pattern from the stimulus.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it involves an expected consequence, but it affirms the consequent (Q, so P) rather than denying it, so its form does not match.
explanation_c: Choice C matches the stimulus: a hypothesis predicts a consequence, the consequence fails to appear, and the hypothesis is therefore rejected (if P then Q; not Q; so not P).
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it reasons about consequences, but it chains forward from an expected cause to its effect, not backward by denying a consequence.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because of the shared setting, but it affirms the antecedent (P, so Q), the opposite of the stimulus's deny-the-consequent form.

stimulus: Last spring a print shop produced many of its promotional flyers on a press with a misregistered color plate, so the colors in those flyers came out slightly out of alignment; this was especially noticeable on photographs and even drew a few complaints. Even so, the local shops that used flyers from this printer tended to see larger increases in foot traffic during that period than shops that used flyers from other printers.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the discrepancy described above?
choice_a: Most people who received the misaligned flyers set them aside without reading them.
choice_b: Most of the shops that used this printer's flyers were restaurants.
choice_c: Not all of the misaligned flyers included photographs.
choice_d: People are more likely to remember a flyer they have seen if its colors were slightly out of alignment.
choice_e: Most local shops during that period did not rely heavily on printed flyers.
prediction_text: If the odd look made the flyers more memorable, the flaw could actually help draw customers.
correct_answer_job: Find the fact that makes a visible flaw consistent with better results.
conclusion: (discrepancy to explain)
support: Flawed flyers coincided with larger foot-traffic gains.
gap: Something must connect the misalignment to a marketing advantage.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns the flyers, but if recipients ignored them it would make the larger foot-traffic gains harder, not easier, to explain.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it describes the shops, but what kind of business they were does not explain why the flawed flyers coincided with bigger gains.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because photographs are mentioned, but that some flyers lacked them does nothing to explain why the flawed flyers outperformed the others.
explanation_d: Choice D most helps explain the discrepancy: if the odd misalignment made the flyers more memorable, then the very flaw that drew complaints could have drawn more customers to the shops that used them.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns flyer use, but a general lack of reliance on flyers does not explain why these particular flawed flyers coincided with larger gains.

stimulus: Reports of black-bear encounters along the trails of Cedar Range have risen sharply over the past fifteen years, according to the park service's own annual incident logs. Yet the number of bears now living in the range has not grown at all during that time, and the bears have no less food available to them within the range than they did before.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the increase in the incidence of bear encounters?
choice_a: Rangers in Cedar Range sometimes relocate bears they believe to be responsible for encounters.
choice_b: About forty bears live in the section of Cedar Range where most encounters occur.
choice_c: More bear encounters occur in Cedar Range than in any other range in the region.
choice_d: The adult bears of Cedar Range are generally unafraid of hikers.
choice_e: Hikers now travel through far more of Cedar Range's backcountry than they did fifteen years ago.
prediction_text: If people now use much more of the range, encounters would rise even with a stable, well-fed bear population.
correct_answer_job: Find the fact that raises human-bear contact without more or hungrier bears.
conclusion: (discrepancy to explain)
support: Encounters rose while bear numbers and food held steady.
gap: Something must increase human exposure to the bears.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns encounters, but relocating problem bears would tend to reduce encounters, so it does not explain their rise.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it gives a figure, but a static count of bears in one area does not explain why encounters have increased over time.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns encounter numbers, but comparing Cedar Range to other ranges does not explain the rise within Cedar Range itself.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it involves bears and hikers, but a longstanding trait of the bears does not explain why encounters have changed over the past fifteen years.
explanation_e: Choice E most helps explain the increase: if people now range across much more of the bears' territory, encounters would rise even though the bear population and their food supply have stayed the same.

stimulus: Ito: When we enforce the community garden's rules about how members keep up their plots, we go wrong by urging gardeners to report violations committed by the people beside them. Doing so breeds resentment among neighbors and produces tips prompted by spite. Vasquez: It is not a mistake. Without rules about how members keep up their plots, one neglected plot could spoil the look of the whole garden.
question_stem: Vasquez's response is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choice_a: treats a criticism of the way in which certain rules are enforced as though it were a criticism of the rules themselves
choice_b: attacks the motives behind Ito's objection rather than the reasoning Ito offers
choice_c: confuses a criticism of the consequences of having a set of rules with a criticism of the particular provisions of those rules
choice_d: takes for granted that because something is likely to happen on some occasions, it will happen on every occasion
choice_e: confuses a cause of resentment among neighbors with a consequence of resentment among neighbors
prediction_text: Ito attacked the reporting method, not the rules; Vasquez defends the rules, missing the point.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: answering an objection to how rules are enforced as though it were an objection to the rules.
conclusion: Encouraging gardeners to report neighbors is not a mistake.
support: Without upkeep rules, one neglected plot could spoil the garden's appearance.
gap: A defense of having rules does not answer a criticism of how those rules are enforced.
explanation_a: Choice A correctly names the error: Ito objected only to the practice of encouraging gardeners to report one another, yet Vasquez defends having upkeep rules at all, which Ito never questioned.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because responses often go after motives, but Vasquez says nothing about why Ito raises the objection; the error lies in what Vasquez defends.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it also describes a mismatch, but the mismatch here is between enforcement and the rules themselves, not between the rules' consequences and their provisions.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because Vasquez does speak of what one gardener could do, but the argument does not slide from sometimes to always; that is not the flaw.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because resentment is mentioned, but Vasquez never reverses its cause and effect; the reply simply answers a criticism that was not made.

stimulus: Academy director: Although our tuition is the highest of any school in the district, our program is also the finest available anywhere in the district. After all, consider any less costly program offered by one of the schools that competes with us. If that program were as good as ours, or better than ours, then it would cost as much as ours does, or more.
question_stem: The reasoning in the academy director's argument is flawed in that the argument
choice_a: fails to draw a needed distinction between the finest program currently offered and the finest program that could be offered
choice_b: relies on a premise that presupposes the truth of the conclusion it is meant to support
choice_c: treats a cause of a program's being the most costly as though it were an effect of the program's being the most costly
choice_d: presumes that because something is true of each program a school offers, it is also true of the school as a whole
choice_e: rests its conclusion on claims that cannot all be true at the same time
prediction_text: The premise that a program as good as theirs would cost as much simply assumes the conclusion that the priciest program is the best.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: the supporting premise already assumes that price tracks quality, which is what is to be shown.
conclusion: The academy's program is the finest in the district.
support: Any cheaper competing program, were it as good, would cost as much or more.
gap: The premise presupposes the very link between price and quality the argument is meant to establish.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because a distinction does lurk nearby, but the argument's fault is that its premise already assumes what it sets out to prove, not that it conflates actual with possible programs.
explanation_b: Choice B correctly names the error: saying that an equally good program would cost at least as much already takes for granted that the costliest program is the best, which is exactly the conclusion.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because price and quality are causally entangled here, but the argument never inverts cause and effect; it assumes its conclusion in a premise.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting as a familiar error, but no inference runs from individual programs to a school as a whole, so composition is not the flaw.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the reasoning feels defective, but the director's claims are consistent with one another; the trouble is that one of them assumes the conclusion.

stimulus: Coach Ramirez: The team reviewed the match footage together on Tuesday afternoon. Any of my players who watched that footage from the opening whistle would have found it instructive, and I happen to know for a fact that at least some of my players did find the footage instructive. So some of my players must have watched the footage from the opening whistle.
question_stem: Coach Ramirez's argument does not follow logically from its premises because of the possibility that
choice_a: some of Coach Ramirez's players are keenly interested in match analysis but were unable to view the footage at all
choice_b: many people who are not Coach Ramirez's players did not find the footage instructive even though they watched it from the opening whistle
choice_c: no one who watched the footage from the opening whistle and found it instructive was one of Coach Ramirez's players
choice_d: some of Coach Ramirez's players arrived a few minutes late to the footage and did not find it instructive
choice_e: not everyone who arrived on time was able to see the whole footage, because of interruptions caused by those arriving late
prediction_text: Players could have found it instructive without watching from the start; the ones who watched from the start and found it instructive might not be his players at all.
correct_answer_job: Name the overlooked possibility that severs the inference from 'found it instructive' back to 'watched from the start.'
conclusion: Some of Ramirez's players watched the footage from the opening whistle.
support: Some of his players found the footage instructive.
gap: Finding the footage instructive does not require having watched from the opening whistle.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns his players, but players who never saw the footage are outside the argument, which is about those who did find it instructive.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it addresses watching from the start, but the premise concerns only Ramirez's players, so what non-players experienced cannot expose the gap.
explanation_c: Choice C names the overlooked possibility: if the people who both watched from the start and found it instructive were not his players, then his players who found it instructive must have joined late, and the conclusion fails.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it introduces late arrivals, but this possibility is perfectly consistent with the conclusion and so does nothing to undermine the inference.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it complicates who saw what, but it does not address how players who found the footage instructive might have missed the opening.

stimulus: Media commentator: Reporters frequently settle on a story's framing chiefly on social grounds: because colleagues at other outlets have already embraced that framing, or because of the professional standing of whoever first advanced it in print. But this practice does journalism no harm whatever, since comparable social pressures shape the work that is done in every single occupation that people anywhere practice.
question_stem: The media commentator's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choice_a: takes for granted that the only legitimate reasons for adopting a story's framing are social ones
choice_b: fails to consider that reporters who adopt a framing for social reasons generally also weigh the available evidence before adopting it
choice_c: fails to consider that many reporters are unaware that they adopt story framings largely for social reasons
choice_d: takes for granted that whether a practice obstructs the goals of a particular occupation depends on how common comparable practices are in other occupations
choice_e: takes for granted that a practice that does not harm journalism will not harm any other occupation
prediction_text: That other fields have the same pressures says nothing about whether the practice frustrates journalism's own goals.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: assuming a practice's harmfulness to one field depends on how common the practice is elsewhere.
conclusion: Adopting story framings for social reasons does journalism no harm.
support: Comparable social pressures shape work in every occupation.
gap: Prevalence elsewhere does not determine whether a practice obstructs this field's goals.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because social reasons dominate the passage, but the commentator never claims they are the only legitimate reasons; that is not what the argument assumes.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it would soften the worry, but the argument's defect is its appeal to other occupations, not its silence about how reporters weigh evidence.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because awareness seems relevant to blame, but whether reporters notice the influence has no bearing on whether the practice harms journalism.
explanation_d: Choice D correctly names the error: the commentator infers harmlessness to journalism from the mere prevalence of similar pressures elsewhere, which leaves untouched whether the practice defeats journalism's own aims.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it also links journalism to other fields, but it reverses the argument's direction, which reasons from other occupations to journalism, not the other way around.

stimulus: Newsletter editor: Many candidates for our residents' association board campaign on a pledge to cut the dues that members pay. But residents in fact elect candidates who promise instead that the association will fund solutions to the problems residents complain about most. Funding solutions costs money, however, and the association's money can come only from dues. So the dues our members pay will seldom be substantially cut.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the newsletter editor's argument?
choice_a: Candidates never promise to do what they actually intend to do once they join the board.
choice_b: The problems that residents complain about most are problems about money.
choice_c: Dues in communities whose boards are appointed rather than elected are no more burdensome than dues in communities like this one.
choice_d: Candidates who promise to do what they sincerely believe ought to be done are seldom elected.
choice_e: Candidates who win seats on the board usually carry out the promises they made while campaigning.
prediction_text: The argument needs the elected candidates to actually do what they promised; otherwise dues might be cut anyway.
correct_answer_job: Add the fact that makes the winners' promises actually determine what happens to dues.
conclusion: Members' dues will seldom be substantially cut.
support: Residents elect candidates who promise funded solutions, and funding comes only from dues.
gap: Winners must actually carry out the promises on which they were elected.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns promises, but if winners ignore their promises entirely, the funded solutions might never be paid for, which weakens rather than strengthens the case.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns residents' complaints, but what the complaints are about does not affect whether funding them keeps dues high.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it compares dues across communities, but the argument concerns why dues stay high where boards are elected, not how they compare elsewhere.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns candidates and elections, but sincerity has no bearing on whether elected candidates' funded solutions keep dues from being cut.
explanation_e: Choice E most strengthens the argument: it secures the step the argument needs, since only if winners actually fund the solutions they promised will the association keep needing the dues that pay for them.

stimulus: Sales of powdered laundry detergent climbed sharply once the powder began to be sold in pre-measured pods, which spared customers the bother of scooping out each dose. Executives at a fertilizer company have begun to consider offering their plant food in pre-measured pods too. Just as it was with detergent in pods, this counts as a shrewd marketing decision on their part.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choice_a: Selling plant food in pre-measured pods will spare gardeners the bother of measuring out each dose.
choice_b: Before pods were introduced, surveys showed that customers were dissatisfied with how hard it was to scoop detergent out of the box.
choice_c: Many gardeners find that boxes of plant food are awkward to store on a shelf.
choice_d: Earlier changes to the packaging of plant food have often been well received by gardeners.
choice_e: Putting plant food into pods will create no greater manufacturing difficulty than putting detergent into pods created.
prediction_text: Detergent sold because pods made dosing easy; the analogy holds only if pods make plant food easy to dose too.
correct_answer_job: Confirm the analogy by showing the new packaging brings the same benefit that drove the original gain.
conclusion: Selling plant food in pre-measured pods is a shrewd marketing decision.
support: Pods made detergent easier to dose, and detergent sales rose.
gap: Pods must deliver the same ease-of-use gain for plant food that they delivered for detergent.
explanation_a: Choice A most strengthens the argument: the detergent's success came from the ease of dosing that pods provided, so establishing that pods bring gardeners that same ease makes the analogy hold.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it explains why detergent pods succeeded, but it says nothing about whether pods will do anything for plant food, which is what the conclusion is about.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it names a drawback of the current packaging, but easier storage is a different benefit from the ease of dosing that drove the detergent's sales.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it suggests gardeners accept change, but a general willingness to accept new packaging does not show that pods will repeat the detergent's particular success.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it removes an objection about production, but ease of manufacture does not show that customers will buy more plant food.

stimulus: Music historian: Scholars who write the history of a decade's recording industry must, naturally, examine the rosters and business strategies of that decade's labels. But scholars almost certainly examine labels that produced hit records more often than they examine labels that quietly folded. It is therefore reasonable to think that histories of the recording industry overstate how successful the labels of the past really were.
question_stem: Which one of the following would, if true, most support the music historian's argument?
choice_a: The particular missteps that cause a label to fail often cannot be inferred from surviving records of its activity.
choice_b: The contracts and session tapes of labels that folded are thrown out far more often than those of labels that endured.
choice_c: Scholars who read the first-person recollections of past executives inevitably bring present-day assumptions to them.
choice_d: The licensing filings that labels were required to submit provide a record more objective than the labels' own internal memos.
choice_e: Scholars who study the labels of the past are usually trained in effective music-business management.
prediction_text: If the paper trail of failed labels vanishes, scholars cannot study them, and histories skew toward successes.
correct_answer_job: Supply a fact explaining why unsuccessful labels are systematically underrepresented in the record.
conclusion: Histories of the recording industry overstate how successful past labels were.
support: Scholars study hit-making labels more often than labels that folded.
gap: Something must explain the systematic gap in what survives to be studied.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns failed labels, but the difficulty of diagnosing failure from records does not explain why scholars study failures less, nor why histories skew toward success.
explanation_b: Choice B most supports the argument: if the materials left by failed labels are routinely destroyed, then scholars are pushed toward studying successes, which is exactly why histories would overstate past success.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it names a bias, but a bias in interpreting recollections is not the selection effect the argument needs, which concerns which labels get studied at all.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it compares sources, but the relative objectivity of filings says nothing about whether failed labels are underrepresented among the labels scholars examine.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it describes the scholars, but their training does not explain a systematic tilt toward successful labels in the histories they write.

recipe_title: Weaken by Severing a Chain Link
stimulus: Hydrologist: Warming ocean temperatures are expected to make monsoon surges over valley V more frequent in the decades ahead, and such surges bring unusually heavy summer rainfall to the valley. Since frog populations in the valley typically climb during long stretches of continuous rain, we should expect average frog numbers in valley V to climb as well over the decades that lie ahead.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the hydrologist's argument?
choice_a: In valley V there is typically far less rainfall in winter than there is in summer.
choice_b: Frog populations in valley V often fall during long stretches in which there is no rain at all.
choice_c: In valley V, summers marked by unusually heavy rainfall have usually not included long stretches of continuous rain.
choice_d: In many valleys that get substantially more summer rain than valley V does, average frog populations are considerably lower than in valley V.
choice_e: Warmer ocean temperatures produce a number of effects besides making monsoon surges more frequent.
prediction_text: Heavy rain is not the same as sustained rain; if the heavy summers are not the long-continuous-rain kind, the frogs get no benefit.
correct_answer_job: Break the link between 'unusually heavy rainfall' and 'long stretches of continuous rain.'
conclusion: Average frog populations in valley V will climb.
support: More surges bring heavier summer rain, and frogs climb during long stretches of continuous rain.
gap: Heavy rainfall need not take the form of long continuous stretches.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns rainfall in the valley, but a contrast between the seasons leaves untouched whether heavier summer rain will come in continuous stretches.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links frogs to rain, but it reinforces the idea that rain drives frog numbers and so supports the argument rather than weakening it.
explanation_c: Choice C most weakens the argument: it severs the crucial link, since the wetter summers the hydrologist predicts would not be the continuous-rain kind that frog populations depend on.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it seems to detach rain from frogs, but conditions in other valleys may differ in many ways, so this does not undermine the reasoning about valley V.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it hints at complications, but unspecified additional effects do not challenge the step from heavier rainfall to more frogs.

recipe_title: Weaken by Attacking the Buyer Profile
stimulus: Although sales of graphic novels have climbed steadily over the past three years, we can confidently expect that trend to reverse itself before very long. Historically, more than three quarters of all the graphic novels sold in this country have gone to readers aged twelve through fifteen, a group whose total population is projected to shrink steadily over the coming decade.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument?
choice_a: Most people sixteen years of age or older have never bought a graphic novel.
choice_b: Library borrowing of graphic novels has fallen over the past three years.
choice_c: New technology will surely make entirely new entertainment options available over the coming decade.
choice_d: Most of the people who have bought graphic novels during the past three years are older than fifteen.
choice_e: The number of distinct graphic-novel genres available is unlikely to shrink in the near future.
prediction_text: If recent buyers are mostly older readers, a shrinking pool of young readers won't reverse the trend.
correct_answer_job: Show that the historical buyer profile no longer describes who is actually buying.
conclusion: The rise in graphic novel sales will reverse before long.
support: Most buyers historically were twelve to fifteen, and that group will shrink.
gap: The historical profile may no longer hold for current buyers.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns older readers, but it reinforces the idea that the young are the market, which strengthens rather than weakens the prediction.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns graphic novels, but borrowing is not buying, so a decline in borrowing does not bear on future sales.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because new competition sounds threatening, but if anything it supports a coming decline in sales rather than undermining it.
explanation_d: Choice D most weakens the argument: if recent buyers are mostly older than fifteen, then a shrinking population of twelve-to-fifteen-year-olds gives little reason to expect sales to fall.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because variety can affect sales, but a stable range of genres says nothing about whether the shrinking young readership will drag sales down.

recipe_title: Weaken by Showing the Research Has Another Use
stimulus: By transferring a gene taken from a hardy arctic moss into the cells of strawberry plants, researchers at an agricultural station have produced strawberries that survive hard frosts without damage. This whole line of research is worthless, however. Even if the berries themselves prove perfectly flavorful, shoppers will simply refuse to buy strawberries that carry the genes of a moss.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
choice_a: The berries from the new plants have not been tested to determine whether they are suitable for making preserves.
choice_b: Every year, strawberry fields in many growing districts are ruined by hard frosts.
choice_c: If growers ever sell fruit containing genetic material from another kind of plant, they will be required to disclose that fact.
choice_d: Some excellent strawberries are grown in districts whose springs are quite cool.
choice_e: The techniques developed in the course of this research could also be used to make strawberries frost-hardy by transferring genes from frost-hardy wild strawberry species.
prediction_text: If the same techniques can confer frost-hardiness using only strawberry genes, the work is valuable even if moss-gene berries never sell.
correct_answer_job: Show the research has value along a path the shoppers' objection does not touch.
conclusion: This line of research is worthless.
support: Shoppers will refuse to buy strawberries carrying moss genes.
gap: The research might yield frost-hardy berries without the objectionable foreign genes.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it raises a doubt about the berries, but an untested use does not show that the research has value despite shoppers' refusal.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it shows frost damage matters, but the argument grants that frost hardiness is desirable; the claim is that shoppers will not buy the resulting berries.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns the foreign genes, but mandatory disclosure would make shoppers' refusal more effective, which supports the argument rather than weakening it.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns cool-weather strawberries, but that good berries already grow in cool districts does not show this research has value.
explanation_e: Choice E most weakens the argument: if the same techniques can yield frost-hardy berries carrying only strawberry genes, the research is valuable even if shoppers reject berries with moss genes.

stimulus: Truffle orchards thrive only in chalky ground, and in very little else besides. Sandy ground, though seldom chalky on its own, can readily be blended with other materials to yield ground that is chalky throughout. Hence truffle orchards can be made to thrive in sandy ground.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choice_a: Sandy ground that has been blended with certain other materials is still sandy ground.
choice_b: Blending a chalky material with another type of material always yields chalky ground.
choice_c: Whenever sandy ground is blended with other materials, chalky ground results.
choice_d: Some crops do not thrive in chalky ground.
choice_e: Truffle orchards do as well in treated sandy ground as they do in naturally chalky ground.
prediction_text: If blending makes it stop being sandy ground, the conclusion about sandy ground would not follow.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for the blended ground still to count as sandy ground.
conclusion: Truffle orchards can be made to thrive in sandy ground.
support: Sandy ground can be blended with other materials to yield chalky ground.
gap: The blended, chalky ground must still be sandy ground.
explanation_a: Choice A is the required assumption: the conclusion is about sandy ground, so if blending turned the sandy ground into something no longer sandy, nothing would have been shown about sandy ground at all.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because blending and chalkiness are central, but the argument needs only that some blend of sandy ground is chalky, not that every such blend is.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting but far too strong: the argument requires only that sandy ground can be made chalky, not that blending always makes it so.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns chalky ground, but what other crops do is irrelevant to whether truffle orchards can be made to thrive in sandy ground.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it compares the two grounds, but the conclusion claims only that the orchards can be made to thrive, not that they do equally well.

stimulus: Harbor commissioners have denied that any of their decisions harmed the bay's oyster beds. The evidence points the other way. Three summers back, after heavy lobbying by a group of shipping firms, the commission struck down a longstanding rule that had barred the dumping of dredged silt in the bay's shallows. In the time since, dozens of the bay's oyster beds have been smothered under a thick blanket of silt, and beds that once yielded steadily now yield almost nothing.
question_stem: The argument relies on which one of the following assumptions?
choice_a: Had the shipping firms not urged the change, the commission would not have lifted the rule barring silt dumping.
choice_b: If the rule barring the dumping of dredged silt had not been lifted, considerably less silt would have settled over the oyster beds.
choice_c: The shipping firms that urged the change were among those whose dumping smothered the oyster beds.
choice_d: The commission is generally more responsive to pressure from shipping firms than to pressure from conservationists.
choice_e: The commissioners who deny that their decisions harmed the oyster beds do not really believe what they say.
prediction_text: The harm must be attributable to the repeal; if the silt would have arrived anyway, the decision harmed nothing.
correct_answer_job: Identify the causal link the argument needs between lifting the rule and the smothering.
conclusion: The commissioners' decisions harmed the bay's oyster beds.
support: After the rule was lifted, dozens of oyster beds were smothered under silt.
gap: Sequence alone does not establish that lifting the rule made the difference.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it explains why the rule was lifted, but the argument needs the repeal to have caused the harm, not an account of what caused the repeal.
explanation_b: Choice B is the required assumption: unless the repeal made a difference to how much silt reached the beds, the smothering cannot be laid at the commissioners' door and the argument collapses.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it ties the firms to the harm, but the argument blames the commission's decision, and it does not matter which particular firms did the dumping.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it fits the story, but a general tendency in the commission's responsiveness is not needed for this particular decision to have caused this harm.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the denials, but the argument shows the decisions did harm, and it needs nothing about whether the commissioners are being sincere.

stimulus: Ethics board member: A study is permissible if it would reasonably be expected to increase the total welfare of the people taking part in it. A study counts as impermissible exactly when, and only when, it would reasonably be expected to reduce the total welfare of the people taking part in it. Thus, studies that would reasonably be expected to leave the total welfare of their participants unchanged are permissible as well.
question_stem: The ethics board member's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: Only impermissible studies would reasonably be expected to reduce the total welfare of their participants.
choice_b: No study is both permissible and impermissible.
choice_c: Any study that is not impermissible is permissible.
choice_d: There are studies that would reasonably be expected to leave the total welfare of their participants unchanged.
choice_e: Only permissible studies have good outcomes.
prediction_text: A welfare-neutral study is not impermissible; to call it permissible we need everything not impermissible to be permissible.
correct_answer_job: Supply the principle that closes the gap between 'not impermissible' and 'permissible.'
conclusion: Studies expected to leave participants' total welfare unchanged are permissible.
support: Such studies would not reduce welfare, so by the biconditional they are not impermissible.
gap: Being not impermissible must guarantee being permissible.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it echoes the second rule, but it merely restates half of what is already given and does nothing to make a welfare-neutral study permissible.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it sounds like the needed tidy-up, but ruling out overlap still leaves room for a study that is neither permissible nor impermissible.
explanation_c: Choice C lets the conclusion follow: a welfare-neutral study would not reduce welfare, so it is not impermissible, and this principle then makes it permissible.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the very studies at issue, but asserting that such studies exist does not show that they are permissible.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links permissibility to results, but good outcomes play no part in the argument, so this cannot bridge the gap.

stimulus: Curator: Some historians hold that the first institution other than a monastery to lend books without charge to any resident was the Boston Public Library, founded in 1854. These historians are mistaken. During a shortage of schoolbooks in the mill town of Ashfield in 1791, the town could not afford to put up a library building. Instead a communal collection of books was housed in the town hall and lent, free of charge, to any resident who asked for one.
question_stem: The curator's conclusion is properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: Monasteries did not lend books without charge to residents at any time during the 1700s.
choice_b: Communal collections of books were not available to residents of Boston before 1854.
choice_c: The founding of the Boston Public Library was not prompted by a shortage of schoolbooks.
choice_d: The communal collection of books housed in Ashfield's town hall was an institution.
choice_e: Every town that lent books without charge during the 1700s left records showing that it did so.
prediction_text: The historians' claim is about institutions; the argument needs Ashfield's collection to have been one.
correct_answer_job: Supply the premise making the Ashfield collection count as the kind of thing the historians' claim is about.
conclusion: The historians are mistaken that Boston's 1854 library was the first such institution.
support: Ashfield's town-hall collection lent books free to any resident in 1791.
gap: The town-hall collection must qualify as an institution.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because monasteries are named, but the historians' claim already sets monasteries aside, so ruling out monastic lending does nothing for the curator's counterexample.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns Boston, but what Boston lacked before 1854 does not establish that Ashfield's collection was the sort of institution at issue.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because a shortage figures in the Ashfield story, but why Boston's library was founded has no bearing on whether Ashfield's collection came first.
explanation_d: Choice D enables the conclusion: the historians' claim concerns institutions, so only if Ashfield's town-hall collection was an institution does its free lending in 1791 show them mistaken.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because records make the case knowable, but the curator needs Ashfield's collection to qualify as an institution, not a guarantee that all such lending was recorded.

stimulus: Blind code review should be used whenever it is practical to do so on software teams. It helps head off the skewed judgments that so often arise from the opinions reviewers already hold about their colleagues, and reviewers plainly ought to be scrupulous about avoiding such skewed judgments.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?
choice_a: Reviewers' objectivity may be impeded when they judge code on the basis of opinions they already hold about their colleagues.
choice_b: Reviewers sometimes neglect to give adequate weight to the risk of judging code on the basis of prior opinions.
choice_c: Whenever it is practical, reviewers should refrain from judging code on the basis of previously formed opinions.
choice_d: Blind code review is often an effective way of securing objectivity in a software team.
choice_e: It is advisable for software teams to use blind code review in as high a proportion of their reviews as they can.
prediction_text: The recommendation to use blind review as widely as practical is the point; the rest explains why.
correct_answer_job: Identify the claim the rest of the passage is offered to support.
conclusion: Software teams should use blind code review whenever practical.
support: It prevents skewed judgments, which reviewers ought to avoid.
gap: Distinguish the recommendation from the reasons offered for it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it captures the passage's worry, but this is the reason offered in support, not the recommendation the passage is advancing.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it sounds like a criticism the passage might endorse, but the passage never says reviewers neglect this risk, so it cannot be the conclusion.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it is a recommendation, but the passage recommends a specific practice, blind review, rather than urging reviewers to set their opinions aside by an effort of will.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it praises blind review, but this states why blind review works, which the passage offers in support of its actual recommendation.
explanation_e: Choice E is the main conclusion: the claims about skewed judgments and reviewers' obligations are offered precisely to support this recommendation to use blind review wherever practical.

stimulus: One hears constantly nowadays that pocket calculators have eaten away the arithmetic skills that mental computation once demanded and sharpened. But two centuries ago the grievance was that certain skills, such as the prodigious mental reckoning that was intrinsic to a merchant's training, were being wiped out by the spread of printed multiplication tables. So what lies ahead of us is probably a mere shift in the habits of the mind rather than their decay.
question_stem: The reference to the grievance of two centuries ago that prodigious mental reckoning was being wiped out plays which one of the following roles in the argument?
choice_a: an example of a change in culture that did not necessarily have a damaging effect on the mind overall
choice_b: evidence supporting the claim that the arithmetic skills sharpened by mental computation are being eaten away by calculators
choice_c: an illustration of the general hypothesis, advanced here, that mental abilities cannot be separated from the tools with which people compute
choice_d: evidence that the claim that arithmetic skills are being lost is entirely unwarranted
choice_e: possible evidence, raised and then set aside, that supporters of the criticized view might have cited
prediction_text: The old complaint is offered as a past case where a similar change altered rather than ruined the mind.
correct_answer_job: Identify what work the historical grievance does: it is a precedent for harmless change.
conclusion: What lies ahead is a shift in mental habits rather than their decay.
support: An earlier, parallel complaint accompanied a change that did not ruin the mind.
gap: Distinguish a cited precedent from the hypothesis it is used against.
explanation_a: Choice A correctly describes the role: the old grievance is cited as a precedent in which a comparable change altered how people think without ruining their minds, which is what supports the conclusion.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the two complaints are parallel, but the old grievance is used against the modern worry, not as evidence for it.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because tools and abilities are linked in the passage, but no such general hypothesis is advanced; the old grievance serves as a reassuring precedent.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting but too strong: the passage allows that skills change, concluding only that the mind is altered rather than degraded, not that the worry is baseless.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the grievance is introduced with 'but,' yet the passage embraces it as a precedent rather than raising and dismissing it.

stimulus: Rivera's Feed Barn sells a very large volume of hay each season. The vast bulk of it is sold in bales to commercial buyers, and most of those bales go to horse stables. Rivera's also sells grooming tools, most of which are bought at retail by hobby riders.
question_stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choice_a: Rivera's earns a larger profit from selling hay than from selling all of its other products combined.
choice_b: A bale of hay bought from Rivera's is more likely to have been bought by a horse stable than by a hobby rider.
choice_c: Among Rivera's regular customers there are more commercial buyers than hobby riders.
choice_d: Rivera's sells a few grooming tools in bulk to horse stables.
choice_e: Most of those who make regular bulk purchases from Rivera's have never bought a grooming tool there.
prediction_text: Most hay goes to commercial buyers, and most of those are stables, so a bale most likely went to a stable.
correct_answer_job: Draw the supported claim about which buyer a given bale most likely went to.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Most hay is sold to commercial buyers, most of whom are stables.
gap: Keep the inference to hay, and to comparative likelihood.
inference_or_resolution: A given bale of hay more likely went to a horse stable than to a hobby rider.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because hay dominates by volume, but nothing is said about profit, which can differ sharply from volume.
explanation_b: Choice B is most strongly supported: the vast bulk of hay goes to commercial buyers, and most of those are horse stables, so any given bale most likely went to a stable.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because commercial buyers take most of the hay, but a few large buyers can account for a large volume, so their number cannot be inferred.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because both products and both buyer types appear, but the passage says most tools are bought at retail and never says any are sold in bulk.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the two products have different buyer profiles, but nothing rules out bulk hay buyers also purchasing grooming tools.

stimulus: A truly static display form, a mosaic for example, is one whose appreciation makes no essential demand on time. Viewing a mosaic does take time, of course, yet its portions may be taken in in any order whatever, and no particular span must be spent before it. By contrast, most display forms, such as film and dance, have time built into them at the root: they call for enactment, and so must be taken in through a fixed order and across a roughly fixed span. A comic strip, though printed and so seemingly static, must in fact be enacted, even when the enactment is only a silent reading panel by panel.
question_stem: If the statements above are true, then on the basis of them which one of the following must be true?
choice_a: A comic strip is less like film than it is like a mosaic.
choice_b: Spatiality and temporality are mutually exclusive components of display forms.
choice_c: Truly static display forms do not essentially involve enactment.
choice_d: Display forms that must be examined for a long period in order to be understood are essentially temporal.
choice_e: Anything capable of being enacted is either cinematic or choreographic, or both.
prediction_text: Enactment brings a fixed order and span, which time-independent forms lack; so truly static forms do not require enactment.
correct_answer_job: Deduce the guaranteed claim linking static forms and enactment.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Enactment implies fixed order and span; static forms have neither.
gap: Chain the definition of static with what enactment requires.
inference_or_resolution: Truly static display forms do not essentially involve enactment.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because comic strips are printed like mosaics, but the passage groups the comic strip with forms that must be enacted, and it makes no overall similarity ranking.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the passage contrasts two kinds of forms, but it never says a form cannot have both spatial and temporal aspects.
explanation_c: Choice C must be true: enactment imposes a fixed order and a roughly fixed span, and in a truly static form time plays no essential part, so such a form cannot essentially require enactment.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it invokes time, but taking a long time to grasp a work differs from requiring a fixed span, so this does not follow.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because film and dance are the examples given, but the comic strip is enacted too, so enactable things are not confined to those two kinds.

stimulus: For years, Larkspur High had the highest average entrance-exam score of any school in its district. This year Larkspur has only the third highest average score in the district. Therefore students at Larkspur must be scoring lower on the exam now than Larkspur students used to score.
question_stem: Which one of the following arguments demonstrates most effectively by parallel reasoning that the argument above is flawed?
choice_a: Because Omar's sapling needs less water than his shrub does, the sapling must be hardier than the shrub.
choice_b: Because Omar's sapling was planted a week before his shrub, Omar must have acquired the sapling first.
choice_c: Because Omar's sapling drops fewer leaves than his shrub does, the sapling is unlikely to become bare.
choice_d: Because Omar's sapling was taller than his shrub a while ago but is now shorter than the shrub, the sapling must have shrunk.
choice_e: Because Omar's sapling has grown closer to his shrub recently, the shrub must have grown closer to the sapling.
prediction_text: A parallel case where something falls in rank only because the others rose, so no decline occurred.
correct_answer_job: Match the error: treating a drop in relative rank as proof of a drop in absolute value.
conclusion: Larkspur students are scoring lower than they used to.
support: Larkspur fell from first to third in the district.
gap: Rank can fall while the underlying value holds steady or rises.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it compares two plants, but it infers hardiness from water needs, which is not the rank-versus-value error committed above.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it reasons from timing, but it involves no change in rank over time and so does not expose the flaw in question.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it draws a conclusion from a comparison, but it is a single-time comparison with no shift in ranking, so the parallel fails.
explanation_d: Choice D parallels the flaw exactly: the sapling's fall in relative height is treated as proof that it lost height, when the shrub may simply have grown faster, just as rival schools may simply have improved.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it involves a changing relation, but it turns on the symmetry of 'closer to,' not on mistaking a fall in rank for a fall in value.

stimulus: Of all the fuels households commonly burn for heat, coal gives off the most soot per unit of heat produced, and soot adds to the pollution of the air indoors. Yet when households that give up burning coal are tracked carefully for a full year afterward, the pollution of the air inside their homes is often found to rise rather than fall.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?
choice_a: Although coal gives off a great deal of soot, it also burns steadily and cheaply, which benefits households overall.
choice_b: Among households with poor ventilation, coal burning and high indoor pollution are strongly correlated.
choice_c: Households that give up burning coal generally do so out of concern about the quality of the air they breathe.
choice_d: Many households that burn coal regularly have about the same level of indoor pollution as households that have never burned coal.
choice_e: Many households that give up burning coal take up burning unseasoned wood, which is heavy in fine particulates, and fine particulates worsen indoor air more than soot does.
prediction_text: They switch to a fuel that produces something worse for indoor air than soot.
correct_answer_job: Find the fact that lets giving up the sootiest fuel still worsen the air.
conclusion: (discrepancy to explain)
support: Coal is sootiest, yet quitting coal often raises indoor pollution.
gap: Another pollutant, from the replacement fuel, must matter more than soot.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it defends coal, but other virtues of coal do not explain why indoor air gets worse once households stop burning it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links coal to pollution, but it deepens the puzzle rather than resolving it, since it makes quitting coal look even more helpful.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it explains why households quit, but their motive does not explain why the air actually worsens afterward.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it compares pollution levels, but it does not explain a rise in pollution following the switch away from coal.
explanation_e: Choice E most helps resolve the discrepancy: households replace the sootiest fuel with one that emits a pollutant that harms indoor air even more, so quitting coal can leave the air dirtier.

stimulus: Athletic director: I intend to assemble a winning relay squad for this season by picking out gifted, self-reliant runners who would rather not train as part of a close-knit group. This approach simply cannot fail, because a recent study shows that where a shared goal is present, the adaptability of loosely bound squads lets them perform better than close-knit squads do.
question_stem: The reasoning in the athletic director's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choice_a: overlooks the possibility that runners who would rather not train in close-knit squads may have trouble committing to a shared goal
choice_b: presumes that factors which are together sufficient for success are also each necessary for success
choice_c: relies on a study that bears no apparent relevance to the plan the director proposes
choice_d: takes for granted that adaptable squads always perform significantly better than rigid ones
choice_e: confuses the goals the director is trying to achieve with the goals that the squad's members must hold in common
prediction_text: Runners who avoid close-knit training may be just the ones who will not commit to a shared goal, so the study's finding may not apply.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: the study's benefit requires a shared goal, which the chosen runners may not supply.
conclusion: The director's approach to assembling the squad cannot fail.
support: Loosely bound squads with a shared goal outperform close-knit squads.
gap: The runners chosen may never form the shared goal the study's finding depends on.
explanation_a: Choice A correctly names the error: the study's advantage holds only where a shared goal is present, and the very trait the director selects for may prevent that condition from being met.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because conditions for success are in play, but the director never treats jointly sufficient factors as individually necessary; the flaw lies elsewhere.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the study is doing heavy lifting, but the study is plainly relevant to loosely bound squads; the trouble is whether its condition will hold here.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it overstates the study, but the argument does not need adaptability to win always; its defect concerns the shared goal the study presupposes.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because two sorts of goals appear, but the director does not run them together; the error is ignoring that the chosen runners may not share any goal.

stimulus: Fleet owner: In this province, strict rules forbid a boat captain from working any cove in which a rare harbor seal has been sighted. These rules turn the presence of a seal into a costly burden for many captains, and so give captains reason not to look after the seals in the waters they fish. It follows that the seals would very likely suffer no harm if the rules on cove fishing were lifted.

support: The analogy maps behavior toward a life onto behavior toward the voyage.
gap: Keep the object of attention the voyage, mirroring the career case.
inference_or_resolution: Crew near a voyage’s end become absorbed in the record of the voyage just ending.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because careers are named in the analogy, but the analogy maps behavior onto the voyage, so the object of their attention should be the voyage.
explanation_b: Choice B completes the analogy correctly: as someone near a career's end reviews that career, so the crew near a voyage's end dwell on the voyage itself.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting as a natural human response, but the analogy is to looking back over what is ending, not ahead to what comes next.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the analogy invokes a life's end, but it takes the comparison literally rather than tracking the behavior it describes.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it does look back at the voyage, but the analogy speaks of reviewing milestones generally, not of second-guessing mishaps.

stimulus: Editorialist: Trade papers seldom report in depth on the decisions of the port authority, and the authority's business is usually conducted behind closed doors. Each of these factors tends to isolate the authority's officers from the dockworkers they serve. That isolation lowers the odds that any given petition from dockworkers will meet with a favorable response from the officers, and this in turn leaves dockworkers disinclined to petition the authority at all.
question_stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the editorialist's statements?
choice_a: Petitions from dockworkers would be likely to draw a favorable response if the authority's officers were less isolated from them.
choice_b: The authority's business should be conducted less secretively, because doing so would avoid discouraging petitions.
choice_c: More frequent in-depth reporting on the port authority's decisions would reduce at least one source of discouragement from petitioning the authority.
choice_d: The most important factor in a dockworker's decision to petition is the chance that the petition will draw a favorable response.
choice_e: If dockworkers were not discouraged from petitioning, the authority's officers would become less isolated from them.
prediction_text: Thin coverage is one of two isolating factors, so more coverage would cut one source of discouragement.
correct_answer_job: Read off what removing one named factor would do to the discouragement.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Both factors isolate officers, and isolation discourages petitions.
gap: Attend to 'at least one source' rather than a claim about the whole chain.
inference_or_resolution: More in-depth reporting would reduce at least one source of discouragement.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it reverses the stated chain, but the passage says isolation reduces the chance of a favorable response, not that less isolation makes one likely.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because secrecy is one culprit, but the passage describes effects and does not support a recommendation about what ought to be done.
explanation_c: Choice C is most strongly supported: thin coverage is one of the two factors that isolate the officers, and isolation is what discourages petitions, so more coverage would remove one such source.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because that chance figures in the chain, but nothing ranks it against the other considerations a dockworker might weigh.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links the same terms, but it runs the causal chain backward, from petitioning to isolation rather than the other way.

stimulus: Chef: I have never been given a stall at the town market, even though several of my dishes are widely loved and sell out at every fair I enter. I know five other well-liked cooks who applied for stalls and fared no better than I did. Thus, being given a stall at the town market proves that a cook is no good.
question_stem: The pattern of flawed reasoning in which one of the following arguments most closely resembles that in the chef's argument?
choice_a: Engineer: I have never been given a booth at the Maker Expo, though several of my devices hold patents and have sold briskly. Other inventors report the same. Therefore the organizers are choosing booths on some basis other than commercial success.
choice_b: Baker: I am always given a booth at the Maker Expo, even though shoppers find my pastries strange and unappetizing. Other bakers report the same. Thus being given a booth proves that one's baking does not suit most people's taste.
choice_c: Curator: The same sculptures that were passed over one year at the Regional Salon took the top award another year. So the sculptures are not judged entirely on merit.
choice_d: Volunteer: The parks board never takes my petitions seriously, even when most residents sign them. Others have brought forward widely signed petitions, and the board has not seriously weighed theirs either. So the parks board takes only worthless petitions seriously.
choice_e: Courier: When I plan my routes most carefully, dispatch cuts my bonus. When I rush, they send me thank-you notes. I conclude that dispatch wants to discourage careful planning.
prediction_text: Find the argument that leaps from good applicants being rejected to the conclusion that only bad ones are accepted.
correct_answer_job: Match the error: from 'the good are refused' infer 'those accepted are bad.'
conclusion: Being given a stall proves a cook is no good.
support: Several popular cooks, including the speaker, were refused stalls.
gap: That good cooks are refused does not show the accepted ones are bad.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it opens identically, but it concludes only that some other criterion is in use, which is a far weaker and non-parallel step.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because its conclusion has the same shape, but its speaker is always accepted rather than always refused, so the premises run the opposite way.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it also attacks a selection process, but it reasons from inconsistent verdicts on the same works, not from good work being refused.
explanation_d: Choice D parallels the flaw exactly: from the fact that worthy petitions are refused a hearing, it leaps to the claim that whatever is heard must be worthless, just as the chef leaps from refusals to the worthlessness of those accepted.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because good work again goes unrewarded, but it infers an intention behind the pattern rather than a verdict on those who are rewarded.

stimulus: When competing for a research grant, scientists sometimes pledge to pursue particular lines of work that they privately believe would be of no benefit at all to their field. Once the grant has actually been awarded, however, a researcher who has won it should try to carry out any pledge at all that the researcher believes would not set the field back.
question_stem: The principle stated above, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?
choice_a: Osei won a grant by pledging to digitize the archive. Once funded, it became plain that digitizing would require cutting fieldwork that colleagues value. Thus Osei should not digitize the archive.
choice_b: Park believes that building the new wind tunnel will not benefit the field, but that pledging to build it will help Park win the grant, and that Park's winning is in the field's best interest. Thus it is not wrong for Park to make the pledge.
choice_c: Lund pledged to preserve funding for the seed vault. Once funded, Lund came to doubt that keeping the pledge would provide any benefit to the field. Thus Lund should break the pledge.
choice_d: Iqbal pledged to restructure the laboratory. Once funded, Iqbal concluded that restructuring would set the field back. Thus Iqbal never should have pledged to restructure the laboratory.
