choice_e: Ferrar pledged to expand the fossil survey while competing for the grant, though Ferrar believed at the time that expanding it would set the field back. Once funded, Ferrar concluded that expanding the survey would in fact benefit the field. So Ferrar should carry out the pledge.
prediction_text: The principle licenses keeping a pledge once the researcher believes it harmless, whatever was believed before.
correct_answer_job: Find the case where the funded researcher now believes the pledge would not set the field back.
conclusion: (principle application)
support: The principle keys on the researcher's post-award belief.
gap: Match the belief state the principle requires.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because Osei has second thoughts, but the principle speaks to setting the field back, not to whether colleagues would be displeased.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns making a pledge, but the principle governs whether a funded researcher should keep a pledge, not whether making one is permissible.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because Lund's belief changed, but doubting a benefit is not believing the pledge would set the field back, so the principle does not license breaking it.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the belief now points at harm, but the principle says nothing about whether the pledge ought to have been made in the first place.
explanation_e: Choice E is justified by the principle: Ferrar is a funded researcher who now believes the pledge would not set the field back, which is precisely the case in which the principle says the pledge should be carried out.

stimulus: Columnist: Practitioners of every trade agree, with near unanimity, that a master craftsman is morally bound to shield an apprentice from ruin. So hardly anyone would object when a master, knowing full well that an apprentice has been falsely blamed for a botched commission, conceals that apprentice from the guild inspectors who arrive to seize the apprentice's tools. What follows is that people generally must also grant that standing in the way of an inspector doing his rounds is, on occasion, the morally correct thing to do.
question_stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that this argument
choice_a: fails to consider the possibility that other moral principles would be widely recognized as overriding any obligation to shield an apprentice from ruin
choice_b: uses a single type of example for the purpose of justifying a broad generalization
choice_c: presumes, without providing justification, that letting inspectors seize an innocent apprentice's tools serves rather than obstructs fairness
choice_d: takes for granted that there is no moral obligation to comply with the rules of one's guild
choice_e: takes for granted that the master in the example is not mistaken about the apprentice's innocence
prediction_text: Many would say competing principles override the duty to shield an apprentice, so the sweeping acceptance does not follow.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: the accepted duty may be widely thought to yield to other principles.
conclusion: It is likely widely accepted that obstructing guild inspectors is sometimes morally right.
support: Few would deny that a master should hide a falsely blamed apprentice.
gap: Other widely held principles may be recognized as overriding the duty to shield an apprentice.
explanation_a: Choice A correctly names the error: the columnist leans on near-universal acceptance of one duty, yet people who accept that duty may widely hold other principles that override it in just these cases.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because one case carries the argument, but the trouble is not the number of examples; even many such cases would leave the overriding-principle worry untouched.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because fairness is in the background, but the columnist need not presume anything about what serves fairness; the gap concerns competing duties.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting and near the mark, but the columnist does not deny such an obligation; the flaw is failing to weigh principles that might override the duty invoked.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting, but the example stipulates that the master knows the apprentice was falsely blamed, so no such assumption is being smuggled in.

stimulus: Shopper: According to the newest issue of the Halloran Review, the boxed teas sold by Brightleaf are essentially devoid of any flavor at all. But Marrow Teas, the largest commercial rival Brightleaf has, is the party that commissions the Halloran Review, and its publicity office signs off on each draft before any of it appears in print. Given how plainly the review is slanted, we may conclude that Brightleaf's boxed teas really are full of flavor.
question_stem: The reasoning in the shopper's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choice_a: draws a conclusion based solely on an unrepresentative sample of Brightleaf's products
choice_b: treats evidence that a report is apparently biased as though it were evidence that the report's claims are false
choice_c: fails to take into account the possibility that Brightleaf has as much motivation to create bad publicity for Marrow as Marrow has to create bad publicity for Brightleaf
choice_d: fails to provide evidence that Marrow's boxed teas are not more flavorful than Brightleaf's are
choice_e: presumes, without providing justification, that Marrow's publicity office would not approve a draft that was hostile to Marrow's own products
prediction_text: A biased source may still be right; showing bias does not show the opposite of what it says.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: bias impugns a report's credibility but does not establish that its claims are false.
conclusion: Brightleaf's teas really are full of flavor.
support: The review disparaging them is obviously biased.
gap: Discrediting a claim's source does not establish the claim's negation.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because only boxed teas are discussed, but the shopper's conclusion is about the very products the review examined, so sampling is not the error.
explanation_b: Choice B correctly names the error: bias gives a reason to distrust the review, but the shopper leaps from distrust all the way to the opposite conclusion, which bias never supports.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the rivalry cuts both ways, but Brightleaf's motives do not bear on the leap from the review's bias to the falsity of its findings.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the rival's teas go unmentioned, but the conclusion concerns Brightleaf's teas alone, so no comparison is owed.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because approval is mentioned, but the argument does not rest on that presumption; the fault is inferring falsity from bias.

stimulus: Library director: At a recent forum on nonprofit governance, several cybersecurity specialists maintained that the gravest danger now facing large institutions such as museums and libraries is unauthorized access to private records. In light of that testimony, we should make guarding our patrons' privacy our foremost priority.
question_stem: The library director's argument is most vulnerable to which one of the following objections?
choice_a: The argument confuses the causes of a problem with the appropriate solutions to that problem.
choice_b: The argument assumes that a correlation between two phenomena is evidence that one causes the other.
choice_c: The argument relies on the testimony of experts whose expertise is not shown to be broad enough to support their general claim.
choice_d: The argument draws a general conclusion about a group based on data about an unrepresentative sample of that group.
choice_e: The argument infers that a property belonging to large institutions belongs to all institutions.
prediction_text: Security specialists can say what security dangers exist; whether that danger outranks every other is beyond their field.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: the experts' authority is narrower than the sweeping claim they make.
conclusion: Guarding patrons' privacy should be the library's foremost priority.
support: Cybersecurity specialists called unauthorized access the gravest danger.
gap: Expertise in security does not qualify one to rank all dangers an institution faces.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because a problem and a response both appear, but the director does not mistake one for the other.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting as a stock error, but no correlation figures in the reasoning at all.
explanation_c: Choice C correctly names the error: specialists in cybersecurity are placed to judge security risks, not to rank that danger above every other danger a museum or library faces.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because 'several specialists' sounds like a sample, but the specialists are the authority relied upon, not a sample of institutions.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because large institutions are named, but the director draws a conclusion about this library, which is itself such an institution.

stimulus: Auction catalogs brim with glowing appraisals and with assurances about provenance; yet we should keep in mind why the house prints them at all, which is to draw the highest bids it can. Clearly, then, these appraisals are self-serving, and the assurances made in them are untrustworthy.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument above?
choice_a: The argument presumes, without providing justification, that if an assurance is not self-serving, then that assurance is trustworthy.
choice_b: The argument presumes, without providing justification, that assurances made for self-serving reasons are never honored.
choice_c: The argument confuses the effect of an action with its cause.
choice_d: The argument overlooks the fact that an assurance need not be untrustworthy just because the party that issued it had an ulterior motive for doing so.
choice_e: The argument overlooks the fact that an auction house that issues assurances for self-serving reasons may nonetheless deserve the business it seeks.
prediction_text: An assurance issued for gain can still be perfectly accurate.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: a self-serving motive does not make the assurance unreliable.
conclusion: The assurances in auction catalogs are untrustworthy.
support: They are printed to draw the highest bids.
gap: Ulterior motive does not entail unreliability.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it inverts the reasoning, but the argument never claims anything about assurances that are not self-serving.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting and close, but the conclusion is that the assurances are untrustworthy, not the stronger claim that they are never honored.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting as a stock error, but nothing in the argument reverses a cause and an effect.
explanation_d: Choice D correctly names the flaw: a house that stands to profit may nonetheless describe a lot accurately, so the self-serving motive alone cannot show the assurances are unreliable.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it grants the motive while resisting the verdict, but whether the house deserves business is not what the argument concludes.

stimulus: The Marrow River flows westward into the Coral Sea from its headwaters in the eastern highlands. Rising between the Marrow's basin and the Gulf that lies east of it, the Ridgeback Range today seals the two apart. Yet certain freshwater snails that inhabit the Marrow are descended from now-extinct brackish snails known to have lived in the Gulf but never in the Coral Sea. On these grounds a number of scientists have put forward the conjecture that the Marrow River once ran eastward, emptying into the Gulf.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, provides additional evidence in support of the hypothesis that the Marrow River once flowed eastward into the Gulf?
choice_a: In many cases, freshwater and brackish snails that share certain characteristics do not in fact share a common ancestor.
choice_b: Many snail species that inhabit the Coral Sea are related to species known to inhabit the Gulf.
choice_c: The Ridgeback Range extends from the northernmost to the southernmost limits of the region.
choice_d: There are very few snail species known to be able to survive in both fresh and brackish water.
choice_e: Most of the fossilized remains of the now-extinct brackish snails from the Gulf date to a period prior to the formation of the Ridgeback Range.
prediction_text: If the Gulf snails lived before the Ridgeback rose, the river could have carried them west before the barrier formed.
correct_answer_job: Add a fact showing the ancestral snails could have reached the Marrow before the range existed.
conclusion: The Marrow once flowed eastward into the Gulf.
support: Marrow snails descend from snails found only in the Gulf.
gap: The ancestry requires a route that existed before the mountains blocked it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns snail ancestry, but by loosening the link between shared traits and shared descent it weakens the argument rather than supporting it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links the two bodies of water, but it suggests the Marrow snails could have arrived by way of the Coral Sea, which cuts against the hypothesis.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the barrier matters, but the range's present extent says nothing about whether the river once ran east before the range arose.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the two habitats, but it does not explain how Gulf ancestors reached the Marrow at all.
explanation_e: Choice E supports the hypothesis: the ancestral snails flourished before the mountains rose, so an eastward-flowing Marrow could have carried their descendants inland while a route still existed.

stimulus: Editorial: Any guild is endangered by division into ranks of widely differing pay between which there is little movement. Divisions of that kind embolden quarrelsome factions, and such factions obstruct sound governance. Because a guild whose trade expands affords its members more openings to better their standing, guilds ought to adopt policies that keep trade steadily expanding.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reasoning in the editorial?
choice_a: Expanding trade produces a proportionally greater rise in earnings for members at the lowest pay ranks than for members at other ranks.
choice_b: Discord within a guild tends to widen the inequities in how its members are paid.
choice_c: Quarrelsome factions are sometimes willing to set aside their differences to back policies conducive to expanding trade.
choice_d: Expanding trade cannot occur without significant investment by members at the highest pay ranks.
choice_e: The presence of quarrelsome factions can be an obstacle to expanding a guild's trade.
prediction_text: Expansion helps only if it lifts the lowest ranks relatively more, closing the gap the editorial fears.
correct_answer_job: Add the fact that expansion actually narrows the rank divisions rather than widening them.
conclusion: Guilds should adopt policies ensuring steady expansion of trade.
support: Expansion gives members chances to better their standing.
gap: Expansion must reduce, not deepen, the pay divisions.
explanation_a: Choice A most strengthens the reasoning: the danger is wide pay divisions with little movement, so expansion helps precisely if it raises the lowest ranks fastest and narrows those divisions.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links discord and pay gaps, but it runs from discord to inequity, whereas the editorial needs expansion to shrink inequity.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it makes the policy adoptable, but that factions would support expansion does not show expansion cures the divisions.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns expansion, but a precondition for expansion says nothing about whether expansion narrows the ranks.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because both elements appear, but it makes factions block expansion, which threatens the remedy rather than supporting it.

recipe_title: Strengthen by Confirming in the Field
stimulus: The burrows occupied by striped dormice frequently hold gnawed hazel leaves together with gnawed tansy stems. Because the dormice are known to eat only the hazel, the tansy is probably carried in to serve as a fumigant, cutting down parasites such as mites. This view is backed by a trial in which some mite eggs were incubated among torn hazel leaves and others among torn tansy stems. The hatching rate among the hazel leaves was close to nine in ten, but among the tansy stems only one egg in four ever hatched.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choice_a: Striped dormice that burrow near hazel thickets almost always have hazel leaves in their burrows.
choice_b: Most striped-dormouse burrows that contain no gnawed tansy are overrun with mites.
choice_c: The striped dormouse is the only rodent that has been found to keep gnawed tansy in its burrow.
choice_d: Mites more commonly live on the bodies of striped dormice than in the burrows those dormice occupy.
choice_e: Tansy stems are generally more difficult for striped dormice to gather than hazel leaves are.
prediction_text: If burrows without tansy are mite-ridden, the laboratory effect holds where it matters.
correct_answer_job: Confirm in real burrows that the tansy is what keeps mites down.
conclusion: The tansy stems are carried in as a fumigant against mites.
support: Far fewer mite eggs hatch among tansy than among hazel.
gap: The trial result must be shown to operate in actual burrows.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns burrow contents, but the ready availability of hazel says nothing about what the tansy is for.
explanation_b: Choice B most strengthens the argument: burrows lacking tansy suffer the very infestation tansy is said to prevent, which is exactly what the fumigant explanation predicts in the field.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it singles out the behavior, but whether other rodents do it has no bearing on why the dormouse does.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because mites are the target, but where the mites reside does not show that the tansy in the burrow suppresses them.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the tansy, but the effort of gathering it does not establish that its purpose in the burrow is to repel mites.

recipe_title: Weaken by Supplying the Base Rate
stimulus: Letter to the editor: A deplorable partiality toward motor racing, and against local rowing, is on display in these pages every week. In the past twelve months this paper has printed upward of six race reports for every single report on rowing.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choice_a: Some newspapers run no reports on rowing at all.
choice_b: The paper employs six racing writers but only one rowing writer.
choice_c: The number of races held last year was considerably greater than the number of rowing events held locally.
choice_d: The paper does not have the space in its sports section to report on every race held or every rowing event held locally.
choice_e: The paper ran more reports on rowing last year than it ran two years ago.
prediction_text: If far more races happen than rowing events, proportional coverage would look just like this.
correct_answer_job: Supply a base rate that explains the disparity without bias.
conclusion: The sports page is biased against local rowing.
support: It ran six times as many race reports as rowing reports.
gap: The counts must be compared against how many events of each kind occurred.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it makes this paper look better, but what other papers do says nothing about whether this paper's ratio reflects bias.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it explains the disparity, but a lopsided staff is itself a sign of the very bias charged, so it supports the argument.
explanation_c: Choice C most weakens the argument: if races vastly outnumber rowing events, then running more race reports reflects what happened rather than any bias in the paper.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it constrains coverage, but a shortage of space applies to both sports and does not explain the lopsided ratio.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because rowing coverage improved, but an increase over time leaves the current disparity, and the charge of bias, untouched.

recipe_title: Weaken by Offering a Rival Function
stimulus: An abyssal sea urchin dwelling nine hundred meters beneath the Ross Sea turns out to carry receptors keenly attuned to blue-green light. No such light reaches so far down from the sun overhead. Supposing these receptors arose as an adaptation to life in the deep, their function is probably to pick up the glow thrown off by creatures that make their own light. Granting as much, and noting that the urchin gives off no light of its own, we may conclude that it probably feeds on glowing prey.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the argument?
choice_a: A trait that serves no function at all tends to be lost over many generations.
choice_b: Prey is scarce at the depth where these urchins are found.
choice_c: The urchins can locate others of their own kind by chemical cues rather than by sight.
choice_d: The abyssal sea urchin's most dangerous predators are bioluminescent.
choice_e: Sensitivity to blue-green light takes many generations to develop.
prediction_text: If the urchin's predators glow, the receptors more plausibly serve escape than hunting.
correct_answer_job: Supply a rival purpose for the receptors that fits the facts as well or better.
conclusion: The urchin feeds on bioluminescent prey.
support: Its receptors likely detect the glow of living things, and it does not glow itself.
gap: The glow detected could belong to predators rather than prey.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns adaptation, but a general remark about useless traits leaves the leap from detecting glow to hunting prey untouched.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because scarce prey seems to threaten the hunting story, but scarcity does not show the receptors serve some other purpose.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns how urchins sense things, but finding their own kind by smell says nothing about what the light receptors are for.
explanation_d: Choice D most weakens the argument: if the creatures that hunt the urchin are the ones that glow, its receptors are at least as plausibly for evading predators as for hunting prey.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the receptors' origin, but how long they took to evolve does not bear on what they are used for.

stimulus: Fitting ski lifts with automatic stop sensors may cut a resort's insurance costs, but it does not make the lifts safer. Incidents actually rise at lifts that have sensors: fewer riders are dragged, but far more are bumped by chairs that halt abruptly.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?
choice_a: Stop sensors cost far less to install than most other lift-safety measures do.
choice_b: The sensors are sometimes triggered by blowing snow rather than by a rider in difficulty.
choice_c: Riders who are dragged are usually those who boarded the lift carelessly.
choice_d: Many bumps by halted chairs are never reported to the resort.
choice_e: Being dragged by a moving lift is a far graver threat to life than being bumped by a chair that has halted.
prediction_text: If dragging is far deadlier than a bump, the sensors save lives even as incidents rise.
correct_answer_job: Show the trade favors safety despite the higher incident count.
conclusion: Automatic stop sensors do not make lifts safer.
support: Incidents rise: fewer draggings, more bumps.
gap: A rise in minor incidents may be outweighed by a fall in grave ones.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it favors the sensors, but their low cost has nothing to do with whether they make riders safer.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns the sensors, but a spurious trigger does not bear on the overall harm the sensors prevent or cause.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it discusses dragging, but who is at fault does not affect whether fewer draggings make the lift safer overall.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the bumps, but under-reporting would mean even more bumps occur, which does not help the sensors' case.
explanation_e: Choice E most weakens the argument: if the incidents the sensors prevent are far deadlier than the ones they cause, the lifts become safer even though total incidents rise.

stimulus: A traditional view of the Denisovans holds that they lacked any capacity for symbolic thought. Fresh evidence now tells against that view. Applying a newly devised dating method, researchers established that a carved bone flute recovered from a Siberian cave dates back a minimum of 45,000 years. The likeliest maker of that flute, then, was a Denisovan.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choice_a: The ability to carve a bone flute like the one found in the Siberian cave indicates a capacity for symbolic thought.
choice_b: Denisovans are known to have possessed the manual dexterity required to carve bone flutes like the Siberian one.
choice_c: No species of hominid other than the Denisovans inhabited any part of Siberia 45,000 years ago.
choice_d: The recent evidence about the bone flute is the first evidence to suggest that Denisovans could think symbolically.
choice_e: Any hominid species that cannot carve bone flutes must lack a capacity for symbolic thought.
prediction_text: Even if a Denisovan carved the flute, that refutes the traditional view only if flute-carving shows symbolic thought.
correct_answer_job: Identify the link from carving a flute to possessing symbolic thought.
conclusion: The traditional view of the Denisovans is mistaken.
support: A Denisovan likely carved the bone flute.
gap: Carving such a flute must indicate a capacity for symbolic thought.
explanation_a: Choice A is the required assumption: without it, showing that a Denisovan carved the flute would leave the traditional view about symbolic thought entirely untouched.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because carving takes skill, but the argument concludes a Denisovan did carve it, so dexterity is presupposed by the case rather than needed to reach the view about thought.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting and would support the attribution of the flute, but the argument says only that a Denisovan likely carved it, which does not require that no other hominid was present.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the evidence is called recent, but whether earlier evidence existed makes no difference to whether this argument succeeds.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links the same two ideas, but it states the converse of what the argument needs and is far stronger than required.

stimulus: Astronomer: At many observatories the smaller institutions now agitate to scrap merit-based telescope scheduling, and their reason is plain enough: under it, the hours awarded to the largest institutions have pulled far ahead of the hours awarded to everyone else. Yet scheduling by merit lifts an observatory's scientific yield enormously. What observatories ought to do, then, is fund a shared archive of raw data, so that the yield reaches every member more evenly.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the astronomer's argument?
choice_a: The skew in observing hours is not itself a direct consequence of scheduling by merit.
choice_b: A shared archive of raw data can be funded without materially eroding the scientific yield that scheduling by merit produces.
choice_c: At observatories whose observing hours are badly skewed, the smaller institutions draw little or no benefit from scheduling by merit.
choice_d: Scrapping merit-based scheduling is one effective way of spreading an observatory's scientific yield more evenly.
choice_e: Spreading the yield more evenly will enlarge the total scientific yield that scheduling by merit brings an observatory.
prediction_text: If funding the archive wiped out the yield, recommending it while praising merit scheduling would be self-defeating.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for the shared archive to distribute rather than destroy the yield.
conclusion: Observatories should fund a shared archive of raw data.
support: Merit scheduling lifts scientific yield, and the skew in hours breeds agitation.
gap: The measure must not cancel the very yield it is meant to distribute.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because the skew is what provokes the agitation, but the astronomer grants that merit scheduling produced it, so the argument cannot require denying that.
explanation_b: Choice B is the required assumption: the archive is urged precisely in order to spread the yield that merit scheduling creates, so if funding it destroyed that yield the recommendation would defeat its own purpose.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it describes the smaller institutions' plight, but the recommendation stands whether or not they currently share in the yield.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because scrapping is what the agitators demand, but the astronomer recommends the archive instead and need not concede that scrapping would work.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links distribution to yield, but the argument needs only that the archive not destroy the yield, not that sharing enlarges it.

stimulus: Editorial: Puppet shows suitable for young children are those that are gently playful, mischievous perhaps, but never menacing. Since the new puppet shows written for adults take up grim subjects such as famine and exile, those shows cannot be suitable for young children.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption that would allow the conclusion to be properly drawn?
choice_a: Shows that are playful and mischievous are never menacing.
choice_b: Shows suitable for adults are seldom suitable for young children.
choice_c: Shows that take up grim subjects are menacing.
choice_d: Young children enjoy a show only if it uses puppets.
choice_e: Young children miss some of the details in shows written for adults.
prediction_text: Suitability requires not being menacing; so grim subjects must make a show menacing.
correct_answer_job: Supply the link from 'grim subjects' to 'menacing.'
conclusion: The new adult puppet shows are unsuitable for young children.
support: They take up grim subjects.
gap: Grim subject matter must render a show menacing.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it restates part of the standard, but it says nothing about shows with grim subjects, which is where the argument needs a bridge.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links the two audiences, but 'seldom' cannot deliver the flat conclusion that these shows are unsuitable.
explanation_c: Choice C allows the conclusion: suitable shows are never menacing, so if grim subjects make a show menacing, the new adult shows are thereby unsuitable for young children.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns children and puppets, but what children enjoy is not what the argument's standard of suitability turns on.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns children watching adult shows, but missing details would, if anything, cut against the shows being menacing to them.

stimulus: Archivist: Our foundation's library holds several medieval manuscripts whose ownership is in dispute. The library does possess papers showing that the manuscripts were acquired lawfully. Even so, an overriding principle assigns any important medieval manuscript, by right, to the community in whose monastery it was penned. Because every institution is bound to respect a right of that kind, our library ought to hand the manuscripts back.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion of the archivist's argument?
choice_a: Any important medieval manuscript belongs by rights to the community in whose monastery it was written.
choice_b: The disputed medieval manuscripts were acquired lawfully by the foundation's library.
choice_c: The foundation's library is in possession of several manuscripts whose ownership is in dispute.
choice_d: The foundation's library should hand back the disputed manuscripts.
choice_e: Every institution is bound to respect whatever rights the community of a manuscript's origin may hold over it.
prediction_text: Everything else is offered to support returning the manuscripts.
correct_answer_job: Pick the recommendation the principle and the obligation jointly support.
conclusion: The library should hand back the disputed manuscripts.
support: An overriding principle assigns them elsewhere, and institutions must honor it.
gap: Distinguish the recommendation from the principle that grounds it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it is stated as overriding, but it is the principle invoked in support of the recommendation rather than the recommendation itself.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it is asserted outright, but it is a concession the archivist makes on the way to the conclusion.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it opens the argument, but it merely sets the scene the argument then reasons about.
explanation_d: Choice D is the overall conclusion: the principle about rightful ownership and the obligation to honor such rights are both offered precisely to support returning the manuscripts.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it appears just before the conclusion, but it is the bridging premise that carries the principle to the recommendation.

stimulus: Musicologist: Rhythmic anticipation can occur without any musical training. Researchers have shown that infants of six months, plainly untutored in any musical art, are able to notice when a beat is dropped from a drum pattern. The infants probably compare the pattern they hear against an internal template of a steady pulse. Thus the infants' minds must already harbor a representation of a steady pulse.
question_stem: The statement that the infants' minds must already harbor a representation of a steady pulse plays which one of the following roles in the musicologist's argument?
choice_a: It is attributed to certain researchers as the main conclusion of their reasoning.
choice_b: It is the main point of the musicologist's argument.
choice_c: It is used to refute the claim that infants have no training in music.
choice_d: It states the hypothesis that the musicologist's argument sets out to explain.
choice_e: It is a conclusion drawn from the evidence and used in turn as a premise to support a more general conclusion.
prediction_text: It is inferred from the infants' behavior and then used to establish the general claim about training.
correct_answer_job: Locate the claim: it is derived from the evidence and then supports the broader thesis.
conclusion: Rhythmic anticipation can occur without musical training.
support: Untrained infants must hold a representation of a steady pulse.
gap: Distinguish an intermediate conclusion from the final one.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because researchers are cited, but the claim is the musicologist's own inference, not something credited to the researchers as their conclusion.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it comes last and is emphatic, but the main point is the opening claim that rhythmic anticipation requires no training.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because training is at issue, but the argument grants that the infants are untrained; it never disputes that.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because the argument does explain the infants' ability, but this claim is a result of the reasoning, not the puzzle it begins from.
explanation_e: Choice E correctly describes the role: the claim is inferred from what the infants can do, and it then supports the broader thesis that rhythmic anticipation needs no musical training.

stimulus: Proponents of the hydrogen bus maintain that once the storage problems associated with its fuel tanks are solved, such buses will be widely adopted and, because they emit nothing at the tailpipe, will bring about an easing of the environmental damage caused by diesel exhaust. But short of flooding still more valleys, the hydrogen that fills those tanks must be made using power drawn from plants that burn coal or gas. Considerable environmental damage is done by every one of those three ways of generating power. Thus the hydrogen bus ______.
question_stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choice_a: will have worse environmental consequences than its proponents may believe
choice_b: will probably remain less popular than other kinds of buses
choice_c: requires that purely technical problems be solved before it can succeed
choice_d: will raise the total level of emissions rather than lower it
choice_e: will not bring about a net reduction in environmental damage
prediction_text: The damage is displaced upstream, so the bus is worse than proponents think.
correct_answer_job: Draw the supported conclusion about the proponents' expectation.
conclusion: (completion target)
support: Every way of making the hydrogen does considerable environmental damage.
gap: Stay with what is supported: the proponents' belief is too rosy.
inference_or_resolution: The hydrogen bus will have worse environmental consequences than its proponents may believe.
explanation_a: Choice A most logically completes the argument: the proponents count only the tailpipe, while producing the hydrogen inflicts damage they have not reckoned with.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because adoption is mentioned, but nothing in the passage bears on how popular the bus will end up being.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because storage problems are named, but the passage's point concerns environmental damage, not the technical preconditions of success.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting but goes too far: the passage says each power source does damage, not that the net emissions must rise.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting and nearly right, but the passage does not weigh the magnitudes, so a flat denial of any net reduction is stronger than what follows.

stimulus: Ethicist: A corporation is not a person in any literal sense. It holds no belief, forms no intention, and, strictly speaking, performs no deed at all. It therefore bears no moral duties or entitlements. But no corporation can endure unless many of its employees ascribe such duties and entitlements to it, for nothing else would move them to make the sacrifices that corporate loyalty demands. Obviously, then, a corporation ______.
question_stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the ethicist's argument?
choice_a: cannot continue to exist unless something other than the false belief that it bears moral duties moves its employees to make sacrifices
choice_b: cannot endure unless many of its employees hold some beliefs that are strictly false
choice_c: can never be a fitting object of moral praise or blame
choice_d: is not worth the sacrifices that its employees make on its behalf
choice_e: should always be thought of in metaphorical rather than literal terms
prediction_text: Endurance requires employees to hold beliefs that are strictly false.
correct_answer_job: Combine the two claims: what employees must believe is, by the first claim, false.
conclusion: (completion target)
support: Corporations bear no such duties, yet endurance requires employees to ascribe them.
gap: Connect the falsity of the ascription with the necessity of the belief.
inference_or_resolution: A corporation cannot endure unless many of its employees hold beliefs that are strictly false.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it uses the same terms, but the passage says nothing else would move employees, so this reverses what was stated.
explanation_b: Choice B most logically completes the argument: enduring requires employees to ascribe duties the corporation does not have, and such an ascription is strictly false.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it follows from the first half alone, but it ignores the second half about endurance, which the completion is meant to bring in.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because sacrifices are discussed, but nothing in the passage weighs whether those sacrifices are worthwhile.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the literal and the figurative are contrasted, but the passage supports no recommendation about how we ought to think.

stimulus: All alpine violins are very loud. All valley violins are very quiet. Every violin in Petra's shop is built from an alpine top and a valley back. Therefore Petra's violins are of moderate loudness.
question_stem: Which one of the following uses flawed reasoning that most closely resembles the flawed reasoning used in the argument above?
choice_a: All apprentices who practice daily play well. But some who do not practice daily also play well. Ines practices somewhat daily. Therefore Ines plays somewhat well.
choice_b: All pupils at Ash School live in Fern County. All pupils at Birch School live in Vale County. Members of the Oyelaran family attend both Ash and Birch. Therefore the Oyelaran family lives in both counties.
choice_c: All grade-one dyes are highly colorfast. All grade-two dyes are not at all colorfast. This fabric was dyed with a mixture of a grade-one dye and a grade-two dye, so the fabric is moderately colorfast.
choice_d: All copyists know shorthand. All surveyors know trigonometry. Ada has worked as a copyist and as a surveyor. Therefore Ada knows both shorthand and trigonometry.
choice_e: All of Dara's kites fly very well. All of Ben's kites fly very badly. Half the kites in this shed fly very well and half fly very badly. Therefore half the kites are Dara's and half are Ben's.
prediction_text: Find the argument that mixes an extreme-A ingredient with an extreme-B ingredient and infers a middling result.
correct_answer_job: Match the error: assuming a blend of two extremes yields the average of the extremes.
conclusion: Petra's violins are of moderate loudness.
support: They combine a very loud part with a very quiet part.
gap: A composite of extremes need not be intermediate.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it slides between degrees, but it moves from a partial cause to a partial effect rather than blending two opposite ingredients.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because two categories are combined, but its conclusion attributes both properties rather than an intermediate one, so the pattern differs.
explanation_c: Choice C parallels the flaw exactly: two ingredients at opposite extremes are combined and the result is assumed to fall midway, which need not follow for dyes any more than for violins.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it combines two memberships, but this reasoning is actually sound, and a parallel-flaw answer must reproduce an error.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the same extremes appear, but it reasons backward from observed properties to ownership rather than forward from a blend to a middling property.

stimulus: Foreman: Idris and Petra are the only applicants who hold the certification we require. But Idris has a record of missing deadlines, so we should hire Petra.
question_stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the foreman's argument?
choice_a: Nadia has long wanted to hike the ridge trail and the canyon trail. Permits are unusually cheap right now. So she should book a trip now rather than keep putting it off.
choice_b: Nadia would like to hike either the ridge trail or the canyon trail on her next holiday. This may be her only chance for such a holiday. So she should choose whichever she finds most interesting, whatever the cost.
choice_c: Nadia has been planning to hike either the ridge trail or the canyon trail. Permits for both are inexpensive right now. So she should instead plan to hike both.
choice_d: Nadia has been planning to hike either the ridge trail or the canyon trail. Rockfall has made the canyon trail impassable. So she should hike the ridge trail.
choice_e: Nadia would like to hike the ridge trail and the canyon trail. Permits for the ridge cost less than permits for the canyon. So she should hike the ridge now and the canyon later.
prediction_text: Look for two candidate options, one disqualified by a specific defect, and the other chosen.
correct_answer_job: Match the form: exactly two acceptable options, one ruled out, so take the other.
conclusion: The foreman should hire Petra.
support: Only Idris and Petra qualify, and Idris misses deadlines.
gap: Find the argument with the same eliminate-and-choose structure.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it recommends an action, but nothing is eliminated from a pair of options; it argues about when to act, not which to choose.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because two options are named, but neither is ruled out; the recommendation turns on interest rather than on disqualification.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it starts from the same pair, but it concludes that both should be taken, which is not the eliminate-and-choose pattern.
explanation_d: Choice D matches the reasoning exactly: two options exhaust the field, a specific defect eliminates one, and the remaining option is therefore chosen.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it favors one trail, but it orders both rather than eliminating one, so the structure is not parallel.

stimulus: Many ferry lines have added ways of collecting fares that automatically debit the prepaid accounts of passengers who walk past an electronic scanner, rather than making passengers queue at a booth to pay. Promoters of these systems say the resulting savings hold fares beneath the level they would otherwise reach. A recent study, though, finds that on lines equipped with scanners the fare increases turn out to be 30 percent steeper than on lines lacking them.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?
choice_a: Scanner payment systems have environmental advantages, because they cut the idling associated with queues at fare booths.
choice_b: Not all passengers ride often enough to make it worth their while to set up an account and obtain the equipment a scanner system requires.
choice_c: By taking payment in advance of actual trips, scanner systems gain a financial advantage through the accrual of interest.
choice_d: Fare increases are an effective way of encouraging passengers to travel at off-peak hours, thereby easing crowding.
choice_e: When passengers do not stop to pay the cost of each crossing separately, they are less likely to press the line's managers to hold fares down.
prediction_text: Passengers who never feel the fare stop objecting to raising it.
correct_answer_job: Find the fact that lets a cheaper system coexist with steeper fare increases.
conclusion: (discrepancy to explain)
support: Scanner systems save money yet come with steeper fare increases.
gap: Something must weaken the pressure that keeps fares down.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it praises the systems, but an environmental benefit does nothing to explain why fares rise faster where they are used.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it limits the systems' reach, but partial adoption does not explain steeper increases among the lines that adopt them.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it adds to the savings, but greater savings make the steeper fare increases more puzzling, not less.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it makes increases sound useful, but it does not explain why they should be steeper on lines with scanners.
explanation_e: Choice E most helps resolve the discrepancy: the scanner hides the fare from the passenger, so the pressure that normally restrains increases weakens, and fares climb faster despite the savings.

stimulus: Skater: My teammates keep telling me that one day I will be badly hurt, because the way I skate is reckless. But I have looked into the matter, and it turns out that figure skaters and recreational skaters suffer injuries at far lower rates than speed skaters do. So if I were to give up speed skating for figure skating, my own risk of injury would drop.
question_stem: The reasoning in the skater's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that this argument
choice_a: infers a cause from what may be a mere correlation
choice_b: relies on a sample of skaters that is too narrow to support its conclusion
choice_c: misinterprets evidence that a result is likely as evidence that the result is certain
choice_d: mistakes a condition sufficient for bringing about a result for a condition necessary for doing so
choice_e: relies on a source of information that is probably not well informed
prediction_text: Figure skaters may simply be less reckless people; the discipline may not be what lowers the rate.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: a group's lower injury rate is treated as showing the discipline causes safety.
conclusion: Switching to figure skating would lower the skater's risk of injury.
support: Figure skaters are injured at lower rates than speed skaters.
gap: A difference in rates across groups need not be caused by the activity itself.
explanation_a: Choice A correctly names the error: the lower injury rate among figure skaters may reflect who takes up the sport rather than anything about the sport, so switching need not make this reckless skater safer.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the research is thin on detail, but nothing suggests the injury rates were drawn from too few skaters; the fault is the causal leap.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because risk is at issue, but the skater speaks throughout of rates and of lowering risk, never of certainty.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting as a stock error, but the argument contains no conditional claim whose sufficiency and necessity could be confused.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the research is vague, but the argument's defect lies in what it infers from the rates, not in where the rates came from.

stimulus: Many hospitals across the region have lately begun piping soft music into their waiting rooms, in the hope of lowering the anxiety felt by patients who are waiting to be seen by a doctor. However, nearly all the patients sitting in these particular waiting rooms are already quite calm. So the hospitals' use of piped music is unlikely to accomplish what it was meant to accomplish.
question_stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choice_a: fails to consider whether hospitals that do not now pipe in music would lower their patients' anxiety if they began doing so
choice_b: fails to consider that even if patients are already calm, piped music may make them calmer still
choice_c: takes for granted that, with respect to their patients' anxiety, hospitals that pipe in music are representative of hospitals generally
choice_d: fails to consider that even if piped music lacks one particular beneficial effect, it may have similar effects that are equally beneficial
choice_e: does not adequately address the possibility that patient recovery is strongly affected by factors other than anxiety
prediction_text: Being calm is not being maximally calm; music could deepen the calm and so serve its purpose.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: an already-calm patient may still be made calmer.
conclusion: The piped music is unlikely to achieve its purpose.
support: Nearly all patients there are already calm.
gap: Anxiety is a matter of degree, so existing calm does not foreclose further improvement.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it widens the inquiry, but the conclusion concerns the hospitals that do pipe music, so what others might achieve is beside the point.
explanation_b: Choice B correctly names the error: calm admits of degrees, so the music can lower anxiety further and thereby do exactly what it was intended to do.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because representativeness often matters, but the argument confines itself to the hospitals that pipe music and needs no such assumption.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting and close, but the flaw is that the music may have the very effect intended, not merely some other benefit.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because recovery matters clinically, but the argument concerns whether anxiety is lowered, not what else affects recovery.

stimulus: Advertisement: Glosswell leaves a floor bright and free of streaks, and the clean scent it gives off is a pleasure. To prove that Glosswell is the best, we ran a test with more than one hundred homeowners. Each homeowner received one tile that had been cleaned with Glosswell and one tile that had been cleaned without it. Ninety-eight percent of the homeowners preferred the tile cleaned with Glosswell. So Glosswell is the most effective floor polish to be had.
question_stem: The advertisement's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it fails to consider whether
choice_a: any of the homeowners who took part in the test are allergic to floor polish
choice_b: Glosswell is more or less harmful to the environment than other floor polishes are
choice_c: the homeowners who took part in the test had any opportunity to evaluate floor polishes other than Glosswell
choice_d: Glosswell is much cheaper or much more expensive than other floor polishes are
choice_e: the homeowners who took part in the test find the benefits of using a floor polish worth the expense
prediction_text: Beating a bare tile shows nothing about beating other polishes, which the conclusion asserts.
correct_answer_job: Name the omission: no rival polish was ever tested against Glosswell.
conclusion: Glosswell is the most effective floor polish available.
support: Homeowners preferred a Glosswell tile to an untreated tile.
gap: The comparison class in the conclusion was never tested.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns the participants, but an allergy would bear on safety, not on whether Glosswell outperforms rival polishes.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it compares Glosswell with rivals, but environmental harm is not the effectiveness the conclusion asserts.
explanation_c: Choice C names the fatal omission: the test pitted Glosswell against no polish at all, so it cannot show that Glosswell beats the other polishes on the market.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because price shapes what people buy, but cost has nothing to do with the claim that Glosswell is the most effective.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the participants' judgments, but whether polish is worth its price does not bear on relative effectiveness.

stimulus: Some ecologists argue that the marsh warbler could not have come through the last ice age had the species not evolved the ability to nest in a wide range of habitats. Yet the evidence is substantial that the reed thrush, a prehistoric species akin to the early warblers, likewise nested across a wide array of habitats, and it became extinct all the same. Hence the ecologists' claim is false.
question_stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choice_a: takes for granted that if one species had a characteristic that happened to enable it to survive certain conditions, at least one related extinct species must have had that characteristic
choice_b: generalizes, from the fact that one species with a certain characteristic survived certain conditions, that all related species with that characteristic must have survived
choice_c: fails to consider the possibility that the reed thrush had one or more characteristics that lessened its chances of surviving prehistoric times
choice_d: confuses a condition's being required for a given result to occur in one case with the condition's being sufficient for such a result to occur in a similar case
choice_e: fails to consider the possibility that, even if a condition caused a result to occur in one case, it was not necessary to cause the result to occur in a similar case
prediction_text: The ecologists said flexibility was needed, not that it guaranteed survival; the thrush's extinction leaves that untouched.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: treating a necessary condition in one case as sufficient in another.
conclusion: The ecologists' claim is false.
support: A related species with the same trait went extinct.
gap: A condition required for survival in one case need not be enough for survival in another.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because both species share the trait, but the argument does not assume the thrush must have had it; the evidence states that it did.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it invokes both species, but the argument reasons from the extinct thrush to the warbler, not from a survivor to all relatives.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting and would explain the extinction, but the deeper fault is that the ecologists never claimed habitat flexibility was enough to secure survival.
explanation_d: Choice D correctly names the error: the ecologists claimed flexibility was necessary for the warbler, and a related species that had flexibility yet died out does nothing to refute a claim of necessity.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it juggles the same notions, but it describes the reverse confusion, which the argument does not commit.

stimulus: Critic: Among touring theater companies it is broadly the rule that a troupe's renown rises together with the delight its audiences take in it. That strikes me as perfectly just, and no ground whatever for cynicism about whether playgoers can tell fine acting from poor.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strongly supports the critic's view?
choice_a: Some of the finest touring troupes are entirely unknown to the general public.
choice_b: In general, the more celebrated a troupe is, the larger the houses it is able to fill.
choice_c: Even the finest touring troupes cannot act consistently well at every single performance.
choice_d: The very best touring troupes often stage works that audiences find difficult to appreciate.
choice_e: The celebrity of a touring troupe usually reflects the quality of its acting.
prediction_text: If fame reflects acting quality, audiences delighting in famous troupes are responding to merit.
correct_answer_job: Show that celebrity tracks quality, so delight in celebrity is delight in merit.
conclusion: Audiences' greater delight in celebrated troupes gives no ground for cynicism about their discernment.
support: Audiences take more delight in more celebrated troupes.
gap: Celebrity must correspond to the quality audiences are supposed to discern.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns fine troupes, but it severs fame from quality and so tends to license the very cynicism the critic rejects.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links celebrity to a measurable effect, but audience size is not audience delight, still less audience discernment.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it complicates the picture, but occasional lapses by fine troupes do not support the critic's claim about audiences.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the best troupes, but it suggests audiences may delight less in the finest work, which cuts against the critic.
explanation_e: Choice E most strongly supports the view: if fame tracks quality, then audiences who delight most in the most celebrated troupes are in fact responding to fine acting.

stimulus: A recent study followed the particular feeding techniques used by six inshore pods of killer whales belonging to one ecotype, and by two offshore pods belonging to a different ecotype, in tasks such as herding fish and stunning prey. What emerged was that a single inshore pod hunted in ways closer to those of the offshore pods than to those of its own inshore neighbors. The likeliest account, then, is that learning rather than inheritance fixes these techniques.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the argument?
choice_a: Killer whales sometimes copy the feeding techniques of other killer whales, whether or not they are closely related genetically.
choice_b: Whales that join a pod from elsewhere sometimes bring unfamiliar techniques with them, along with unfamiliar inherited traits.
choice_c: The pods studied face markedly different feeding conditions because of the different waters they inhabit.
choice_d: The differences in technique among the pods studied are pronounced enough to tell each pod apart from all the others.
choice_e: Among the pods studied, the six inshore pods range over waters much closer together than the two offshore pods do.
prediction_text: If whales copy techniques regardless of kinship, the cross-ecotype resemblance follows from learning.
correct_answer_job: Make learning, not shared ancestry, the better explanation of the odd resemblance.
conclusion: The feeding techniques are fixed by learning rather than inheritance.
support: One inshore pod resembled the distant offshore pods more than its genetic neighbors.
gap: Something must make copying, rather than shared genes, the source of the resemblance.
explanation_a: Choice A provides the most support: if whales copy techniques irrespective of kinship, an inshore pod feeding like distant offshore pods is exactly what learning would produce.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it introduces new techniques, but by bundling them with inherited traits it keeps a genetic explanation alive.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because environment shapes behavior, but differing conditions would predict differing techniques, not the resemblance that needs explaining.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the techniques, but that pods are distinguishable says nothing about whether learning or genes fixes their techniques.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because proximity can aid copying, but it does not explain why one inshore pod feeds like the distant offshore pods.

recipe_title: Strengthen by Supplying the General Rule
stimulus: Trainer: Deliberate-practice coaching works on changing an athlete's voluntary movements. It is therefore likely to prove more effective at correcting faults of technique than are the rival methods that work on changing involuntary reflexes, since only voluntary movements lie under an athlete's direct conscious control.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the trainer's argument?
choice_a: Faults in performance are frequently caused by involuntary reflexes that coaching could change.
choice_b: It is difficult for any coaching method to be effective without working on processes that lie under the athlete's direct conscious control.
choice_c: Deliberate-practice coaching is the only method that works primarily on an athlete's voluntary movements.
choice_d: No method that works on involuntary reflexes can be effective unless it also addresses voluntary movements.
choice_e: All of an athlete's voluntary movements are under conscious control, though other bodily processes cannot be controlled at all.
prediction_text: The argument needs effectiveness to depend on working with what the athlete can consciously control.
correct_answer_job: Supply the rule that makes conscious control the key to effectiveness.
conclusion: Deliberate-practice coaching is likelier to be effective than reflex-based methods.
support: Only voluntary movements are under the athlete's direct conscious control.
gap: Conscious control must matter to whether a coaching method works.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns reflexes, but it makes the rival methods look useful, which weakens rather than strengthens the trainer's case.
explanation_b: Choice B most strengthens the argument: it supplies the missing rule linking conscious control to effectiveness, which is precisely what turns the trainer's premise into a reason.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it distinguishes the method, but exclusivity does not show that working on voluntary movements makes a method effective.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it constrains the rivals, but it allows those methods to succeed when combined, and it never links control to effectiveness.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it echoes the premise, but restating which processes are controllable adds nothing about what makes coaching effective.

stimulus: Ibarra: Many municipal water plants that now rely on single-use carbon cartridges could rely on ceramic membranes instead. Ceramic membranes are less hazardous to plant workers and leave behind far less waste. What is more, some filtration steps run at a faster rate, or leave fewer unwanted residues, when membranes are used. So water plants should begin using ceramic membranes for many steps that currently use carbon cartridges. Renner: A ceramic membrane carries a purchase price several times over that of a carbon cartridge, so at present membranes are not practical for municipal water plants.
question_stem: Of the following, which one, if true, is the strongest counter Ibarra could make to Renner's argument?
choice_a: The cost of carbon cartridges is only one of many expenses involved in operating a municipal water plant.
choice_b: New methods of disposing of spent carbon cartridges have recently been developed.
choice_c: Ceramic membranes can be cleaned and reused many times over, whereas a carbon cartridge can be used only once.
choice_d: The water industry has historically been quick to adopt new techniques that speed up filtration.
choice_e: For the sake of public relations, plants will sometimes adopt a more environmentally friendly process even when it is slightly more expensive.
prediction_text: If the expensive item is used many times and the cheap one only once, the price comparison misleads.
correct_answer_job: Show the higher unit price does not mean higher cost in use.
conclusion: Ceramic membranes are not impractical for water plants.
support: Renner rests entirely on the higher purchase price of membranes.
gap: Purchase price per unit is not cost per use.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it downplays cartridge costs, but it leaves untouched Renner's point that membranes cost many times as much.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because waste is part of Ibarra's case, but easier disposal of cartridges helps Renner if anything, and says nothing about cost.
explanation_c: Choice C is the strongest counter: if one membrane does the work of many cartridges, its higher purchase price need not make it more expensive in use, which is all Renner's objection rested on.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it predicts uptake, but a willingness to adopt fast techniques does not answer the charge that membranes are too costly.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it explains why a plant might switch, but it concedes the extra expense rather than showing the objection mistaken.

recipe_title: Weaken by Severing a Chain Link
stimulus: Glaciologist: In the decades to come, warmer summers should drive foehn winds across valley W far more often than at present, and a foehn wind sets the snowpack melting at unusual speed. The valley's alpine ponds fill up over long stretches of steady melt, and so the average pond level in W ought to rise as well.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the glaciologist's argument?
choice_a: In valley W there is typically far less snowfall in autumn than there is in winter.
choice_b: Pond levels in valley W often fall during long stretches in which there is no melt at all.
choice_c: In many valleys that receive considerably more meltwater than valley W does, average pond levels are lower than they are in valley W.
choice_d: In valley W, summers marked by unusually rapid snowmelt have usually not included long stretches of steady melt.
choice_e: Warmer summers produce a number of effects besides making foehn winds more frequent.
prediction_text: Rapid melt need not be steady melt; a burst of melt may run off before ponds fill.
correct_answer_job: Break the link between 'rapid melt' and 'long stretches of steady melt.'
conclusion: Average pond levels in valley W will rise.
support: More foehn winds bring rapid melt, and ponds fill during steady melt.
gap: Rapid melt and long steady melt are not the same thing.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns snow in the valley, but a seasonal contrast in snowfall says nothing about whether rapid melt comes in steady stretches.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it ties melt to ponds, but it reinforces the link the argument relies on and so supports the conclusion.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it seems to unhook melt from ponds, but other valleys may differ in drainage and shape, so this does not bear on valley W.
explanation_d: Choice D most weakens the argument: the rapid melt the glaciologist predicts is precisely not the long, steady melt that fills the ponds, so the chain breaks at its crucial link.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it hints at complications, but unnamed additional effects do not challenge the step from rapid melt to rising ponds.

stimulus: A new district policy has been drawn up in order to avert many severe cases of blight. This aim is to be accomplished by the annual inoculation of high-risk orchards: every orchard more than forty years old, together with any orchard whose soil conditions might cause it to suffer complications from the blight fungus. Any given year's inoculation guards solely against whichever strain of the fungus is judged most probable for that season; consequently, in each successive year the orchards on the high-risk list must be inoculated afresh against some other strain entirely.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption that would allow the conclusion above to be properly drawn?
choice_a: The number of orchards in the high-risk group will not change significantly from one year to the next.
choice_b: The likelihood that a severe outbreak of blight will occur varies from year to year.
choice_c: No inoculation against the blight fungus guards against more than one strain of that fungus.
choice_d: Each year's inoculation will have fewer side effects than the previous year's, because the technology will constantly improve.
choice_e: Each year the strain of the blight fungus deemed most likely to prevail will be one that had not previously been deemed most likely to prevail.
prediction_text: A different vaccine each year is needed only if the year's chosen strain is never a repeat of an earlier one.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for a different strain to be needed every single year.
conclusion: Every year high-risk orchards must be inoculated against a different strain.
support: Each inoculation guards only against the strain deemed most likely that year.
gap: The strain deemed most likely must never repeat from one year to another.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns the high-risk group, but how many orchards there are has no bearing on whether a new strain must be targeted each year.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it invokes year-to-year variation, but variation in the size of the risk does not require that the strain differ each year.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it echoes the passage, but this is already given; what is still needed is that the year's chosen strain never repeats.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns successive inoculations, but side effects have nothing to do with why a different strain must be targeted.
explanation_e: Choice E is the required assumption: were a strain from an earlier year chosen again, the orchards would need the same inoculation as before, and the conclusion that a different strain is needed every year would fail.

stimulus: A recent experiment indicates that rats will on occasion behave altruistically rather than from any motive of self-interest. Rats in the experiment looked on while a rat unknown to them struggled inside a narrow tube from which escape was impossible without help. Most of the watching rats threw the latch that opened the tube, even though throwing it demanded that they press a stiff lever repeatedly. Because the rats were promised nothing whatever for their trouble, altruism is plainly what the experiment brought to light.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choice_a: The rats in the experiment did not act in the expectation that they would receive a reward.
choice_b: Had a reward been offered in the experiment, the rats would have behaved differently.
choice_c: Rats are the only rodents that have been shown to behave altruistically.
choice_d: The rats in the experiment regarded throwing the latch as a form of play.
choice_e: The rats would have behaved differently toward a rat that was already familiar to them.
prediction_text: If the rats expected a reward, the act would not be altruistic; so they must not have expected one.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for 'no reward offered' to establish altruism.
conclusion: The experiment revealed altruism.
support: No reward was offered for the helping behavior.
gap: No reward offered does not by itself rule out the rats' expecting one.
explanation_a: Choice A is the required assumption: the conclusion rests on the helping being unrewarded, so had the rats expected a reward, the behavior would not count as altruism at all.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because rewards are central, but the argument needs only that the rats expected none, not that a reward would have changed their conduct.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it praises the rats, but whether other rodents are altruistic is irrelevant to what this experiment shows about these rats.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting as a rival motive, but the argument does not require it; indeed if the rats were merely playing, that would undercut the altruism claim.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the trapped rat was a stranger, but nothing in the argument depends on how the rats would treat a familiar companion.

stimulus: Peaty ground is where cranberries flourish. Chalk soil is rarely peaty on its own, yet blending it with certain other materials will produce ground that is peaty throughout. It follows that chalk soil can be made to support flourishing cranberries.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choice_a: Blending a peaty material with another type of material always produces peaty ground.
choice_b: Chalk soil that has been blended with certain other materials is still chalk soil.
choice_c: Whenever chalk soil is blended with other materials, peaty ground results.
choice_d: There are plants that fail to thrive in peaty ground.
choice_e: Cranberries do as well in treated chalk soil as they do in naturally peaty ground.
prediction_text: If blending stops it from being chalk soil, nothing has been shown about chalk soil.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for the blended, peaty ground still to count as chalk soil.
conclusion: Cranberries can be made to flourish in chalk soil.
support: Chalk soil can be blended to yield peaty ground.
gap: The blended ground must remain chalk soil.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because blending and peatiness are central, but the argument needs only that some blend of chalk soil is peaty, not that every blend is.
explanation_b: Choice B is the required assumption: the conclusion speaks of chalk soil, so if blending turned it into something that was no longer chalk soil, nothing would follow about chalk soil.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting but far too strong: the argument needs only that chalk soil can be made peaty, not that blending always makes it so.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns peaty ground, but what other plants do has no bearing on whether cranberries can be made to flourish in chalk soil.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it compares the two grounds, but the conclusion claims only that cranberries can be made to flourish, not that they do equally well.

stimulus: Retail analyst: A new rule requires every energy-drink can to carry caffeine warnings, unsettling images of sleep loss, and no brand artwork. This rule will not change the drinking habits of most people who drink these beverages regularly, since most of those people rarely look at the can when they take one from the fridge.
question_stem: The conclusion of the retail analyst's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: If regulations on the design of cans would change the habits of those who drink these beverages regularly, then those regulations should be imposed.
choice_b: If those who drink these beverages regularly look at unsettling images of sleep loss frequently, it is likely to change their habits.
choice_c: The new can design cannot change the habits of people who drink these beverages regularly unless they frequently look at the can when taking one.
choice_d: Almost all people who drink these beverages regularly are already familiar with the risks that caffeine poses to their health.
choice_e: Most people who drink these beverages regularly would be unable to describe the artwork on their usual brand if asked to do so.
prediction_text: If the new can can only affect habits when people look at it, then people who rarely look are unaffected.
correct_answer_job: Supply the conditional making frequent looking necessary for the rule to work.
conclusion: The rule will not change the habits of most regular drinkers.
support: Most regular drinkers rarely look at the can.
gap: Looking at the can must be necessary for the design to change habits.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns the same regulations, but it recommends policy and says nothing about whether this rule will in fact change habits.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links looking to habits, but it runs the wrong way: it tells us what frequent looking would do, not that looking is required.
explanation_c: Choice C lets the conclusion follow: if frequent looking is required for the design to have any effect, then drinkers who rarely look at the can cannot have their habits changed by it.
