explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it would explain the rule's futility, but it offers a different reason and does not make the stated conclusion follow.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it supports the claim that drinkers rarely look, but reinforcing a premise does not supply the link the conclusion needs.

stimulus: If you heat your workshop with a kiln, you ought to use a pellet kiln rather than a cordwood kiln. Because the pellets are pressed from mill leavings that would otherwise be dumped, heating a workshop with a pellet kiln will not cause any more trees to be cut. The same cannot be said of a cordwood kiln. Pellet kilns, then, do less harm to the environment than cordwood kilns.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choice_a: Pellets are pressed from mill leavings, waste that would otherwise not be reused at all.
choice_b: Where a workshop is heated, a pellet kiln does less environmental harm than a cordwood kiln.
choice_c: Using a pellet kiln to heat one's workshop does not cause trees to be cut.
choice_d: People who heat their workshops with kilns should use pellet kilns instead of cordwood kilns.
choice_e: Using a cordwood kiln to heat one's workshop causes trees to be cut.
prediction_text: The environmental comparison is offered to support the opening recommendation.
correct_answer_job: Separate the recommendation from the environmental claim that supports it.
conclusion: People who heat workshops with kilns should use pellet kilns instead of cordwood kilns.
support: Pellet kilns are better for the environment.
gap: Distinguish the practical recommendation from its supporting comparison.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it explains the whole case, but it is the fact on which the argument builds rather than the point it is making.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it is stated last and is itself a conclusion, but it is drawn in order to support the recommendation with which the argument opens.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it is inferred from the mill-leavings premise, but it is a step along the way, not the argument's destination.
explanation_d: Choice D is the overall conclusion: the facts about mill leavings, felled trees, and environmental effect are all marshalled to support this recommendation.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it is asserted by contrast, but it serves as one half of the comparison rather than as the argument's main point.

stimulus: A conceptual artist's Ledger Stack is a heap of ledgers that cannot be told apart, by the eye, from the record books kept in an actual county office. Ledger Stack counts as a work of art, whereas an identical heap of ordinary ledgers would not count as one. It is therefore not true that appearance by itself entirely settles whether a thing counts as a work of art.
question_stem: The argument proceeds by
choice_a: highlighting the differences between things that are believed to have a certain property and things that actually have that property
choice_b: demonstrating that an opposing argument relies on an ambiguity
choice_c: suggesting that two things that cannot be told apart must be things of the same type
choice_d: questioning the assumptions that underlie a particular theory
choice_e: showing that something that would be impossible if a particular thesis were correct is actually true
prediction_text: If appearance settled the matter, two identical heaps could not differ in status; yet they do.
correct_answer_job: Describe the method: exhibiting a case that could not occur if the thesis held.
conclusion: Appearance alone does not settle whether something counts as a work of art.
support: Two visually identical heaps differ in whether they count as art.
gap: Identify the refutation structure rather than a rival description.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because status and appearance come apart, but no contrast is drawn between what is believed and what is actually the case.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because a single term governs the dispute, but the argument never charges the opposing thesis with trading on two senses of a word.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because indistinguishable heaps are central, but the argument insists on the opposite, that indistinguishable things can differ in type.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because a theory is under attack, but the argument does not probe assumptions; it produces a case the theory cannot accommodate.
explanation_e: Choice E correctly describes the method: were appearance alone decisive, two indistinguishable heaps could not differ in status, yet the argument exhibits precisely such a pair.

stimulus: Museum curators have learned that visitors are more readily led to form favorable views of objects toward which they are at first indifferent, or even hostile, when those objects are linked, by image rather than by wall text alone, to things about which the visitors already feel warmly. Therefore curators are likely to ______.
question_stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?
choice_a: mount displays containing images of things that most members of the expected audience like
choice_b: use little if any wall text in the displays they mount
choice_c: try to encourage favorable views of objects that can be better shown by image than described in text
choice_d: place their displays in the entry hall rather than in the side galleries
choice_e: point up an object's appealing features by contrasting them, in images, with the unappealing features of a rival object
prediction_text: Curators will mount displays that include images of things the expected audience already likes.
correct_answer_job: Draw the action the finding recommends: put liked things, as images, into the display.
conclusion: (completion target)
support: Pictorial links to already-liked things shift attitudes favorably.
gap: Stay with what the finding licenses, not a broader ban on text.
inference_or_resolution: Curators will mount displays containing images of things most of the expected audience likes.
explanation_a: Choice A most logically completes the argument: the finding says favorable attitudes transfer through images of already-liked things, so curators would supply exactly such images.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because images outperformed text alone, but the finding compares linking methods and never recommends abandoning text.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it invokes images, but the finding concerns what the objects are linked to, not which objects photograph well.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting as a curatorial choice, but nothing in the finding bears on where a display should be placed.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it uses images, but the finding is about linking to liked things, not about contrasting with disliked ones.

stimulus: Modern engineering rests on proposing designs and stress-testing them against the world, which is in essence an attempt to show that those designs will fail. Nothing brings an engineer more standing than toppling a received design. No wonder, then, that a few engineers cast doubt on the safety margins for suspension cables that nearly everyone else accepts. The remarkable thing, rather, is this: though hundreds of researchers labor to make their names in cable science, scarcely any of them turn up evidence that the margins are unsafe.
question_stem: The information above provides the most support for which one of the following statements?
choice_a: Most engineers who are reluctant to accept the safety margins are not acting in accordance with the accepted standards of engineering debate.
choice_b: Most researchers in cable science have substantial motive to find evidence that would discredit the accepted safety margins.
choice_c: There is evidence that conclusively shows the accepted safety margins to be correct.
choice_d: Engineers who are skeptical about the safety margins have offered no alternative account of the cable data.
choice_e: Research in cable science is driven primarily by a desire for standing within the profession.
prediction_text: Because overturning wins standing, researchers have strong motive to discredit the margins.
correct_answer_job: Read off what the incentive structure implies about researchers' motives.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Standing comes from toppling received designs, and hundreds seek standing.
gap: Confine the inference to motive, not to what the evidence proves.
inference_or_resolution: Most researchers in cable science have substantial motive to discredit the accepted safety margins.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because skeptics are mentioned, but the passage calls their skepticism unsurprising and never faults how they conduct themselves.
explanation_b: Choice B is most strongly supported: the greatest standing comes from toppling a received design, and hundreds of researchers are striving to make their names.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because so few find contrary evidence, but the absence of refutation is not conclusive proof of correctness.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the skeptics, but the passage says nothing at all about what accounts they have or have not offered.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because standing is highlighted, but that it brings the most recognition does not show it is the primary driver of the research.

stimulus: Barn owls in the loft regularly drop pellets just inside the doorway. The keeper's first supposition was that the dropping happened by accident, though a territorial marker is the likelier account. Were it accidental rather than a marker, we should expect owlets and females to drop pellets there as well, yet only the adult males do so.
question_stem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following arguments?
choice_a: If the river were running high, the ferry would probably be delayed. But the river is low today. So the ferry will most likely run on time.
choice_b: I expect the surveyor to find the beam cracked. If the beam is cracked, the hall will be closed. So the hall will most likely be closed.
choice_c: If the kiln had reached full temperature, we should expect the glaze to have vitrified. But the glaze is still dull, so the kiln probably never reached full temperature.
choice_d: If the pump had failed, we should have expected the tank to overflow. The tank did overflow. So the pump probably failed.
choice_e: If the crew finish early, I would expect them to celebrate. Since the crew will probably finish early, they will probably celebrate.
prediction_text: The parallel rejects an explanation because a prediction it makes does not hold.
correct_answer_job: Match the form: a hypothesis predicts a consequence; the consequence fails; the hypothesis is rejected.
conclusion: The pellet-dropping is a territorial marker, not an accident.
support: The accident hypothesis predicts behavior that is not observed.
gap: Find the deny-the-consequent argument among the choices.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it uses a conditional, but it denies the antecedent rather than the consequent, which is an entirely different and invalid pattern.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it reasons about consequences, but it runs forward from an expected finding to its effect, not backward from a failed prediction.
explanation_c: Choice C matches the stimulus: a hypothesis predicts an observable consequence, the consequence is absent, and the hypothesis is therefore rejected.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it also weighs a hypothesis against a consequence, but it affirms the consequent instead of denying it.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because of the same conditional shape, but it affirms the antecedent, which is the opposite of the stimulus's move.

stimulus: We should approve the plan to pave over the old orchard, because the heritage league, which fiercely opposes it, is run by people who have no stake in the town's long-term prosperity. Keeping old orchards blocks new housing, and housing is vital to the town's growth.
question_stem: The flawed reasoning exhibited by the argument above is most similar to that exhibited by which one of the following arguments?
choice_a: Our province ought to safeguard the buildings it judges to be of national significance. Such buildings may not be recognized as significant by every resident, but the judgment of the province should prevail.
choice_b: Records important to local heritage ought to be archived properly for future generations. For if even one such record is lost, the town's past becomes harder to recover.
choice_c: The council ought to endorse postponing the new bypass. Many residents of the neighborhoods that would be affected are fervently opposed to building it now.
choice_d: You should replace your roof no more often than once every thirty years. After all, roofers advise replacing it every twenty years, and they stand to profit handsomely from the work.
choice_e: One should not borrow even small sums unless it is absolutely necessary. Once a few dollars are borrowed, interest begins to accumulate, and over the long run the burden grows heavy.
prediction_text: Find the argument that discounts a recommendation solely because those making it stand to gain or lack the right stake.
correct_answer_job: Match the error: dismissing advice because the advisers have interests of their own.
conclusion: The plan to pave the orchard should be approved.
support: Its opponents have no stake in the town's prosperity.
gap: The advisers' interests say nothing about whether their position is correct.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns preservation, but it commits no comparable error and does not discount anyone's advice on account of their interests.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because heritage is the topic, but it argues straightforwardly from consequences and impugns no one's motives.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it invokes opponents, but it defers to their opposition rather than dismissing advice because of who gives it.
explanation_d: Choice D parallels the flaw exactly: the roofers' advice is set aside merely because they have an interest in giving it, just as the league's opposition is set aside because of its leaders' lack of stake.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it warns against a course of action, but it reasons from accumulating consequences and never impugns an adviser's motives.

stimulus: Some years back, brewers took up a method that strips gluten from barley malt while leaving the malt's flavor largely unharmed. Yet many beer drinkers, when the resulting gluten-free beer first appeared on shop shelves, reported that it tasted rather poor.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the statements above?
choice_a: The share of beer drinkers who drink only gluten-free beer is far larger today than it was when the method was introduced.
choice_b: Many beer drinkers would refuse to drink gluten-free beer even if they believed that it tasted just as good as ordinary beer.
choice_c: The taste of any beer can be affected by the foods that are consumed along with it.
choice_d: Beer made gluten-free by this method generally costs more than ordinary beer does.
choice_e: During the years when the method was introduced, brewers used only low-grade barley for their gluten-free products.
prediction_text: Something other than the method spoiled the taste, such as poor ingredients.
correct_answer_job: Find the fact that makes bad-tasting beer consistent with a flavor-preserving method.
conclusion: (discrepancy to explain)
support: The method preserves flavor, yet the product tasted poor.
gap: The flaw must lie outside the gluten-stripping method itself.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns gluten-free beer, but a rise in its later popularity does not explain why the early product tasted poor.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns drinkers' attitudes, but a refusal to drink the beer is not a report that it tasted poor.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it offers another influence on taste, but it applies to all beers alike and explains nothing about this one.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because price affects how a product is received, but cost has nothing to do with reports about how the beer tasted.
explanation_e: Choice E most helps resolve the discrepancy: the gluten-stripping method may leave flavor intact while the beer still tastes poor, because the malt it started from was of poor quality.

stimulus: Alpine newts must contend with a skin fungus that raises lesions capable of interfering with their swimming. Among populations of alpine newts that have not dispersed to fresh ponds, as many as ninety-five percent carry heavy infections of the fungus, whereas fewer than fifteen percent of the newts in dispersing populations are infected at all. This shows that dispersal allows alpine newts to escape the fungus.
question_stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument overlooks the possibility that
choice_a: alpine newts infected with the fungus are typically unable to disperse
choice_b: alpine newts are unable to detect which ponds are free of the fungus
choice_c: long dispersals are no better protection from the fungus than short dispersals are
choice_d: populations of alpine newts that have not dispersed are much larger than dispersing populations
choice_e: populations of alpine newts tend not to disperse when they have a stable supply of food
prediction_text: Infection may prevent dispersal rather than dispersal preventing infection.
correct_answer_job: Name the overlooked possibility that reverses the direction of the causal claim.
conclusion: Dispersal allows alpine newts to escape the fungus.
support: Dispersing populations are far less often infected.
gap: The infection could be what keeps newts from dispersing.
explanation_a: Choice A names the overlooked possibility: if lesions keep infected newts from swimming to fresh ponds, then dispersing populations would be free of infection without dispersal doing anything to prevent it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns how newts choose ponds, but whether they can detect clean ponds leaves the causal direction untouched.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it questions how much dispersal helps, but the argument claims only that dispersal helps, not that longer helps more.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it compares the populations, but the figures cited are proportions, which a difference in size does not disturb.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it explains why some newts stay, but a stable food supply does not explain why those that stay are the infected ones.

stimulus: Rancher: Grazing cattle on imported feed, though harder on the soil than rotational grazing is, lets a rancher raise more cattle on the same acreage. Were every rancher to take up rotational grazing, they would prove unable to raise enough cattle for the region's growing demand. Hence, if enough cattle are to be raised, the currently fashionable practice of rotational grazing must spread no further.
question_stem: The reasoning in the rancher's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on which one of the following grounds?
choice_a: It takes for granted that grazing on imported feed is only slightly harder on the soil than rotational grazing is.
choice_b: It overlooks the possibility that even if the practice of rotational grazing continues to spread, many ranchers will choose not to adopt it.
choice_c: It fails to consider the possibility that, at some points in the region's past, enough cattle were raised without any use of imported feed.
choice_d: It overlooks the possibility that a consequence that would surely follow if all ranchers adopted rotational grazing would ensue even if not all of them did.
choice_e: It takes for granted that damage to the soil from the continued use of imported feed would not be detrimental to human health.
prediction_text: The practice can spread a good deal while many ranchers still decline it, so demand could still be met.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: further spread of a practice is not universal adoption of it.
conclusion: Rotational grazing must spread no further.
support: Universal rotational grazing would fail to meet demand.
gap: Spreading further is not the same as being adopted by everyone.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because soil damage is conceded, but the argument's conclusion does not depend on how much harder imported feed is on the soil.
explanation_b: Choice B correctly names the error: the premise concerns what would happen if every rancher adopted the practice, whereas the conclusion forbids any further spread at all.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it questions the necessity of imported feed, but past demand was smaller, so history does not touch the argument about growing demand.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it also concerns partial adoption, but it would help the rancher's case rather than expose the flaw in it.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because soil damage may well have further costs, but human health plays no part in the reasoning being assessed.

stimulus: Ethicist: Within every healing profession it is granted, almost without exception, that a physician must shield a patient from avoidable ruin. Scarcely anyone, then, would object when a physician who knows that a patient has been wrongly named in a fraud inquiry withholds that patient's file from the inspectors who have arrived to demand it. It follows that people at large must also grant that thwarting an official inquiry is, now and again, the right thing for a person to do.
question_stem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that this argument
choice_a: uses a single type of example for the purpose of justifying a broad generalization
choice_b: presumes, without providing justification, that letting inspectors examine an innocent patient's file serves rather than thwarts justice
choice_c: fails to consider the possibility that other moral principles would be widely recognized as overriding any obligation to shield a patient from ruin
choice_d: takes for granted that there is no moral obligation to cooperate with an official inquiry
choice_e: takes for granted that the physician in the example is not mistaken about the patient's innocence
prediction_text: Many who accept the duty would hold that other principles override it here, so no general acceptance follows.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: the accepted duty may be widely thought to yield to competing principles.
conclusion: People at large must grant that thwarting an official inquiry is sometimes right.
support: Scarcely anyone would object to the physician's withholding the file.
gap: Other widely held principles may be recognized as overriding the duty invoked.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because one case bears the whole weight, but multiplying cases would not answer the worry about principles that override the duty.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because justice hovers behind the case, but the ethicist need presume nothing about what serves justice; the gap lies among competing duties.
explanation_c: Choice C correctly names the error: those who accept the physician's duty may nonetheless hold that duties of candor to lawful inquiries override it, in which case no general acceptance follows.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting and lies near the mark, but the ethicist never denies such an obligation; the failure is to weigh it against the duty invoked.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting, but the example stipulates that the physician knows the patient was wrongly named, so nothing is being smuggled in.

stimulus: Columnist: Many candidates for the county board pledge to shrink the paperwork the county imposes upon its farmers. What farmers do at the ballot box, however, is choose whichever candidate undertakes to have the county pay for programs addressing the troubles they complain of most. Funding such programs requires records and forms, and keeping records is itself a species of paperwork. So the paperwork imposed on farmers will seldom be reduced by any great amount.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the columnist's argument?
choice_a: Candidates never pledge to do what they actually intend to do once they are in office.
choice_b: The troubles that farmers complain of most are troubles about paperwork.
choice_c: Paperwork imposed on farmers in counties whose boards are appointed is no more burdensome than in counties like this one.
choice_d: Candidates who win seats on the county board usually carry out the promises they made while campaigning.
choice_e: Candidates who pledge to do what they sincerely believe ought to be done are seldom elected.
prediction_text: The argument needs elected candidates to carry out the programs they promised.
correct_answer_job: Add the fact that makes winners' promises determine what actually happens.
conclusion: Paperwork imposed on farmers will seldom be greatly reduced.
support: Farmers elect candidates promising funded programs, which generate records.
gap: Winners must actually deliver the programs on which they were elected.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns pledges, but if winners ignore their promises the programs may never be funded, which weakens the columnist's case.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because paperwork recurs, but what farmers complain about does not bear on whether funding programs keeps paperwork high.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it compares counties, but the argument explains why paperwork persists here, not how this county compares with others.
explanation_d: Choice D most strengthens the argument: only if winners actually fund the programs they promised will the county keep generating the records that make up the paperwork.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns candidates and elections, but sincerity has no bearing on whether the funded programs keep paperwork from shrinking.

stimulus: Ranger: In the weeks that follow calving, female muskoxen repeatedly chew the bitter bark of the dwarf willow, a shrub they leave untouched at every other season. The bark is probably chewed for its medicinal properties, since the compounds it releases kill the gut fluke.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the ranger's argument?
choice_a: Muskoxen rarely chew the bark of any shrub other than the dwarf willow.
choice_b: Caribou have also been observed chewing bitter bark in the weeks that follow calving.
choice_c: Of the bitter shrubs available to muskoxen, the dwarf willow is by far the most common.
choice_d: Dwarf willow bark is easier to strip from the branch when it is damp.
choice_e: The weeks that follow calving are when muskoxen are most likely to be infested by gut flukes.
prediction_text: If muskoxen are most vulnerable to gut flukes just after calving, the medicinal account fits the timing.
correct_answer_job: Match the timing of the behavior to the medical need it is said to serve.
conclusion: The bark is chewed for its medicinal properties.
support: The bark's compounds kill the gut fluke, and muskoxen chew it only after calving.
gap: The behavior's timing must line up with when the medical benefit is needed.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it singles out the willow, but exclusive use of one shrub does not show that the use is medicinal.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it shows the behavior is widespread, but what caribou do says nothing about why muskoxen do it.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it explains the choice of shrub, but abundance supplies a rival, non-medicinal reason for chewing that bark.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns handling the bark, but ease of stripping bears on how the muskoxen chew it, not on why.
explanation_e: Choice E most strengthens the argument: the muskoxen chew the bark exactly when the parasite it kills is most threatening, which is what a medicinal purpose predicts.

stimulus: A tally showed that most of the burst pipes reported by tenants last winter were in south-facing flats. This suggests that bursts in north-facing flats are likelier than south-facing bursts to go unreported, since ______.
question_stem: The conclusion of the argument is strongly supported if which one of the following completes the passage?
choice_a: it is very likely that just as many pipes burst in north-facing flats as burst in south-facing ones
choice_b: tenants differ a great deal in how promptly they report a burst pipe
choice_c: pipes that burst usually have other defects in addition to the one that caused the burst
choice_d: the signs of a burst in a north-facing flat tend to differ from the signs of a burst in a south-facing flat
choice_e: other tallies suggest that a great many minor burst pipes go unreported
prediction_text: If pipes burst about equally often in both orientations, the lopsided tally must reflect under-reporting.
correct_answer_job: Supply the base rate that makes unequal reporting, not unequal bursting, the explanation.
conclusion: North-facing bursts more often go unreported than south-facing bursts do.
support: Most reported bursts were in south-facing flats.
gap: Rule out that south-facing flats simply suffer more bursts.
explanation_a: Choice A strongly supports the conclusion: if bursts occur equally often in both orientations, a tally dominated by south-facing reports can only mean that north-facing bursts go unreported.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns reporting, but variation among tenants does not explain a lopsided split between the two orientations.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns burst pipes, but additional defects say nothing about which flats' bursts get reported.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because differing signs hint at differing detection, but by itself it does not establish that north-facing bursts go unreported more often.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns unreported bursts, but general under-reporting affects both orientations alike and supports no comparison.

recipe_title: Weaken by Making the Rare Case the Dangerous One
stimulus: Vance: Almost every case of hantavirus in humans comes from contact with an infected rodent, and deer mice do carry hantavirus. But there is little to justify the notices urging the removal of any deer mice nesting in barns where people work. Deer mice are timid creatures that rarely approach a person, and the overwhelming majority of them carry no virus at all.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens Vance's argument?
choice_a: An infected deer mouse is far likelier to infect another deer mouse than to infect any other kind of animal.
choice_b: Infected deer mice are less mobile than other deer mice, but they are far bolder around people.
choice_c: Most animals that carry hantavirus belong to species that, under ordinary conditions, very rarely approach people.
choice_d: The deer-mouse populations with the highest rate of infection do not nest in barns.
choice_e: People are likelier to notice contact with a deer mouse when the contact occurs inside a barn.
prediction_text: If the infected mice are the bold ones, timidity in the majority is no comfort.
correct_answer_job: Show that the infected minority behaves in just the way that makes contact likely.
conclusion: The notices urging removal of deer mice are unjustified.
support: Deer mice are timid and mostly uninfected.
gap: The traits that make mice safe must hold of the infected ones too.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns transmission, but spread among mice does not bear on the danger those mice pose to the people working in the barn.
explanation_b: Choice B most weakens the argument: Vance rests on the timidity of deer mice, yet the very mice that carry the virus are the ones that approach people, so the notices may be well founded.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns carriers, but it reinforces Vance's picture of shy carriers and so tends to support the argument.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns where infected mice live, but it makes the barns safer, which strengthens rather than weakens Vance's case.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns barns, but noticing contact does not make contact more dangerous or more frequent.

recipe_title: Weaken by Attacking the Donor Profile
stimulus: Donations of blood at the regional centre have risen three years running, and yet a reversal is to be looked for shortly. Its own records show that better than three quarters of everything the centre collects has always come from donors in their forties and early fifties; and people of that age are set to dwindle in number, year upon year, for a decade to come.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the argument?
choice_a: Most people under forty have never once given blood at the centre.
choice_b: Plasma collection at the centre has fallen away across the past three years.
choice_c: Most of what the centre has collected during the past three years came from people under forty.
choice_d: New medical technology will surely reduce the need for donated blood over the next decade.
choice_e: The number of collection sessions the centre holds each month is unlikely to fall in the near future.
prediction_text: If recent donations come mostly from younger people, a shrinking older band will not reverse the rise.
correct_answer_job: Show the historical donor profile no longer describes who is actually giving.
conclusion: Donations at the centre will soon begin to fall.
support: Most donations historically came from a band whose population will dwindle.
gap: The historical profile may no longer hold of current donors.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns younger people, but it reinforces the claim that the older band is the source of donations, and so supports the prediction.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns the centre, but plasma is not blood, so a decline there bears on nothing in the argument.
explanation_c: Choice C most weakens the argument: if recent donations come mostly from people under forty, then the dwindling of the older band gives little reason to expect collections to fall.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it looks ahead a decade, but a falling need for blood would, if anything, accompany a fall in collections rather than undercut the prediction.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because sessions affect how much can be collected, but a steady number of sessions says nothing about the dwindling pool of donors the argument relies on.

stimulus: Passengers are owed protection from avoidable harm, and that obligation falls upon the operators of ferries. So, since carbon-monoxide leaks pose substantial risks to passengers, and since detectors can significantly reduce the danger such leaks present, ferry operators must institute policies that make the installation of detectors mandatory aboard every vessel.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choice_a: Crew members do not regard a mandatory installation policy as a violation of their rights.
choice_b: Carbon-monoxide leaks are the most harmful hazard to which passengers risk exposure aboard a ferry.
choice_c: Most passengers aboard ferries are unaware of the danger that carbon-monoxide leaks present.
choice_d: Voluntary detector-installation policies would not adequately protect passengers from the risks posed by carbon-monoxide leaks.
choice_e: Society has already accepted the idea of mandatory safety devices in other settings.
prediction_text: If voluntary installation would protect passengers just as well, nothing forces the mandatory policy.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for a mandatory policy, rather than a voluntary one, to be required.
conclusion: Ferry operators must make detector installation mandatory.
support: Detectors reduce a substantial risk that operators must guard against.
gap: A voluntary policy must be inadequate to discharge the duty.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because mandates raise objections, but the argument concerns protecting passengers and needs nothing about how crews regard the policy.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it elevates the hazard, but the argument needs only that the risk is substantial, not that it is the very worst.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because ignorance heightens danger, but what passengers know is not required for the duty to generate a mandatory policy.
explanation_d: Choice D is the required assumption: were a voluntary policy sufficient to protect passengers, the duty would be discharged without any mandate, and the conclusion would not follow.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because precedent makes the mandate palatable, but the argument rests on the operators' duty, not on what society has accepted elsewhere.

stimulus: Commentator: One cannot rightly defend the current practice of recruiting divers for deep salvage work by merely pointing out that those divers volunteer, that the hazards are disclosed to them, and that they are paid for facing those hazards. For while nothing is amiss in paying a person to undertake a task freely chosen, matters stand otherwise where duress has shaped the choosing.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the commentator's argument?
choice_a: No transaction can be justified merely on the grounds that those taking part in it do so voluntarily.
choice_b: Anyone who acts without complete freedom is acting under some form of externally imposed duress.
choice_c: There is nothing wrong with accepting money for putting oneself at risk.
choice_d: People should be permitted to perform any action so long as that action is freely chosen.
choice_e: Possessing information about the possible consequences of the choices one makes does not ensure that one's choices are free.
prediction_text: Unless information can leave a choice unfree, the defense would succeed and the argument would collapse.
correct_answer_job: Identify why being informed and paid fails to establish a free choice.
conclusion: The appeal to informed, paid volunteering does not defend the practice.
support: Payment is wrong when the choice is made under duress.
gap: Being informed of consequences must not guarantee that a choice is free.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because voluntariness is at issue, but the commentator grants that free choice does justify payment, so this sweeping denial is not required.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because duress is the pivot, but the argument needs only that information fails to guarantee freedom, not this stronger equation.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because payment for risk is the practice under scrutiny, but the argument concerns whether the defense succeeds, not whether accepting money is permissible.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because free choice looms large, but a permission principle is not what the argument requires.
explanation_e: Choice E is the required assumption: if being informed did ensure a free choice, then the defense the commentator rejects would go through, and the argument would fail.

stimulus: Antlers recently taken from deer that were mounted and preserved in the 1890s have been found to hold only half as much cadmium as antlers recently taken from living deer of the very same species. Since the cadmium that gathers in a deer's antlers as they grow is drawn from the lichens the deer browses, these results indicate that cadmium levels in upland lichens are higher now than they stood a century ago.
question_stem: The argument depends on assuming that
choice_a: the process used to preserve mounted deer in the 1890s did not substantially reduce the amount of cadmium in the antlers
choice_b: the proportion of a deer's diet consisting of lichens was not, on average, as high in the 1890s as it is today
choice_c: the amount of cadmium in a lichen depends on the amount of pollution in the air above it
choice_d: cadmium drawn from lichens is essential to the normal growth of a deer's antlers
choice_e: the mounted deer whose antlers were tested for cadmium were not fully grown
prediction_text: If mounting stripped cadmium from the antlers, the old readings would be low for reasons having nothing to do with lichens.
correct_answer_job: Identify the assumption protecting the old specimens from having lost cadmium.
conclusion: Cadmium in upland lichens is higher now than a century ago.
support: Antlers from 1890s specimens hold half as much cadmium as modern antlers.
gap: The preservation process must not itself have reduced the cadmium.
explanation_a: Choice A is the required assumption: were the mounting process itself to have leached cadmium away, the lower readings would say nothing about the lichens of that era.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because diet affects intake, but this would explain the difference without any change in lichens, so the argument cannot assume it.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it explains why lichens might grow more toxic, but the argument concludes only that they have, not how.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns cadmium and antlers, but whether the metal is essential to growth is beside the point.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because immature antlers might hold less, but the argument requires the opposite, that the old antlers were comparable to the new.

stimulus: Jurist: Any ruling that may reasonably be looked to for a gain in the overall security of the parties it touches is a sound ruling. A ruling counts as unsound just in case, and only in case, it may reasonably be looked to for a loss in that overall security. Rulings that would leave the overall security of those parties exactly where it stood are therefore sound rulings too.
question_stem: The jurist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: Only unsound rulings would reasonably be expected to reduce the total security of the parties they affect.
choice_b: Any ruling that is not unsound is sound.
choice_c: No ruling is both sound and unsound.
choice_d: There are rulings that would reasonably be expected to leave the total security of the affected parties unchanged.
choice_e: Only sound rulings have good consequences.
prediction_text: A neutral ruling is not unsound; to call it sound we need everything not unsound to be sound.
correct_answer_job: Close the gap between 'not unsound' and 'sound.'
conclusion: Security-neutral rulings are sound.
support: Such rulings do not lower security, so by the biconditional they are not unsound.
gap: Being not unsound must guarantee being sound.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it echoes the second rule, but it merely repeats half of what is given and does nothing to make a neutral ruling sound.
explanation_b: Choice B lets the conclusion follow: a security-neutral ruling does not reduce security, so it is not unsound, and this principle then makes it sound.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it tidies the categories, but ruling out overlap still leaves room for a ruling that is neither sound nor unsound.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it concerns the very rulings at issue, but asserting that such rulings exist does not show them to be sound.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links soundness to results, but good consequences play no part in the jurist's reasoning.

stimulus: Geographer: Most people, reflecting on how far inland the Kessel Basin lies, take its mild autumns to be owed to the Vantar Current, whose warm water runs southward along the coast. But this belief is mistaken. It is true enough that the Vantar carries warm water past the basin; yet on the far side of the continent the analogous Oray Current carries warm water only as far inland as the Selm Hills. And the lowlands well beyond those hills have mild autumns too.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the geographer's argument?
choice_a: It is widely believed that the Kessel Basin's mild autumns must be owed to the Vantar Current.
choice_b: It is true that the Vantar Current carries warm water past the Kessel Basin.
choice_c: The belief that the Kessel Basin's mild autumns must be owed to the Vantar Current is mistaken.
choice_d: On the far side of the continent, the Oray Current carries warm water only as far inland as the Selm Hills.
choice_e: The lowlands beyond the Selm Hills have mild autumns.
prediction_text: The point is that the popular explanation is wrong.
correct_answer_job: Pick the claim the comparison with the Oray Current is offered to establish.
conclusion: The belief that the Vantar Current explains the basin's mild autumns is mistaken.
support: An analogous current elsewhere fails to explain mild autumns beyond its reach.
gap: Distinguish the rejected belief from the rejection of it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it opens the passage, but it reports the view the geographer sets out to overturn, not the geographer's own claim.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it is asserted plainly, but it is a concession granted on the way to the conclusion.
explanation_c: Choice C is the conclusion: the comparison with the Oray Current and the lowlands beyond the Selm Hills is offered precisely to show that the popular explanation fails.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it is central to the case, but it is one of the facts marshalled in support of the conclusion.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it delivers the sting of the comparison, but it too is evidence rather than the point being argued for.

stimulus: Artificial roosts put up in disused quarries are said to furnish bats with shelter they badly need, and supporters read that benefit as proof that the practice does the ecology good. However, the practice may be ecologically harmful even if it does give shelter, for it may draw bats deep into the quarry workings in ways that nobody can foresee.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the practice may draw bats deep into the quarry workings in ways that nobody can foresee?
choice_a: It is a summary of the argument's overall position.
choice_b: It is a claim that the argument sets out to refute.
choice_c: It is a claim the argument says is not enough to establish what supporters take it to establish.
choice_d: It is a premise offered in support of the argument's conclusion.
choice_e: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
prediction_text: It is the support offered for the claim that the practice may be harmful.
correct_answer_job: Locate the claim's function: a stated reason for the argument's own conclusion.
conclusion: The practice may be ecologically harmful even if it gives shelter.
support: It may draw bats into the workings in unforeseeable ways.
gap: Distinguish a supporting premise from the conclusion it supports.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it is prominent, but it restates no more than one reason within the argument rather than the whole of it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the argument does refute the supporters, but this particular claim is the argument's own, not the view it opposes.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting, but that describes how the argument treats the shelter claim, not the claim about the quarry workings, which the argument endorses.
explanation_d: Choice D correctly describes the role: the unforeseeable drawing of bats into the workings is the reason given for concluding that the practice may be harmful.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it is a strong claim, but the main conclusion is that the practice may be harmful; this claim is what supports that.

stimulus: Lecturer: From the earliest days, people have gone to oracles to learn where their lives were heading. In just this respect the pronouncements of clinical prognosis differ not at all from the utterances of the priestess at Delphi. Whether a prognosis is true, as with an oracle, comes to nothing more than the question how well it helps a person bear an uncertain future. So although prognosis can point to a number of real triumphs, that it falls short of the whole truth is amply shown by how often it has hardened patients into despair.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main conclusion of the lecturer's argument?
choice_a: Clinical prognosis is at least partly responsible for hardening patients into despair.
choice_b: Clinical prognosis is no more true than the utterances of the priestess at Delphi.
choice_c: Clinical prognosis is merely a form of oracle.
choice_d: Clinical prognosis, like an oracle, attempts to say where a person's life is heading.
choice_e: Clinical prognosis falls short of being completely true.
prediction_text: Everything else is offered to show that prognosis is not wholly true.
correct_answer_job: Separate the single main claim from the comparisons and observations supporting it.
conclusion: Clinical prognosis falls short of being completely true.
support: It is like an oracle, its truth is mere usefulness, and it often breeds despair.
gap: Distinguish the conclusion from the supporting comparison and evidence.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it closes the passage, but it is the evidence offered, not the claim that evidence is offered to support.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because the comparison is vivid, but it is a premise that sets up the main point rather than the point itself.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting but overshoots: the lecturer claims prognosis falls short of the whole truth, not that it is nothing but oracle-mongering.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it is stated early, but it is the background that frames the argument, not what the argument establishes.
explanation_e: Choice E is the main conclusion: the comparison to the oracle, the account of truth as usefulness, and the record of despair are all marshalled to establish just this.

stimulus: Okonkwo's Timber Yard sells a large volume of planking. The vast bulk of it goes in pallets to trade buyers, most of them boatwrights. Hand tools are sold at Okonkwo's as well, and weekend hobbyists buy nearly all of those, one at a time, over the counter.
question_stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choice_a: A plank bought from Okonkwo's is more likely to have been bought by a boatwright than by a weekend hobbyist.
choice_b: Okonkwo's earns a larger profit from planking than from all of its other goods combined.
choice_c: Among Okonkwo's regular customers there are more trade buyers than weekend hobbyists.
choice_d: Okonkwo's sells a few hand tools in pallets to boatwrights.
choice_e: Most of those who buy planking in pallets from Okonkwo's have never bought a hand tool there.
prediction_text: Most planking goes to trade buyers, and most of those are boatwrights, so a plank most likely went to a boatwright.
correct_answer_job: Draw the supported claim about which buyer a given plank most likely went to.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: The bulk of planking goes to trade buyers, mostly boatwrights.
gap: Keep the inference to planking, and to comparative likelihood.
inference_or_resolution: A given plank more likely went to a boatwright than to a weekend hobbyist.
explanation_a: Choice A is most strongly supported: the vast bulk of planking goes to trade buyers, most of whom are boatwrights, so any given plank most likely went to one.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because planking dominates by volume, but nothing is said about profit, which can diverge sharply from volume.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because trade buyers take most of the planking, but a few large buyers can account for a great volume, so their number cannot be inferred.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because both goods and both buyer types appear, but the passage says tools are mostly bought at retail and never that any go in pallets.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because the two goods have different buyer profiles, but nothing rules out pallet buyers also purchasing hand tools.

stimulus: Call an artifact wholly silent when nothing in the appreciating of it turns essentially upon sound; a woven tapestry will serve as the example. The ear is idle before a tapestry. Which of its passages one takes in first is fixed by no order at all, and no listener is held to any particular span of time. With most art forms it is otherwise. Opera and recitation alike demand utterance, and whatever demands utterance must be received through a settled order of sounds, over a span of time that is roughly settled too. A printed ballad, though set down on paper and so to all appearances silent, must nevertheless be uttered, even where the uttering is only a murmur beneath the reader's breath.
question_stem: If the statements above are true, then on the basis of them which one of the following must be true?
choice_a: A printed ballad is less like an opera than it is like a tapestry.
choice_b: Wholly silent artifacts do not essentially involve utterance.
choice_c: Silence and sound are mutually exclusive components of artifacts.
choice_d: Artifacts that must be examined for a long period in order to be understood have sound built into them at the root.
choice_e: Anything capable of being uttered is either operatic or recited, or both operatic and recited.
prediction_text: Utterance brings a fixed order and span, which a silent artifact never demands; so silent artifacts do not require utterance.
correct_answer_job: Deduce the guaranteed claim linking wholly silent artifacts and utterance.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Utterance implies fixed order and span; silent artifacts demand neither.
gap: Chain the definition of silence with what utterance requires.
inference_or_resolution: Wholly silent artifacts do not essentially involve utterance.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because a ballad sits on paper as a tapestry hangs on a wall, but the passage groups the ballad with what must be uttered, and it ranks no similarities.
explanation_b: Choice B must be true: utterance imposes a fixed order of sounds and a fixed span, whereas a wholly silent artifact makes no essential demand upon sound at all.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because two kinds of artifact are contrasted, but the passage never denies that an artifact might have both silent and sonorous aspects.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it invokes time, but taking long to grasp a work differs from requiring a fixed span of listening, so this does not follow.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because opera and recitation are the examples given, but the printed ballad must be uttered too, so utterable things are not confined to those two.

stimulus: Commentator: The reported epidemic of overcrowding in our schools is a myth. Across the last eight years the average class gained only a single pupil. That is not a substantial increase, and so the proportion of classes that are overcrowded cannot have increased substantially either.
question_stem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to the flawed reasoning contained in the argument above?
choice_a: The average summer temperature over the past five years must have risen, since most people believe that summers are growing hotter.
choice_b: The proportion of flats in the old quarter must have risen substantially in recent years, since a substantial number of workshops there have been converted into flats.
choice_c: The proportion of employees who earn very high wages must not have risen more than slightly over the last year, since the average wage has risen only slightly in that time.
choice_d: The average weight of adults must have risen in recent years, since restaurants have raised the proportion of rich dishes on their menus.
choice_e: The average price of a house must be rising, since the proportion of household income spent on housing has risen over the last eight years.
prediction_text: A small change in a mean is compatible with a large change in the share above a threshold.
correct_answer_job: Match the error: inferring the behavior of a proportion at the tail from a small change in an average.
conclusion: The proportion of overcrowded classes has not risen substantially.
support: The average class size rose only slightly.
gap: An average can barely move while the tail of the distribution shifts a great deal.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it reasons about an average, but it rests on popular belief rather than on inferring a proportion from a mean.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns a proportion, but it argues from a substantial change to a substantial proportion, which is not the stimulus's error.
explanation_c: Choice C parallels the flaw exactly: a slight rise in the mean is treated as showing that the share at the top of the distribution barely moved, which need not hold in either case.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because averages and proportions both appear, but it runs from a proportion to an average, the reverse of the stimulus.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it also links a proportion to an average, but it infers the average from the proportion rather than the proportion from the average.

stimulus: Auditor: The reviewers, in reaching their finding that no funds had been misdirected, leaned almost wholly upon figures nobody is able to check. That gives us fair ground for doubting whether their finding holds. Yet to convert such ground for doubt into a demonstration that funds were in fact misdirected would be no less objectionable.
question_stem: Which one of the following conforms most closely to the principle illustrated above?
choice_a: A magazine printed a thorough account of both sides of a quarrel without questioning either view. So although the magazine let each side make its case, the account favored neither side over the other.
choice_b: Although Okafor's remedy appears to be a workable solution, we should not adopt it yet. Many other remedies undoubtedly exist, and we cannot know which is best until we have weighed them all.
choice_c: If an agent earns a commission on a sale, it is reasonable to suppose that the agent's view of the goods might be biased. However, the mere possibility of bias should not be confused with actual bias.
choice_d: Marlowe has declared that she will never miss a deadline. So long as Marlowe keeps working, no one can establish that declaration, whose truth answers only to what actually comes to pass. All the same, one would err in reading that as showing that Marlowe is going to miss a deadline.
choice_e: The makers of Brightwash claim it is a better detergent than Purecloth because Purecloth is ineffective. Purecloth may well be ineffective, but claims about Brightwash should rest on Brightwash's own performance.
prediction_text: A claim that cannot be verified is doubtful, but its unverifiability does not show it false.
correct_answer_job: Find the case where doubt is warranted yet the contrary is not thereby established.
conclusion: (principle to be matched)
support: Unverifiable grounds warrant doubt but not the contrary conclusion.
gap: Match both halves: doubt warranted, contrary not established.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns even-handedness, but it says nothing about doubt being mistaken for proof of the contrary.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it counsels withholding judgment, but it concerns comparing alternatives rather than confusing doubt with disproof.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting and close, since it warns against an inference from possibility, but it distinguishes possible bias from actual bias rather than doubt from proof of the contrary.
explanation_d: Choice D conforms most closely: the declaration cannot be verified, which gives reason to doubt it, yet that unverifiability is expressly denied to establish the contrary claim.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it faults an inference, but it concerns arguing from a rival's failings rather than mistaking doubt for disproof.

stimulus: Delgado: The riverside greenway ought to be extended by several kilometers at once. The beauty of the restored wetlands along that stretch would draw more visitors to the town, and the extra spending those visitors bring would benefit every resident. Okonjo: We must proceed with care. Extend the greenway and the moorage fees charged to houseboats along its present margins will climb, and such a climb would throw the households that pay them into real disarray.
question_stem: On the basis of their statements, Delgado and Okonjo are committed to disagreeing about the truth of which one of the following?
choice_a: The increased visitor traffic along an extended greenway would be a benefit to the town.
choice_b: Some of the residents at the edges of the greenway would see their moorage fees rise.
choice_c: Some people would be adversely affected by the extension of the greenway.
choice_d: The greenway should not be extended.
choice_e: The greenway should be extended without hesitation.
prediction_text: Delgado says extend at once; Okonjo says proceed carefully, so they clash over acting without hesitation.
correct_answer_job: Locate the claim one asserts and the other denies.
conclusion: (disputed claim)
support: Delgado urges immediate action; Okonjo counsels caution.
gap: Beware claims that only one speaker addresses.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because Delgado asserts it, but Okonjo never denies that visitors would benefit the town; she raises a separate cost.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because Okonjo asserts it, but Delgado says nothing about moorage fees and so is not committed to denying it.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it captures Okonjo's worry, but Delgado's claim that residents would benefit on the whole is consistent with some being harmed.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because Okonjo resists, but she counsels care rather than opposing extension outright, so she need not deny that it should happen.
explanation_e: Choice E is the point at issue: Delgado urges extension at once, while Okonjo insists that care be exercised, so the two are committed to opposite verdicts on this claim.

stimulus: It has often been said that grasping a proof completely convinces one of its conclusion entirely. If that is so, then complete conviction in the theorems one has proved oneself must lie beyond our reach, for a complete grasp of one's own reasoning, however desirable a thing it may be, is unattainable.
question_stem: A flaw in the reasoning in the argument above is that this argument
choice_a: treats the failure to satisfy a condition that brings about a particular outcome as though satisfying that condition were the only way of realizing the outcome
choice_b: confuses something that is necessary for an action to occur with something that necessarily results from that action
choice_c: takes for granted that something that has merely been said to be true is, in fact, true
choice_d: ignores the possibility that a state of affairs is desirable even if it cannot be attained
choice_e: uses the difficulty of attaining a state of affairs as a reason for not attempting to attain it
prediction_text: Conviction might arrive by some path other than a complete grasp, so failing that path proves nothing.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: a sufficient route to an outcome is treated as the only route.
conclusion: Complete conviction in one's own theorems is beyond reach.
support: A complete grasp of one's own reasoning is unattainable.
gap: A condition that brings about an outcome need not be the only way to reach it.
explanation_a: Choice A correctly names the error: a complete grasp is said to bring entire conviction, but conviction might be reached by other routes, so its unattainability settles nothing.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because conditions and results are both in play, but nothing here is treated as necessary for an action, nor as flowing necessarily from one.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the passage opens with what has been said, but the argument is explicitly conditional upon that saying, which it does not endorse.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting, but the argument expressly grants that a complete grasp is desirable though unattainable, so it ignores nothing of the kind.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because attainability is central, but the argument recommends nothing about whether the attempt should be made.

stimulus: Researcher: In a trial, five hundred households were given a home-repair manual, while five hundred similar households were given none. Across the following year, the average number of calls to tradespeople fell by twenty percent among the households that had received the manual, yet held steady among the rest. Since a house kept in better repair leads to fewer calls to tradespeople, the trial indicates that keeping a repair manual at home improves the state of a house.
question_stem: The reasoning in the researcher's argument is questionable in that
choice_a: it is possible that the households in the trial that were given no repair manual acquired repair manuals on their own
choice_b: two different states of affairs could each causally contribute to the same effect even though neither causally contributes to the other
choice_c: the households in the trial could have gained access to repair information from sources other than manuals
choice_d: a state of affairs could causally contribute to two or more different effects
choice_e: certain states of affairs that lead households to call tradespeople less often could also make them likelier to keep a repair manual at home
prediction_text: Owning the manual may cause households to do repairs themselves rather than call, so fewer calls need not mean better houses.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: the manual may reduce calls without improving the house.
conclusion: Keeping a repair manual at home improves the state of a house.
support: Households with the manual made fewer calls to tradespeople.
gap: Two different things can each reduce the calls without one producing the other.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it would blur the comparison, but such contamination would tend to erase the difference the trial found, not explain it away.
explanation_b: Choice B correctly names the error: having the manual and having a well-kept house might each reduce calls to tradespeople without the manual doing anything to keep the house in repair.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because information could arrive by other routes, but that would affect both groups and does not expose the leap from fewer calls to better repair.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it names a causal complication, but the trouble is two causes converging on one effect, not one cause fanning out to several.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting and would matter in an observational study, but the manuals here were assigned by the researchers, so no such selection can operate.

stimulus: Taken as a whole, the corals that ring the atoll form an intricate, densely linked community that channels nutrients much as the mycelia threading a forest floor do. And like a spreading mycelial network, the reef is extending itself at thousands of points at once. So we may expect that the reef will one day acquire a forest's capacity for self-repair.
question_stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choice_a: equates the intricacy of a system with the capacity of that system
choice_b: fails to consider the possibility that other habitats may acquire a capacity for self-repair before the reef does
choice_c: fails to give any indication of why the characteristics on which it fastens are sufficient for the eventual development of a capacity for self-repair
choice_d: draws a dubious analogy between the nutrients channeled by a mycelial network and those channeled across a reef
choice_e: presumes, without providing justification, that those managing the reef are interested in developing a self-repairing system
prediction_text: Sharing two features with mycelia gives no reason to think those features are enough to yield self-repair.
correct_answer_job: Name the error: nothing shows the cited resemblances suffice for the capacity predicted.
conclusion: The reef will one day acquire a forest's capacity for self-repair.
support: The reef resembles a mycelial network in structure and in growth.
gap: The cited resemblances are never shown to be sufficient for the capacity claimed.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because intricacy is emphasized, but the argument treats intricacy as evidence rather than declaring it identical with the capacity.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it names an omission, but which habitat gets there first has no bearing on whether the reef will get there at all.
explanation_c: Choice C correctly names the error: two shared features are cited, and nothing whatever is said to show that those features are enough to produce the capacity predicted.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because an analogy carries the argument, but the flaw lies in the leap to self-repair, not in whether nutrients travel alike in the two.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because purposes often lurk in such claims, but the argument makes no appeal to anyone's intentions about the reef.

stimulus: The Kavine dialect is spoken only upon the northern plateau, and the Suran escarpment today cuts that plateau off from the coastal lowlands. Certain verb endings in Kavine, however, descend from forms now extinct that are attested only in the old speech of the coast, and never in any of the plateau's other dialects. On this basis some linguists have framed the conjecture that the ancestors of the Kavine speakers once lived along the coast.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, provides additional evidence in support of the conjecture that the ancestors of the Kavine speakers once lived along the coast?
choice_a: In many cases, dialects that share certain verb endings do not in fact share a common ancestor.
choice_b: Many verb endings of the plateau's other dialects are related to endings known from the old speech of the coast.
choice_c: The Suran escarpment runs from the northern to the southern limits of the region.
choice_d: Most of the surviving inscriptions that bear the extinct coastal forms date from a period before the Suran escarpment became impassable.
choice_e: There are very few verb endings that occur both upon the plateau and along the coast.
prediction_text: If the extinct coastal forms were current before the escarpment became impassable, speakers carrying them could have moved up onto the plateau.
correct_answer_job: Add a fact showing the coastal forms could have travelled inland before the barrier closed.
conclusion: The ancestors of the Kavine speakers once lived along the coast.
support: Kavine keeps verb endings descended from forms attested only on the coast.
gap: The descent requires a route that existed before the escarpment closed it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns shared endings, but by loosening the tie between shared forms and shared descent it weakens the conjecture rather than backing it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it links plateau and coast, but it suggests the endings could have reached Kavine through neighbouring dialects, which cuts against the conjecture.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the barrier is central, but the escarpment's present extent says nothing about whether speakers crossed it before it closed.
explanation_d: Choice D supports the conjecture: the coastal forms were in use while a route inland still lay open, so speakers carrying them could have climbed to the plateau and left those endings in Kavine.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns the two speech areas, but scarcity of shared endings does nothing to explain how the coastal forms reached Kavine at all.

stimulus: Trustee: When a college hardens into tiers of sharply unequal prestige, and passage from one tier to another grows rare, the college is in danger. Tiers so fixed give rival factions their footing, and factions of that kind stand in the way of sound governance. Because a college whose endowment grows affords its departments more openings to improve their standing, the wise course for any college is a policy of steady endowment growth.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reasoning in the trustee's argument?
choice_a: Discord within a college tends to widen the inequities among its departments.
choice_b: Rival factions are sometimes willing to set aside their differences to back policies favorable to endowment growth.
choice_c: Endowment growth cannot occur without substantial gifts from alumni of the most prestigious departments.
choice_d: The presence of rival factions can be an obstacle to enlarging a college's endowment.
choice_e: A growing endowment produces a proportionally greater rise in resources for departments in the lowest tiers than for departments in the other tiers.
prediction_text: Growth helps only if it lifts the lowest tiers relatively more, closing the divisions the trustee fears.
correct_answer_job: Add the fact that endowment growth narrows the tier divisions rather than deepening them.
conclusion: Colleges ought to adopt policies keeping the endowment steadily growing.
support: Endowment growth gives departments openings to improve their standing.
gap: Growth must reduce, not deepen, the divisions in prestige.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it links discord and inequity, but it runs from discord to inequity, whereas the trustee needs growth to shrink inequity.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it makes the policy adoptable, but factions supporting growth does not show that growth cures the divisions.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns growth, but a precondition for growth says nothing about whether growth narrows the tiers.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because both elements appear, but it makes factions block the remedy, which threatens the trustee's proposal rather than supporting it.
explanation_e: Choice E most strengthens the reasoning: the danger is wide tiers with little movement, so growth helps precisely if it raises the lowest tiers fastest and narrows those divisions.

stimulus: Economist: Gift cards, which leave the recipient free to pick the actual present, are valued more highly by recipients than are presents chosen for them by other people. One study put to people this question: what sum would they have parted with for a present that somebody else had picked out for them? The figures they named came, on average, to only about two-thirds of what such presents had cost.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the economist's argument?
choice_a: People will not part with a present chosen for them by another unless they are offered roughly one and a half times what the present actually cost.
choice_b: The rate at which presents are returned to shops has climbed steadily since it was first measured.
choice_c: Gift cards presently account for only about fourteen percent of all gift giving.
choice_d: People in the study would have paid more for presents chosen by close friends and relatives than for presents chosen by others.
choice_e: Most shops demand a receipt before allowing a present to be exchanged.
prediction_text: If recipients demand far more than the price to give the present up, they value it above what they would pay for it.
correct_answer_job: Show that willingness to pay understates what recipients actually place on the present.
conclusion: Recipients value gift cards more highly than presents chosen for them.
support: People would pay only two-thirds of the cost of a chosen present.
gap: What one would pay for a thing may misstate what one takes it to be worth.
explanation_a: Choice A most weakens the argument: recipients who demand half again the price to surrender a chosen present plainly value it above its cost, so the willingness-to-pay figure misstates what they think it worth.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because returning a present suggests dissatisfaction, but a rising return rate supports the economist rather than undermining the study's reading.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it concerns gift cards, but how often they are given has nothing to do with how highly recipients value them.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it refines the study, but it still leaves chosen presents valued below their cost and so does not overturn the conclusion.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it concerns what recipients can do with a present, but shop policy does not bear on how highly the present is valued.

recipe_title: Weaken by Supplying the Base Rate
stimulus: Complaint to the trustees: our acquisitions committee is plainly prejudiced in favour of ceramics and against textiles. Across the past decade the committee has bought nine ceramic pieces for every single textile that it has bought.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choice_a: Some museums acquire no textiles whatever.
choice_b: Far more ceramic pieces than textiles came onto the market during the past decade.
choice_c: The committee numbers nine specialists in ceramics but only one in textiles.
choice_d: The museum lacks the storage to acquire every ceramic piece and every textile that comes onto the market.
choice_e: The committee bought more textiles in the past decade than it bought in the decade before.
prediction_text: If far more ceramics than textiles came up for sale, buying proportionally would look exactly like this.
correct_answer_job: Supply a base rate explaining the disparity without prejudice.
conclusion: The acquisitions committee is prejudiced against textiles.
support: It bought nine ceramic pieces for every textile.
gap: The purchase counts must be weighed against what was available to buy.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it flatters this museum by comparison, but what other museums do says nothing about whether this committee's ratio reflects prejudice.
explanation_b: Choice B most weakens the argument: if ceramics vastly outnumbered textiles among the pieces available, then buying more ceramics tracks what was for sale rather than any prejudice.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it explains the disparity, but a lopsided committee is itself a mark of the very prejudice alleged.
