explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because acquisition is constrained, but a shortage of storage presses on both kinds of object alike and explains no lopsided ratio.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because textile buying improved, but an increase over time leaves the present disparity, and the charge of prejudice, untouched.

stimulus: A common complaint about free-verse poems, that a child could write that, holds that their formal likeness to schoolchildren's verses shows them to be no more moving than those clumsy efforts. Yet a psychological study put pairs before its participants, each pair holding one free-verse poem and one schoolchild's verse, and most of them rated the free-verse poem the more moving every time. That refutes the complaint, and so establishes that free-verse poems are moving.
question_stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?
choice_a: People judge how moving a poem is better when they compare it with another poem.
choice_b: Each poem shown to the participants carried a label accurately indicating whether it was a free-verse poem or a schoolchild's verse.
choice_c: Most of the schoolchildren's verses used in the study were not unmoving.
choice_d: Participants who did not consistently rate the free-verse poems as more moving nonetheless rated them so more often than not.
choice_e: There were few formal likenesses between the free-verse poems shown and the schoolchildren's verses paired with them.
prediction_text: Beating something unmoving does not make a poem moving; the comparison class must not be unmoving.
correct_answer_job: Identify what must hold for 'rated more moving' to establish 'moving.'
conclusion: Free-verse poems are moving.
support: They were rated more moving than schoolchildren's verses.
gap: The schoolchildren's verses must not themselves have been unmoving.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because the study used pairs, but the argument needs nothing about whether comparison sharpens judgment.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because labels could sway raters, but the argument would be better off without them, so it cannot require that they were present.
explanation_c: Choice C is the required assumption: if the children's verses were unmoving, then being rated more moving than they were would leave the free-verse poems unmoving too, and the conclusion would fail.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it tidies the study's result, but the argument rests on what most participants did and needs nothing about the rest.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because likeness drives the complaint, but the argument concedes the likeness and answers the complaint on its own ground.

stimulus: By long tradition the Solutreans are held to have lacked any capacity for abstract counting. That tradition is now under pressure. Researchers, using a dating method lately refined, have established that a notched tally bone recovered from a Pyrenean shelter was cut no less than twenty-two thousand years ago. The likeliest maker of that bone, then, was a Solutrean.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choice_a: Solutreans are known to have possessed the manual skill required to cut tally bones like the Pyrenean one.
choice_b: No hominid group other than the Solutreans occupied any part of the Pyrenees twenty-two thousand years ago.
choice_c: The recent evidence about the tally bone is the first evidence to suggest that Solutreans could count abstractly.
choice_d: The ability to cut a tally bone like the one found in the Pyrenean shelter indicates a capacity for abstract counting.
choice_e: Any hominid group that cannot cut tally bones must lack a capacity for abstract counting.
prediction_text: Even if a Solutrean cut the bone, that overturns the view only if cutting such a bone shows abstract counting.
correct_answer_job: Identify the link from cutting a tally bone to a capacity for abstract counting.
conclusion: The traditional view of the Solutreans is mistaken.
support: A Solutrean likely cut the notched tally bone.
gap: Cutting such a bone must indicate a capacity for abstract counting.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because cutting takes skill, but the argument concludes a Solutrean did cut it, so the skill is presupposed by the case rather than needed for the view about counting.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it would secure the attribution, but the argument claims only that a Solutrean was the likeliest maker, which does not require sole occupancy.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because the evidence is called fresh, but whether earlier evidence existed makes no difference to whether this argument succeeds.
explanation_d: Choice D is the required assumption: without it, showing that a Solutrean cut the bone would leave the traditional view about abstract counting entirely untouched.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it links the same two ideas, but it states the converse of what the argument needs and is far stronger than required.

stimulus: Many folk tales feature seers who are supposedly unerring, that is, able to name the outcome of any wager before it is settled. But the naming of an outcome is correct only if that outcome comes to pass. Thus the tales themselves often show that their seers are not truly unerring, since some of the outcomes the seers name never come to pass at all.
question_stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choice_a: It is impossible for anyone to name outcomes correctly with absolute consistency.
choice_b: Tales that portray seers as unerring often leave unstated whether the outcomes they name come to pass.
choice_c: When tales portray seers as unerring, the outcomes those seers name are generally central to the plots of the tales.
choice_d: No folk tale has ever portrayed a truly unerring seer.
choice_e: A seer is truly unerring only if every outcome that seer names comes to pass.
prediction_text: Unless every naming must be correct, a handful of failures would not show the seer errs.
correct_answer_job: Identify what unerringness must require for a few failed namings to refute it.
conclusion: The seers in these tales are not truly unerring.
support: Some outcomes they name never come to pass.
gap: Unerringness must demand that all namings be correct.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns perfect naming, but the argument needs a standard for unerringness, not a claim that nobody could meet it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns what tales show, but the argument relies on cases where the naming plainly fails, so this is not required.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it makes the namings important, but how central they are to a plot is not needed for the argument to go through.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it sounds like the upshot, but the argument concerns the seers in these tales and need not assume so sweeping a claim.
explanation_e: Choice E is the required assumption: the argument moves from some failed namings to the seer's not being unerring, which works only if unerringness demands that all namings be correct.

stimulus: Analyst: A new statute requires every lottery ticket to carry odds disclosures, sobering images of debt, and no scratch-off artwork. Habitual buyers of tickets will not, for the most part, change how they buy, because scarcely any of them so much as glance at a ticket before handing over their money.
question_stem: The conclusion of the analyst's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choice_a: The new ticket design cannot alter the habits of people who buy tickets regularly unless those people frequently look at the ticket before buying.
choice_b: If regulations on the design of tickets would alter the habits of regular buyers, those regulations ought to be imposed.
choice_c: If people who buy tickets regularly look at sobering images of debt frequently, it is likely to alter their habits.
choice_d: Almost all people who buy tickets regularly are already familiar with the odds against them.
choice_e: Most people who buy tickets regularly could not describe the scratch-off artwork on their usual ticket if asked to do so.
prediction_text: If the ticket can only alter habits when buyers look at it, buyers who barely glance are unaffected.
correct_answer_job: Supply the conditional making frequent looking necessary for the design to work.
conclusion: The statute will not alter the habits of most regular buyers.
support: Most regular buyers barely glance at a ticket.
gap: Looking at the ticket must be necessary for the design to change habits.
explanation_a: Choice A lets the conclusion follow: if frequent looking is required for the design to have any effect, then buyers who barely glance cannot have their habits altered by it.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns the same regulations, but it recommends policy and says nothing about whether this statute will alter habits.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it links looking to habits, but it runs the wrong way, telling us what frequent looking would do rather than that looking is required.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it would explain the statute's futility, but it offers a different reason and does not make the stated conclusion follow.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it supports the claim that buyers barely glance, but reinforcing a premise does not supply the link the conclusion needs.

stimulus: Public-health officer: Those bent on cutting drowning deaths usually pour their effort into equipment measures, such as wider use of life jackets, better hull design, and stricter buoyancy standards. Yet nothing would cut drowning deaths so much as trimming the total hours that people spend out on open water. Being out on open water is, in plain fact, a major risk factor.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the public-health officer's argument?
choice_a: Drowning deaths can be cut by improving the equipment that people use on the water.
choice_b: A reduction in the hours that people spend on open water would do more to cut drowning deaths than would any equipment measure.
choice_c: Those bent on cutting drowning deaths should pour their effort into equipment measures.
choice_d: Wider use of life jackets, better hull design, and stricter buoyancy standards all help to cut drowning deaths.
choice_e: Being out on open water, on its own, ranks among the largest risk factors for drowning.
prediction_text: The point is that cutting hours on the water beats any equipment measure.
correct_answer_job: Identify the comparative recommendation the passage builds toward.
conclusion: Reducing hours on open water would cut drowning deaths more than any equipment measure would.
support: Being on open water is itself a major risk factor.
gap: Distinguish the comparative conclusion from the fact that supports it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because equipment measures are discussed, but the officer mentions them as the approach being displaced, not as the point being made.
explanation_b: Choice B is the overall conclusion: the remark that being on open water is itself a major risk factor is offered precisely to support this comparison between the two approaches.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it echoes the opening, but it states the view the officer argues against rather than the officer's own conclusion.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because these appear early, but they describe current practice rather than what the argument sets out to establish.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it is stated emphatically at the end, but it is the evidence offered in support of the comparative claim, not the claim itself.

stimulus: Registrar: More than one party lays claim to several tissue samples held in our university's genome bank. Our files contain consent forms proving that each sample was gathered with permission properly given. Nevertheless a principle that outranks any such form vests in the donor village the power to say what shall be done with a sample it provided. No laboratory may set that power aside, and so our bank must return the choice to those villages.
question_stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion of the registrar's argument?
choice_a: A donor village that provided a tissue sample holds the power to say what shall be done with it.
choice_b: Each of the claimed tissue samples was gathered with permission properly given.
choice_c: The genome bank must return to the donor villages the choice of what shall be done with their samples.
choice_d: More than one party lays claim to several tissue samples held in the university's genome bank.
choice_e: No laboratory may set aside a donor village's power to decide what shall be done with a sample it provided.
prediction_text: Everything else is offered to support returning the choice to the donor villages.
correct_answer_job: Pick the recommendation the principle and the obligation jointly support.
conclusion: The genome bank must return the choice about the samples to the donor villages.
support: A principle outranking consent vests the decision in the villages, and no laboratory may set it aside.
gap: Distinguish the recommendation from the principle that grounds it.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it outranks the consent forms, but it is the principle invoked in support of the recommendation rather than the recommendation itself.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it is asserted outright, but it is a concession made on the way to the conclusion.
explanation_c: Choice C is the overall conclusion: the principle vesting that power in the villages, together with the rule that no laboratory may set it aside, is offered precisely to support returning the choice.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it opens the argument, but it merely sets the scene the argument then reasons about.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it appears just before the conclusion, but it is the bridging premise carrying the principle to the recommendation.

stimulus: Devising secure combinations for strongroom locks is difficult. What a keeper wants is a combination easily recalled, an anniversary perhaps, or the year a relative was born. Such combinations, sadly, are just the ones an outsider bent on the strongroom's contents will guess first. Hardest of all to guess is a random string of digits, though nothing slips a legitimate keeper's memory so readily. Keepers who forget their combinations consume the locksmith's time; moreover, combinations that are very difficult to recall are generally written down by the keepers, and hence pose the gravest security threat of all.
question_stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choice_a: Keepers should not write down their combinations even when those combinations are hard to recall.
choice_b: It is expensive to have locksmiths constantly resetting forgetful keepers' combinations.
choice_c: Combinations that are random strings of digits are the least likely to result in security breaches.
choice_d: Combinations that are very easy to guess pose less of a security threat than combinations that are very difficult to recall.
choice_e: The easier a combination is to recall, the more secure the strongroom.
prediction_text: Hard-to-recall combinations pose the gravest threat, so easy-to-guess ones pose less of a threat than they do.
correct_answer_job: Rank the two threats using the 'gravest of all' clause.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Combinations very hard to recall pose the gravest security threat of all.
gap: Read the superlative as ranking above the easy-to-guess case.
inference_or_resolution: Combinations very easy to guess pose less of a security threat than combinations very difficult to recall.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because writing combinations down is called the gravest threat, but the passage describes what happens and recommends nothing.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because forgetful keepers consume the locksmith's time, but nothing is said about what that time costs.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because such strings are hardest to guess, but they are also the ones most often written down, which the passage calls the gravest threat of all.
explanation_d: Choice D must be true: combinations very difficult to recall get written down and thereby pose the gravest threat of all, so any other threat, including easy guessing, must be lesser.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because hard-to-recall combinations are dangerous, but easy-to-recall ones are the easiest to guess, so no such monotone relation holds.

stimulus: Peat mosses in quick growth lock away more carbon than ever leaves them; let their growth slow to a crawl and the balance tips the other way. Should the carbon reaching the air climb by any substantial amount, the northern lowlands grow warmer, and it is there that the bulk of the world's peat mosses lie. And warmth in those lowlands tells upon the mosses that carpet them: the warmer it gets, the more their average growth slackens.
question_stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choice_a: The amount of carbon given off into the air is bound to rise at a steadily accelerating pace.
choice_b: If the carbon given off into the air rises substantially, most of the world's peat mosses will give off more carbon than they lock away.
choice_c: If the peat mosses begin to grow more sluggishly, the northern lowlands will as a result grow substantially warmer.
choice_d: Any warming of the northern lowlands will be accompanied by a substantial rise in the carbon given off into the air.
choice_e: Peat mosses in the northern lowlands will grow more sluggishly, on average, if they give off enough carbon to raise substantially the total amount given off into the air.
prediction_text: If the mosses give off enough carbon to raise the total substantially, the warming that follows will slow their growth.
correct_answer_job: Follow the stated chain to the conditional it best supports.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Slow growth gives off carbon; a substantial rise warms the lowlands; warmth slows growth.
gap: Link the mosses' own emission to their own slowed growth by way of the warming step.
inference_or_resolution: The mosses will grow more slowly if they give off enough carbon to raise the total substantially.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns carbon given off, but nothing in the passage supports a claim about an ever-accelerating rate.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it uses the passage's terms, but nothing licenses concluding that a substantial rise makes most mosses net emitters.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting but reverses the chain: warming slows growth, so slower growth does not by itself warm the lowlands.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting but states the converse: a substantial rise causes warming, which does not license the claim that every warming is accompanied by such a rise.
explanation_e: Choice E is most strongly supported: a substantial rise in carbon given off warms the lowlands, and warmer lowlands slow the mosses' growth, so their own heavy emission would slow them.

stimulus: Some civic habits, such as punctuality, tend to benefit the person who keeps them; others, such as jury service, do not. No personal habit counts as a civic habit when keeping it works harm upon others.
question_stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choice_a: Being punctual tends to work no harm upon other people.
choice_b: A person wholly lacking in civic habits will tend not to have habits that benefit other people.
choice_c: A civic-minded person tends to benefit other people more than a person who is not civic-minded does.
choice_d: Jury service tends to be to one's own disadvantage but not to the disadvantage of others.
choice_e: If a personal habit that one keeps tends to benefit other people, then that habit is a civic habit.
prediction_text: Punctuality is a civic habit, so it cannot tend to be detrimental to others.
correct_answer_job: Apply the disqualifying rule to the stated example.
conclusion: (inference target)
support: Punctuality is a civic habit; civic habits are not detrimental to others.
gap: Apply the rule to the example given.
inference_or_resolution: Punctuality tends not to be detrimental to other people.
explanation_a: Choice A must be true: punctuality is stated to be a civic habit, and no habit that tends to be detrimental to others counts as one, so punctuality cannot be detrimental to others.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it echoes the terms, but nothing connects lacking civic habits to lacking habits that help others.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting but goes beyond the premises: the rule forbids harming others but ranks nobody's benefit to others against anyone else's.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because jury service is named, but the passage says only that it does not benefit the one who keeps it, never that it disadvantages that person.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting but reverses the rule: not harming others is required of a civic habit, which does not make helping others sufficient to be one.

stimulus: Playwright: Not once has a script of mine been staged at the summer festival, though several of my plays are widely loved and have filled provincial theaters for years on end. Six other playwrights whose work is dearly loved submitted scripts to that same festival, and their fortunes were exactly as poor as mine. It follows that a script staged at the summer festival is proof of a playwright's want of talent.
question_stem: The pattern of flawed reasoning in which one of the following arguments most closely resembles that in the playwright's argument?
choice_a: Vintner: I have never taken a medal at the county show, though several of my wines sell briskly and have won praise in the trade press. Other vintners say the same. Therefore the judges must be using some basis other than commercial success.
choice_b: Applicant: The grants panel never funds my proposals, even when most reviewers commend them. Others have submitted widely commended proposals, and the panel has not funded theirs either. So the grants panel funds only worthless proposals.
choice_c: Confectioner: I always take a medal at the county show, even though fairgoers find my sweets peculiar and unappealing. Other confectioners report the same. Thus taking a medal proves that one's sweets do not suit most people's taste.
choice_d: Archivist: The same photographs that were overlooked one year at the regional salon carried the chief award another year. So the photographs are not judged entirely on merit.
choice_e: Dispatcher: When I plan my rounds with the greatest care, the office trims my bonus. When I rush, they send me thanks. I conclude that the office means to discourage careful planning.
prediction_text: Find the argument leaping from worthy applicants being refused to the worthlessness of those accepted.
correct_answer_job: Match the error: from 'the good are refused' infer 'those accepted are bad.'
conclusion: Being staged at the festival proves a playwright is no good.
support: Several popular playwrights, the speaker among them, were passed over.
gap: That good playwrights are refused does not show the staged ones are bad.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it opens identically, but it concludes only that some other criterion is at work, which is a far weaker and non-parallel step.
explanation_b: Choice B parallels the flaw exactly: from the fact that commended proposals go unfunded it leaps to the claim that whatever is funded must be worthless, just as the playwright leaps from refusals to the worthlessness of those staged.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because its conclusion has the same shape, but its speaker is always accepted rather than always refused, so the premises run the other way.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it also attacks a selection process, but it reasons from inconsistent verdicts on the same works, not from good work being refused.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because good work again goes unrewarded, but it infers an intention behind the pattern rather than a verdict on those who are rewarded.

stimulus: Market studies confirm that travelers booking hotels chiefly seek the cleanest ones. Call a hotel clean when soiled rooms are a great rarity there and its upkeep runs to no more than the average. Oddly, though, several among the very cleanest hotels book poorly with just those travelers who profess to prize cleanliness above all.
question_stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?
choice_a: Travelers booking hotels claim to care more about cleanliness than about price.
choice_b: Some owners of clean hotels are reluctant to refurbish them and tend to keep them as they are for many years.
choice_c: Travelers often choose hotels on the strength of a reputation for cleanliness, and reputations can fall out of date.
choice_d: Some hotels shown to need a great deal of upkeep very rarely have soiled rooms.
choice_e: Some of the most stylish hotels are among the least clean.
prediction_text: Travelers act on reputation, and a reputation may lag behind the facts.
correct_answer_job: Find the fact letting cleanliness-seeking travelers pass over the cleanest hotels.
conclusion: (discrepancy to explain)
support: Travelers who prize cleanliness avoid some of the cleanest hotels.
gap: What travelers act on may not be actual cleanliness.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it concerns what travelers say, but it repeats the very fact that makes the situation puzzling.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns clean hotels, but an unrefurbished hotel is not thereby unclean, so this explains no booking gap.
explanation_c: Choice C most helps resolve the discrepancy: travelers who prize cleanliness may steer clear of a hotel that has become clean, because its reputation has not yet caught up with it.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because it plays with the definition of clean, but it merely identifies hotels that fail one condition and leaves the booking puzzle intact.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because style may draw travelers, but the puzzle concerns travelers who say they care most about cleanliness, not about style.

stimulus: Conservationist: Engineered microbes are being released into municipal water systems at a pace so quick, and under oversight so slack, that fragile watersheds stand at significant risk of harm. One microbe of that kind was already in wide release before any study revealed the threat it posed to native mayflies. Hence no fresh engineered microbe ought to enter a water system until it has first undergone rigorous testing for safety.
question_stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the conservationist's reasoning?
choice_a: An engineered microbe should not be released into a water system if rigorous testing has shown it to be risky.
choice_b: If a microbe has no potential for posing environmental risks, it may be released into a water system without any testing of its safety.
choice_c: If rigorous testing of an engineered microbe already in use shows that it poses environmental risks, its release should be discontinued.
choice_d: No microbe that might present risks to the environment should be permitted into a water system unless its safety has been thoroughly tested.
choice_e: If rigorous studies find no evidence that a microbe would present risks once released, no further testing of its safety is required.
prediction_text: Nothing that might present environmental risk should be released until its safety has been thoroughly tested.
correct_answer_job: Supply the principle licensing a testing requirement for anything that might pose a risk.
conclusion: Rigorous testing should be required before any new microbe is released.
support: Released microbes pose a significant risk of environmental harm.
gap: A principle must carry 'might pose risk' to 'test before release.'
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because it governs risky microbes, but it presupposes that testing has already happened and so cannot justify requiring the testing.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because it concerns testing, but it licenses release in the safe case and says nothing about requiring tests in the risky one.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because it responds to discovered risks, but it addresses withdrawing a microbe already released, not testing before release.
explanation_d: Choice D most helps to justify the reasoning: engineered microbes are said to pose a significant risk, and this principle turns that risk directly into a requirement of thorough testing before release.
explanation_e: Choice E is tempting because it mentions rigorous studies, but it tells us when testing may cease rather than that testing must precede release.

stimulus: Nadia: The city is increasingly split between those who can read a map and those who cannot. The gap between the well-schooled and the poorly schooled is partly to blame for causing this split, but that schooling gap will itself widen because of the growing importance of map literacy. Emeka: I disagree. Employers need staff who can read a map more with every year, and firms will therefore be obliged to give almost every worker that training. That will narrow the split between those who can read a map and those who cannot. So whatever it may be that widens the schooling gap in years to come, the importance of map literacy will not be the cause.
question_stem: Nadia and Emeka disagree over whether
choice_a: the gap between the well-schooled and the poorly schooled will widen
choice_b: the schooling gap is now partly to blame for causing the split between those who can read a map and those who cannot
choice_c: employers' need for staff who can read a map will increase
choice_d: firms will have to train their workers to read a map
choice_e: the gap between the well-schooled and the poorly schooled will widen as a result of the growing importance of map literacy
prediction_text: Nadia says map literacy will widen the schooling gap; Emeka denies exactly that.
correct_answer_job: Locate the proposition one asserts and the other denies.
conclusion: (disputed claim)
support: Nadia affirms and Emeka denies the causal claim about map literacy.
gap: Beware claims only one speaker addresses.
explanation_a: Choice A is tempting because both discuss the gap, but Emeka allows that something else might widen it, so he does not deny that it will widen.
explanation_b: Choice B is tempting because Nadia asserts it, but Emeka says nothing about what currently causes the split and so is not committed to denying it.
explanation_c: Choice C is tempting because Emeka asserts it, but Nadia's claim about the growing importance of map literacy agrees rather than conflicts with it.
explanation_d: Choice D is tempting because Emeka relies on it, but Nadia never addresses what firms will do, so no disagreement is joined here.
explanation_e: Choice E is the point at issue: Nadia asserts precisely this causal claim, and Emeka closes by denying that map literacy will be what widens the gap.
